reversibility.notes: Each prompt is a counted call the provider has seen and billed; nothing on a device changes. A saved result is a new file under the project's ai/bench, never written over, which the run reports and does not remove.

doc.summary: Asks a provider's model a prompt set, scores each answer, and reports the score with every call's tokens, time and cost.
doc.description: Asks the target provider's model each prompt of the set in turn, as ai.chat asks one, and scores each answer with the prompt's scorer; a call that fails counts as failed and the set goes on. It returns each prompt's result (passed, tokens, time, cost, and the error of a failed call), how many passed, the score, and the total cost when every call is priced. Every call's usage record is appended to usage_sink, and with save_as the results, with the answers, are saved under the project's ai/bench. A check makes no call: it validates the set and its scorers and estimates its tokens.

params.name: model
params.description: The model to ask for, as the provider names it.

params.name: prompts
params.description: The prompt set, up to 200: each {id, text or messages, expect}, where expect is one of exact (the answer, trimmed, equals it), contains, regex (RE2) and json_field ({path, equals}: the answer read as JSON holds equals at path, a dotted list of keys).

params.name: save_as
params.description: A file name under the project's ai/bench (run1.json) the results are saved to, with each answer cut to 4 KiB; never written over. Crawl tier only.

params.name: residency
params.description: The use's residency. local refuses a provider whose record says hosted, before contact and at validate; hosted admits either.

params.name: temperature
params.description: Sampling temperature, 0 to 2. A kind that does not accept a parameter reports it ignored and does not send it.

params.name: top_p
params.description: Nucleus sampling, 0 to 1.

params.name: max_tokens
params.description: The most tokens the answer may take, 1 to 1000000. A check prices the answer at this many; without it the answer's cost is unbounded.

params.name: stop
params.description: A sequence, or a list of up to 8, that ends the answer.

params.name: thinking
params.description: A token budget for a model that thinks before it answers (Ollama turns thinking on); a kind without thinking ignores it.

params.name: schema
params.description: A JSON schema the answer must meet, asked for through the kind's own structured output and checked before the task succeeds. It keeps to type, properties, required, additionalProperties, items, enum, const, minimum, maximum, minLength, maxLength, minItems and maxItems; any other keyword is refused rather than half-checked.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long one call may take, retries included, from 1s to 1h.

params.name: retries
params.description: How many times a retryable failure (a rate limit, an overloaded or failing server, a provider never reached) is tried again, with exponential backoff and jitter and honoring Retry-After; 0 to 10. Nothing else is retried, and nothing after the answer began.

params.name: usage_sink
params.description: A file name under the project's ai/usage directory (spend.jsonl) each call's usage record is appended to as one JSON line, proved writable before any call. Crawl tier only.

returns.name: results
returns.description: Each prompt's id, passed, input and output tokens, duration, cost when priced, and error when its call failed.

returns.name: passed
returns.description: How many prompts passed.

returns.name: count
returns.description: How many prompts the set holds.

returns.name: score
returns.description: passed divided by count.

returns.name: cost
returns.description: What the set cost, in currency.

returns.name: currency
returns.description: The price table's currency.

returns.name: saved
returns.description: The results file, relative to the project.

returns.name: estimate
returns.description: The set's estimated input tokens, and each prompt's estimate.

examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Bench
  ai.bench.run:
    model: "qwen3:14b"
    max_tokens: 50
    prompts:
      - {id: capital, text: "Capital of France? One word.", expect: {contains: Paris}}
      - {id: label, text: "Answer {\"label\": \"bug\"} as JSON.", expect: {json_field: {path: label, equals: bug}}}

reversibility.notes: A call is made and cannot be unmade: the provider has seen what was sent and counted what it answered. Nothing on a device changes, so there is nothing a later task could put back.

doc.summary: Asks the target provider's model and returns its answer with a usage record: tokens, time, retries and cost.
doc.description: Sends messages, or a prompt bundle with optional untrusted input, to the model named on the ai_provider device the task targets, through its kind (ollama, anthropic, google, or any server speaking OpenAI's chat completions API), with the device's own key over its own TLS and no redirect followed. Before any call it refuses a use tagged local against a hosted provider, a kind needing a key the device does not have, and a bundle its signing policy does not admit; a parameter the kind does not accept is reported ignored and not sent, and one the provider rejects (a 400 naming it) is reported dropped, the call sent once more without it, and never sent again to that provider for that model in the run. Only rate limits, overload, server errors and a provider never reached are retried, with exponential backoff and jitter and honoring Retry-After, and nothing after the answer began streaming, which could bill twice. With schema the answer is asked for through the kind's structured output and checked against the schema before the task succeeds. Every call ends in a usage record, returned and, with usage_sink, appended to a file in the project; the messages and the answer are never in it. With review rules, an answer crossing a threshold is held for a person before any later task can read it: asked at the terminal when someone is there, otherwise kept in the project's ai/review with the task failing as held until it is decided with pleiades ai review, after which running again reuses the decision with no second call; with nobody to ask at all it fails closed. A signature says who approved a bundle's text and that it is unchanged; it is provenance and integrity, not a promise about what the model does with it. A check makes no call: it validates the key, the residency, the parameters against the kind, the schema and the bundle's signature, and estimates the cost from the prompt's size and max_tokens. It reports changed, since a real run makes a counted call.

returns.name: answer
returns.description: The model's answer, whole: every kind streams, and the task sees one answer.

returns.name: json
returns.description: The answer read as JSON, once it met the schema.

returns.name: stop_reason
returns.description: Why the model stopped, in the provider's own words.

returns.name: usage
returns.description: The usage record: time, method, provider, kind, residency, model asked for and the model that answered, input and output tokens, duration, retries, the parameters ignored and dropped, the cost and currency when the provider's price table prices the model, the prompt's verdict, and the outcome. returns.description: The prompt's verdict: status (verified, unsigned, not checked) and, for a bundle, its name, version, SHA-256 and signing key.

returns.name: ignored

returns.name: review
returns.description: The answer's review: not held, or approved with the key, the rules it matched, who decided and when; in a check, the rules and any decision already on record. A held answer is never returned: the task fails as held.

returns.name: reused

examples.name: Ask a local model for a structured answer

- name: Classify

doc.summary: Loads a model into an Ollama host's memory, unloading every other model first so one is resident at a time.
doc.description: Loads the model to stay in memory (keep_alive -1), after unloading every other resident model, so the host never holds two; a model already alone in memory is no change. It runs only against an ai_provider whose kind is ollama and whose record declares ai_host_guard: single_resident, and keeps to it: at most one model in memory. It speaks only Ollama's HTTP API, so it never restarts, stops or signals the host, or the machine or distribution it runs in.

doc.summary: Asks a use's providers in fallback order and returns the first answer, refusing any provider the use's residency forbids.
doc.description: Routes a call by use: the routing table names, for each use, its residency (local or hosted), its signing policy and its providers in fallback order, each an ai_provider device with the model to ask it for. Before any call it resolves every provider in the use's order (each must be an onboarded ai_provider, with a key when its kind needs one) and refuses the route as a whole when one would take a local use's data to a hosted provider, which pleiades validate refuses already for a literal table. The use, not the task, decides the signing policy and the residency, so the task may set neither, nor model; a prompt bundle must be for the routed use. It then calls the providers in order, as ai.chat calls one, and moves to the next only when a provider could not be reached or kept failing in a way only time mends (rate limits, overload, server errors) after its retries, before any answer began; a refused request, a refused key or an answer missing its schema fails the task instead, since the next provider would be asked the same wrong thing or hide a broken credential. Every attempt's usage record is appended to usage_sink. It runs once, with no target device (no hosts:), and reaches providers through the project, so it runs on the Crawl tier; on the Walk tier target the provider and use ai.chat. A check makes no call: it resolves the route and estimates each provider's cost.

returns.description: The answer read as JSON, once it met the schema.

returns.name: stop_reason
returns.description: Why the model stopped, in the provider's own words.

returns.name: usage
returns.description: The usage record: time, method, provider, kind, residency, model asked for and the model that answered, input and output tokens, duration, retries, the parameters ignored and dropped, the cost and currency when the provider's price table prices the model, the prompt's verdict, and the outcome. It never holds what was sent or answered.

returns.name: prompt
returns.description: The prompt's verdict: status (verified, unsigned, not checked) and, for a bundle, its name, version, SHA-256 and signing key.

returns.name: ignored
returns.description: Parameters the provider's kind does not accept, which were not sent.

returns.name: dropped
returns.description: Parameters the provider rejected, removed and never sent to it for that model again in the run.

returns.name: estimate
returns.description: What a check reports instead of a call: the prompt's tokens (four characters a token), max_output_tokens or output_unbounded, the parameters that would be ignored and dropped, and, when the model is priced, input_cost, and max_cost when the output has a cap that is sent, with the currency.

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: What the provider's record allows that a run must say: a key sent over plain http://, weakened TLS.

returns.name: review
returns.description: The answer's review: not held, or approved with the key, the rules it matched, who decided and when; in a check, the rules and any decision already on record. A held answer is never returned: the task fails as held.

returns.name: reused
returns.returned: when a decided answer is reused
returns.description: True when the answer was approved earlier for this very request and returned from its review with no call; usage is the original call's.

returns.name: provider
returns.description: The provider that answered.

returns.name: model
returns.description: The model it was asked for.

returns.name: use
returns.description: The use routed.

returns.name: attempts
returns.description: Each provider tried, in order, with its model, outcome and, for a failure, why.

examples.name: Summarize locally, falling back to a second local server
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Summarize
  ai.route:
    use: summarize
    routes:
      summarize:
        residency: local
        signing: optional
        providers:
          - {provider: workstation, model: "qwen3:14b"}
          - {provider: lab-vllm, model: qwen3-14b}
    messages:
      - {role: user, content: "Summarize the release notes in three lines."}
    max_tokens: 300

reversibility.notes: A run that created an absent archive emits a file.remove naming it, which is a real, restorable inverse for the archive itself. A run that found the archive already present emits nothing. What no inverse here can restore is whatever remove=true deleted once the archive was written: those source paths are gone, and the archive holding their bytes is exactly what the inverse would just have deleted.

doc.summary: Creates an archive (tar or tar.gz) from files on the target.
doc.description: Creates path as a tar archive of src, entirely from files already on the target -- this is community.general.archive without a zip option. Idempotency here is existence-only: a run finding path already there reports no change and reads none of src, the same way file.copy's checksum comparison decides on bytes rather than a name but simpler still, since this does not even open the archive to compare. remove, when true, deletes src once the archive has been written; the archive itself is not touched a second time to verify it. A check reads what a real run reads and runs no tar. A src, or the directory the archive would go in, that is missing when a check runs makes the call unchecked rather than failed, since an earlier task in the same run may be what creates it.

params.name: path
params.description: The archive file to create.

params.name: src
params.description: The paths on the target to include, at least one.

params.name: format
params.description: The archive format. tgz is accepted as a synonym for tar.gz.

params.name: remove
params.description: Delete src once the archive has been written.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The archive this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What path looked like before this task and after it (exists, kind, mode, owner, group, size, mtime). Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Archive a directory
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Archive the release build
  archive.create:
    path: /tmp/release.tar.gz
    src:
      - /opt/app/dist

examples.name: Archive and remove the originals
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Archive old logs and delete them
  archive.create:
    path: /var/backups/logs-2026-08.tar.gz
    src:
      - /var/log/app/2026-08
    remove: true

reversibility.notes: Extracting an archive can create any number of files and directories under dest, and this method does not enumerate them as it goes. A safe inverse would have to delete exactly what was created and nothing dest already held, which needs that enumeration; without it, the only honest choices are refusing to record an inverse or recording one that might delete more than this run added. This method refuses, the same call pkg.upgrade makes for an installed build a repository may no longer offer.

doc.summary: Extracts an archive (tar or tar.gz) on the target.
doc.description: Extracts src into dest, where src is an archive already present on the target -- this is community.general.unarchive with remote_src implied true always; nothing in this platform can transfer a file from wherever a runbook runs to the target (file.copy explicitly refuses that too), so a src living anywhere else is out of scope. Compression is auto-detected by tar itself, so there is no format parameter here the way archive.create has one. Idempotency is opt-in: naming creates skips extraction when that path is already there, and naming none means every run extracts again, the same honesty exec.command already has for a command with no built-in idempotency of its own. A check reads what a real run reads and extracts nothing. A src missing when a check runs, or a dest that is there but is not a directory, makes the call unchecked rather than failed, since an earlier task in the same run may be what fixes it.

params.name: src
params.description: The archive on the target to extract. Never a path on the machine running this task.

params.name: dest
params.description: The directory to extract into, created if it does not exist.

params.name: remove
params.description: Delete src once it has been extracted.

params.name: creates
params.description: A path whose existence means extraction already happened; when it is already there, this task reports no change and does not extract again. Left unset, every run extracts.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The directory this task extracted into.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What dest looked like before this task and after it (exists, kind, mode, owner, group, size, mtime). Recorded even on a run that skipped extraction because creates was already there.

examples.name: Extract a build already staged on the target
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Unpack the release
  archive.extract:
    src: /tmp/release.tar.gz
    dest: /opt/app

examples.name: Extract only once
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Unpack the SDK if it is not already there
  archive.extract:
    src: /tmp/sdk.tar.gz
    dest: /opt/sdk
    creates: /opt/sdk/bin/sdk

reversibility.notes: It reads files and, with resolve, asks the registry; it writes nothing.

doc.summary: Lists every container image reference in a build's files that is not pinned by both tag and digest.
doc.description: Reads the named files on the device and checks each image reference in them: pinned means named by both tag and digest (name:tag@sha256:...), since a tag alone moves underneath a build and a digest alone says nothing about what it is. A reference built from a build argument with no default, or from a variable a Compose file is interpolated with, cannot be read as written and is an offender too. With resolve, each pinned reference's tag is also resolved to the digest it names now, through the device's container engine (its own network, proxy, mirrors and registry logins, and the run's credential for that registry when it has one), and a pinned digest the tag no longer names is reported as drift. Any offender fails the task, its error naming them, and the task's returns are reported with the failure. Nothing is written.

params.name: files
params.description: The files on the device to read, each recognized by its name and content: a Dockerfile or Containerfile (each FROM, COPY --from and RUN --mount from that names an image, a FROM through an ARG read from the ARG's default), a Compose file (each service's image), or Kubernetes manifests (every container's image, in every document). A file of none of these kinds is refused by name. Each is read whole, at most 1 MiB.

params.name: resolve
params.description: Also resolve each pinned reference's tag through the device's container engine and report drift. The device must have its engine onboarded.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: references
returns.description: Every reference found: file, line, reference, where (FROM, COPY --from, RUN --mount, ARG NAME, image), pinned, problem (empty when there is none), and current (the digest its tag names now, when it drifted).

returns.name: offenders
returns.description: How many references are offenders, which is zero for a task that succeeded.

examples.name: Check a project's images are pinned
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Check image pins
  build.digests.check:
    files: [/srv/app/Dockerfile, /srv/app/compose.yaml, /srv/app/k8s/deploy.yaml]

reversibility.notes: Its undo writes back each reference it changed, as it was, from a record it keeps on the device before writing anything (the journal holds only the record's id); a file edited since is refused rather than overwritten.

doc.summary: Pins every container image reference in a build's files to the digest its tag names now.
doc.description: Reads the named files on the device, resolves each reference's tag to the digest it names now through the device's container engine (for a multi-platform image the index's digest, which pins every platform, never one platform's), and rewrites each reference that changes as name:tag@sha256:..., keeping its own spelling of the name. Every reference is resolved before anything is written, so a registry refusing one (gone, rate limited, unauthorized) leaves every file as it was. A reference with no tag, or one built from a build argument with no default, is refused, since nothing says what to refresh it to. Each file is rewritten once, only if it still holds what was read, and keeps its mode, owner and group: the new content is written beside it and renamed over it, or, when a new file cannot be given its owner and group by this login, copied into it in place (named in warnings); a write that fails puts back every file it had rewritten. Each change is reported as file, line, from and to. With set, the given rewrites are made instead of resolving any: each names a file, a line, the reference there now and the one to write. Before writing anything, a run keeps the references it replaces in an undo record on the device, in the login's own state directory (${XDG_STATE_HOME:-~/.local/state}/pleiades/build-digests, private to it, records older than 90 days removed by the next run), and its recorded undo is this method with undo naming that record, which writes each reference back only where the file still holds what the run wrote. A check resolves every reference as a run does and reports the changes it would make, writing nothing.

params.name: files
params.description: Required unless undo is given. The files on the device to read, each recognized by its name and content: a Dockerfile or Containerfile (each FROM, COPY --from and RUN --mount from that names an image, a FROM through an ARG read from the ARG's default), a Compose file (each service's image), or Kubernetes manifests (every container's image, in every document). A file of none of these kinds is refused by name. Each is read whole, at most 1 MiB.

params.name: set
params.description: Exact rewrites to make instead of resolving: each a mapping of file, line, from (the reference written there now) and to (the reference to write, which must parse). A file must also be in files. An entry whose from is not on that line refuses the task.

params.name: undo
params.description: The id of an undo record an earlier run of this method kept on the device: the references it names are written back as they were, and files, when not given, are the files it names. Cannot be combined with set. A run that writes keeps a record of its own, and the record it replayed is removed.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: changes
returns.description: Each reference changed, or that a check would change: file, line, from and to.

returns.name: warnings
returns.returned: when a file was written in place
returns.description: Each file written in place rather than renamed over, and why.

examples.name: Move a project's image pins forward
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Refresh image pins
  build.digests.refresh:
    files: [/srv/app/Dockerfile, /srv/app/compose.yaml]

reversibility.notes: It reads a lockfile and its manifest, and writes nothing.

doc.summary: Checks that a lockfile covers its manifest, carries an integrity hash for every entry, and draws only from allowed sources.
doc.description: Reads a lockfile and its manifest on the device and reports every way the lockfile falls short: a dependency the manifest declares that the lockfile does not lock (or locks for a different range), an entry the manifest no longer declares, an entry with no integrity hash or checksum (or only a sha1 one), an entry fetched over plain http, a git dependency not pinned to a commit, and an entry from a source not on the allowed list. npm's package-lock.json (lockfile versions 2 and 3) with package.json, and Cargo's Cargo.lock (versions 3 and 4) with Cargo.toml, are read; a format is a plug-in, so more can be added. An npm entry bundled inside its parent, or a workspace link, carries its parent's integrity and is not a separate source; a Cargo path crate has no source. Any finding fails the task, its error naming them, and the task's returns are reported with the failure. Nothing is written.

params.name: lockfile
params.description: The lockfile's path on the device. Its format is recognized by its name (package-lock.json, Cargo.lock) unless format names one.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The manifest's path, when it is not the lockfile's sibling of the usual name (package.json, Cargo.toml). A Cargo workspace member is checked by naming its own Cargo.toml with the workspace's Cargo.lock.

params.name: format
params.description: The lockfile's format, npm or cargo, when its name does not say.

params.name: sources
params.description: The sources entries may come from. For npm, registry host names (default registry.npmjs.org), git and file; for Cargo, Cargo's source strings (default both spellings of crates.io) and git.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: findings
returns.description: Each shortfall: package (with its version where the lockfile has one) and problem; empty for a task that succeeded.

examples.name: Verify an npm lockfile
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Verify the lockfile
  build.lock.verify:
    lockfile: /srv/app/package-lock.json

examples.name: Verify a Cargo lockfile, allowing a private registry
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Verify the lockfile
  build.lock.verify:
    lockfile: /srv/app/Cargo.lock
    sources:
      - sparse+https://index.crates.io/
      - sparse+https://crates.example.internal/

reversibility.notes: A run that launched a fresh instance (name did not already exist among non-terminated instances) emits a cloud.aws.ec2.terminate naming the launched instance_id. A run that found an existing match emits nothing, the same as every other converged run in this catalog, even though this method does not compare that existing instance's image or type against what was requested.

doc.summary: Launches an EC2 instance via the AWS API.
doc.description: Makes sure an instance tagged Name=name exists among the account/region's non-terminated instances, launching one from image_id if none does. This is a narrow slice of amazon.aws.ec2_instance: idempotency here is existence of the Name tag only, not a comparison of a matching instance's configuration against what was requested. An instance already present under that name is left exactly as it is, regardless of whether its image or instance type match; this method never recreates. The target device is the AWS account/region context itself (an aws_account inventory item), not a device this task reaches over any transport. A check looks the name up and, when nothing matches, predicts a launch without sending RunInstances, not even as a dry run; it leaves the instance ID and state out, since AWS assigns both.

params.name: name
params.description: The Name tag to find or create an instance under.

params.name: image_id
params.description: The AMI id to launch from. Ignored when an instance already exists under name.

params.name: instance_type
params.description: The EC2 instance type (e.g. t3.micro). Ignored when an instance already exists under name.

returns.name: instance_id
returns.description: The instance this task found or launched.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the account reported about the Name-tagged instance before this task and after it (exists, instance_id, state). Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

returns.name: inverse
returns.returned: when this task launched a new instance
returns.description: The cloud.aws.ec2.terminate task that undoes this run.

examples.name: Launch a small instance
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Launch the build agent
  cloud.aws.ec2.create:
    name: build-agent-1
    image_id: ami-0abcdef1234567890
    instance_type: t3.micro

reversibility.notes: A terminated instance's storage (unless an EBS volume was explicitly detached beforehand, which this method does not do) and identity are gone; there is nothing a cloud.aws.ec2.create could restore.

doc.summary: Terminates an EC2 instance via the AWS API.
doc.description: Terminates the instance named by instance_id. A no-op if AWS has no record of that id at all, or if it is already terminated. Unlike cloud.aws.ec2.create, this takes an exact instance_id rather than a Name-tag lookup: terminating by a fuzzy match is a worse default than requiring the exact resource for a destructive action.

params.name: instance_id
params.description: The instance id to terminate.

returns.name: instance_id
returns.description: The instance this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the account reported about the instance before this task and after it (exists, instance_id, state). Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Terminate an instance
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Tear down the build agent
  cloud.aws.ec2.terminate:
    instance_id: i-0123456789abcdef0

reversibility.notes: A run that created the bucket (it did not already exist) emits a cloud.aws.s3.delete_bucket naming it. A run that found the bucket already present emits nothing, the same as every other converged run in this catalog.

doc.summary: Creates an S3 bucket via the AWS API.
doc.description: Makes sure bucket exists in the account/region, creating it if it does not. Idempotent on existence alone: this method has no bucket configuration surface (versioning, encryption, policy) to compare or converge, the same restraint every other narrowly-scoped method in this catalog applies against its own upstream's larger surface. The target device is the AWS account/region context itself (an aws_account inventory item), not a device this task reaches over any transport.

params.name: bucket
params.description: The bucket name to create or leave alone.

returns.name: bucket
returns.description: The bucket this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether the bucket existed before this task and after it. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

returns.name: inverse
returns.returned: when this task created the bucket
returns.description: The cloud.aws.s3.delete_bucket task that undoes this run.

examples.name: Create a bucket
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Create the release artifacts bucket
  cloud.aws.s3.create_bucket:
    bucket: my-release-artifacts

reversibility.notes: Bucket names are globally unique across all of AWS, so a bucket this task just deleted may be claimed by an unrelated account before any inverse would run; there is no safe cloud.aws.s3.create_bucket to record.

doc.summary: Deletes an S3 bucket via the AWS API.
doc.description: Deletes bucket if it exists; a no-op otherwise. This method does not empty a non-empty bucket first: AWS itself refuses to delete one that still holds objects, and that refusal is the safety rail, not an error this method routes around. A check reads the bucket and whether it holds anything, deleting nothing; one that holds objects makes the call unchecked rather than failed, since an earlier task in the same run may be what empties it.

params.name: bucket
params.description: The bucket name to delete.

returns.name: bucket
returns.description: The bucket this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether the bucket existed before this task and after it. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Delete a bucket
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remove the release artifacts bucket
  cloud.aws.s3.delete_bucket:
    bucket: my-release-artifacts

reversibility.notes: The bytes a file held before are not kept, so the write cannot be undone; a container recreated from its image has the image's file again.

doc.summary: Puts one file into a container.
doc.description: Makes the file at dest inside the container named name hold content, or the bytes of src, a file in the project directory, with mode. The file is read first and written only when its bytes or mode differ, so a second run with the same bytes writes nothing. src is read by the command line, which holds the project (relative, inside it, through no symbolic link, never .pleiades, at most 64 MiB); a Walk-tier Runner cannot see the project, so there src is refused and content is the way. The container may be running or stopped. The bytes the file held before are not kept, so the write has no undo. A check reads and compares, and writes nothing. The engine is reached the first way onboarding proved for the device (this machine's socket, an SSH channel to the engine's socket, the engine's own dial-stdio over SSH, or mutual TLS), its identity checked against the one onboarding recorded, and every request outside the operations this method declares is refused before it reaches the engine.

params.name: name
params.description: The container's name.

params.name: dest
params.description: The file's absolute path inside the container; its directory must exist.

params.name: content
params.description: The bytes the file should hold. Set content or src, not both.

params.name: src
params.description: A file in the project directory whose bytes the file should hold, relative to it.

params.name: mode
params.description: The file's mode, in octal.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task, when the engine is reached over SSH. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The container's name.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The file's path inside the container.

returns.name: checksum
returns.description: The SHA-256 of the bytes it holds.

returns.name: size
returns.description: Their size.

examples.name: Drop a configuration file into a running container
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Web config
  container.copy_in:
    name: web
    dest: /etc/nginx/conf.d/site.conf
    src: files/site.conf

reversibility.notes: It reads what the engine reports, and changes nothing.

doc.summary: Reads one text file out of a container.
doc.description: Returns the text of the file at src inside the container named name, running or stopped, with its size and SHA-256. A file over max_bytes, or one that is not valid UTF-8 text, is refused rather than cut or mangled. It changes nothing, so a check is the same read. The engine is reached the first way onboarding proved for the device (this machine's socket, an SSH channel to the engine's socket, the engine's own dial-stdio over SSH, or mutual TLS), its identity checked against the one onboarding recorded, and every request outside the operations this method declares is refused before it reaches the engine.

params.name: name
params.description: The container's name.

params.name: src
params.description: The file's absolute path inside the container.

params.name: max_bytes
params.description: The largest file read, in bytes, up to 16 MiB.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task, when the engine is reached over SSH. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The container's name.

returns.name: content
returns.description: The file's text.

returns.name: size
returns.description: Its size in bytes.

returns.name: checksum
returns.description: Its SHA-256.

examples.name: Read the app's version file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Version
  container.copy_out:
    name: web
    src: /opt/app/VERSION
  register: version

reversibility.notes: A run that created the container records its removal, by ID; one that found it as declared records nothing.

doc.summary: Makes a container exist as declared, without starting it.
doc.description: Makes the container named name exist from image as the task declares it, without starting it: container.run's declaration, comparison and refusals, with no start. An existing container that matches is left as it is, running or not; one that differs is refused, naming container.recreate. A check pulls and creates nothing. The engine is reached the first way onboarding proved for the device (this machine's socket, an SSH channel to the engine's socket, the engine's own dial-stdio over SSH, or mutual TLS), its identity checked against the one onboarding recorded, and every request outside the operations this method declares is refused before it reaches the engine.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task, when the engine is reached over SSH. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The container's name.

returns.name: id
returns.description: The container's ID.

returns.name: state
returns.returned: when the container exists or would
returns.description: The container's state as the engine names it (created, running, exited, paused), after the task.

returns.name: image
returns.description: The image by digest: the one the container runs, or would.

returns.name: image_digest
returns.description: The image's digest.

returns.name: image_id
returns.returned: when the image is on the engine
returns.description: The engine's ID for the image.

returns.name: pulled
returns.description: Whether the image had to be pulled (by a check, would be).

returns.name: env_names
returns.description: The environment variables the task set, by name only.

examples.name: Create a job container to start later
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Backup job
  container.create:
    name: backup
    image: restic/restic:0.17.3
    command: [backup, /data]
    volumes: ["appdata:/data"]

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: the method reads the engine's own report and changes nothing.

doc.summary: Reads the container engine's own report of itself.
doc.description: Reads the device's container engine as it reports itself, for a later task's when: Docker's info and version, or Podman's libpod info, which says what Docker's form does not. Both are reported under the same names: the engine and its version, the newest API version it speaks, its storage driver, whether it runs rootless, the cgroup version and driver, the OS and architecture (in Go's names, linux and amd64), the kernel, the host's operating system, its container and image counts, CPUs and memory. On a device running both engines, engine chooses which. Reading changes nothing, and a check reads the same way. The engine is reached the first way onboarding proved for the device (this machine's socket, an SSH channel to the engine's socket, the engine's own dial-stdio over SSH, or mutual TLS), its identity checked against the one onboarding recorded, and every request outside the operations this method declares is refused before it reaches the engine.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task, when the engine is reached over SSH. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: engine
returns.description: The engine: docker or podman.

returns.name: carrier
returns.description: How the engine was reached: local, socket, stdio or tls.

returns.name: version
returns.description: The engine's release.

returns.name: api_version
returns.description: The newest API version the engine speaks.

returns.name: storage_driver
returns.description: The storage driver (overlay2, overlay, btrfs, ...).

returns.name: rootless
returns.description: Whether the engine runs without root.

returns.name: cgroup_version
returns.description: The cgroup version, 1 or 2.

returns.name: cgroup_driver

reversibility.notes: Its undo removes the archive it created; it never replaces one, so nothing else is lost.

doc.summary: Dumps a database with the device's pg_dump into a new archive on the device.
doc.description: Runs pg_dump on the device in its custom format into dest, which must not exist: a dump never replaces an archive. The archive is written beside dest and linked to it once complete, so a failed or interrupted dump never leaves a partial archive under the name a restore would read. pg_dump must be at least the server's major version, which is checked before anything is written. The password reaches the device on standard input and is written by the shell's own printf into a password file (PGPASSFILE, mode 0600) in a private directory, in memory where the host keeps one per user, removed however the run ends, as PostgreSQL recommends over PGPASSWORD: it is never on a command line or in any process's environment, though the device's login user and root can read the file while the run lasts; every PG variable the device's login carries is cleared first, so its own PGSERVICE or PGHOST cannot redirect the dump; a pinned CA is written to a private directory removed however the run ends. pg_dump runs under timeout -k, so a hung one is stopped on the device. Its removal is recorded as the undo as soon as the archive is in place, then its size and SHA-256 are read back and returned; a read back that fails is a warning, not a failure that would drop the undo. The database reaches pg_dump as a connection string naming it alone, quoted, so a name holding = is only ever a name. A check makes every refusal a run makes and writes nothing. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

doc.summary: Compares the privileges granted to a role with a declared set, and fails naming each extra and each missing one.
doc.description: Reads, in one snapshot, every privilege granted to role itself in the database (on the database, schemas, tables, views, sequences, functions and columns, outside the system schemas, each with whether it carries the grant option), the roles it is a member of, and the objects it owns, and compares them with expect. A pattern schema.* stands for every object of its kind in the schema that exists; an exact object that does not exist is missing. Privileges reached through PUBLIC or through another role's membership are that grant's to answer for and are not compared; an owner holds everything on what it owns, so ownership is compared as its own entry, extra unless owns declares it. A column grant is its own entry, never folded into its table's. A grant option held but not declared is extra, and one declared but not held is missing. Default privileges are not compared. It only reads, so a check of it is the task itself. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

params.description: The name of a database connection: one stored with pleiades add-database-connection, or a PostgreSQL Connection credential bound to the template. It holds the server as the device sees it, the login and its password, the TLS mode and the live databases; a task never carries any of them.

params.name: database
params.description: The database to connect to.

params.name: expect

A privilege is its SQL name (SELECT, USAGE, EXECUTE, ...), ALL for every one its kind has on this server (before PostgreSQL 17, a table has no MAINTAIN, and declaring it there is refused), and may end WITH GRANT OPTION.

reversibility.notes: SQL has no inverse the method can derive; write the reverse as a rollback: list, or as a new forward migration.

doc.summary: Applies a directory of numbered SQL files in order, each in its own transaction, recording each in a version table.
doc.description: Reads every .sql file in dir on the device, named <version>_<name>.sql and applied in numeric order. Another .sql name, in any letter case (1_x.SQL), is refused rather than skipped, as is a .down.sql file (this applies forward only) and a version two files share. Every file is read and checked before any runs: a file may not commit or roll back its own transaction, and a statement that cannot run in a transaction (CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, VACUUM) needs a file of its own starting -- pleiades: no-transaction, holding exactly that one statement. With additive_only, a file that drops, truncates, deletes, revokes, renames or changes a column's type is refused unless it says why (-- pleiades: destructive: <why>), which the result lists, and so is one whose effect the lint cannot read: a DO block, a CALL, an EXECUTE, a COPY to or from a program, or a query on its own (SELECT f() does whatever f does); a statement that runs another (WITH, PREPARE, EXPLAIN, COPY of a query) is judged by the one it runs. The check is a SQL lexer, so a keyword in a string or comment does not count, and it does not see into a function or trigger that an INSERT, UPDATE or CREATE sets off. Each file runs in its own transaction, as role when given, with a statement timeout and a lock timeout (a busy table fails the migration rather than stalling the application), and its version, name, SHA-256 and duration are recorded in the version table in the same transaction. An applied file whose checksum changed is refused, as is a pending version below the newest applied one unless allow_out_of_order is set. Runs against one version table are serialized by the version itself, with no lock: each file claims its version as the table's primary key before it runs, so a second run applying the same file waits on the first's claim and then reads its record rather than applying it again; a no-transaction file's claim is recorded first as unfinished and marked finished once its statement succeeds (removed if it fails), so a run that died midway is named rather than guessed at. The lint reads a backslash in a string literal as the standard does, so before each file is sent the session must have standard_conforming_strings on, and a file that turns it off stops the run before the next. A check reads and checks every file, reads the version table and reports the pending files, applying nothing. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

params.description: The name of a database connection: one stored with pleiades add-database-connection, or a PostgreSQL Connection credential bound to the template. It holds the server as the device sees it, the login and its password, the TLS mode and the live databases; a task never carries any of them.

params.description: The database to connect to.

doc.summary: Runs one SQL statement and returns its rows as CSV, read-only unless the task says otherwise.
doc.description: Prepares exactly one statement (the server refuses more than one in a prepared statement) and runs it in a transaction with a statement timeout and a lock timeout set for that transaction alone. Without write, the transaction is read-only and rolled back; with write, it is committed, and a data change without RETURNING is run for the count of rows it changed. The rows are returned as RFC 4180 CSV with a header row, NULL as an empty field and the empty string as ""; more than max_rows rows, or more than 1 MiB of CSV, fails the task rather than return part. A read-only transaction stops writes to the database's tables but is not a sandbox: a superuser, or a member of pg_execute_server_program, pg_read_server_files or pg_write_server_files, can still act outside the database (COPY TO PROGRAM, server files), so such a login is refused unless allow_privileged_role is set, which the run warns about. Give queries a role of their own with only the privileges they need. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

params.description: The name of a database connection: one stored with pleiades add-database-connection, or a PostgreSQL Connection credential bound to the template. params.description: Run in a read-write transaction and commit it. A task with write cannot be checked (check_mode is refused at validation).

params.description: The statement timeout, as a duration such as 30s or 5m, up to 1h.

doc.summary: Restores an archive on the device into a database the task names, in one transaction, refusing a live one unless told why.
doc.description: Runs the device's pg_restore with --single-transaction and --exit-on-error, so a restore that fails leaves nothing of itself behind. The target database is named by the task, never defaulted. A database is live when its connection lists it, or when it says so itself (ALTER DATABASE app SET pleiades.live = on): restoring over one is refused unless allow_live is set with a live_reason, which the result records and the run warns about. A database that does not exist is refused unless create is set, in which case it is created first and dropped again if the restore fails; one that already holds tables, views or sequences is refused unless clean is set (--clean --if-exists). By default objects are restored owned by the connection's login and without the archive's grants (no_owner, no_privileges), which suits a copy restored for verification; turn both off to restore a database as it was. The archive is listed (pg_restore --list) before anything changes, which refuses a file that is not one. The database reaches pg_restore as a connection string naming it alone, quoted, so a name holding = is only ever a name and never another server. A check makes every refusal a run makes and writes nothing. It cannot be undone: dump the target first to keep a way back. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

params.name: connection
params.description: The name of a database connection: one stored with pleiades add-database-connection, or a PostgreSQL Connection credential bound to the template. It holds the server as the device sees it, the login and its password, the TLS mode and the live databases; a task never carries any of them.

params.name: database

params.name: src

params.name: create

params.name: clean

params.name: allow_live
params.description: Allow restoring over a live database. Needs live_reason.

params.name: live_reason
params.description: Why a live database is being overwritten, recorded in the result and warned about.

params.name: no_owner
params.description: Restore objects owned by the connection's login rather than the archive's owners (--no-owner).

params.name: no_privileges
params.description: Leave out the archive's grants (--no-privileges).

params.name: maintenance_database
params.description: The database connected to while the target is checked, created or dropped.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long pg_restore may run, up to 24h, after which it is stopped on the device and its transaction rolled back.

reversibility.notes: It counts rows in read-only transactions, and writes nothing.

doc.summary: Counts every table's rows exactly, and with compare fails naming each table whose counts differ from a second database's.
doc.description: Counts the rows of every table outside the system schemas with count(*), in a REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY transaction per database, so each side's counts are one moment; partitions are counted through their parent, once. With compare, a second database (on the same connection, or another named one, reached through the same device) is counted the same way and the two are compared table by table: a different count, or a table only one side has, fails the task. Comparing a live database with a copy of it differs by whatever was written since; the comparison is for copies at rest, such as a restore checked against the dump's source taken at the same time. Planner estimates are never used. It only reads, so a check of it is the task itself. The connection is made from the device, through its SSH session (a direct-tcpip channel, or direct-streamlocal to a socket), so the database sees the connection its own network and pg_hba.conf already allow; TLS, when the connection asks for it, is negotiated and verified by this platform against the connection's pinned CA or the system's roots, and nothing of the machine running pleiades (a .pgpass, a certificate, a PG variable) is read.

params.name: connection
params.description: The name of a database connection: one stored with pleiades add-database-connection, or a PostgreSQL Connection credential bound to the template. It holds the server as the device sees it, the login and its password, the TLS mode and the live databases; a task never carries any of them.

params.name: database
params.description: The database to connect to.

params.name: compare
params.description: The database to compare with: database, and connection when it is on another server. Any other key is refused.

params.name: schemas
params.description: Count only the tables in these schemas, each of which must exist.

params.name: exclude
params.description: Tables not to count, as schema.table or schema.*.

params.name: max_tables
params.description: The most tables one side may count, up to 10000; past it the task fails rather than count part.

params.name: timeout
params.description: Each count's statement timeout, up to 1h.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: tables
returns.description: Each table counted: table, rows, and compare_rows with compare.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: How many tables' counts differ, which is zero for a task that succeeded.

returns.name: only_here
returns.description: Tables only the first database has.

returns.name: only_there
returns.description: Tables only the compared database has.

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: What the run allowed that it must say: a connection that crosses a network unencrypted, a privileged login, a live database overwritten, a version mismatch.

doc.summary: Checks a Cloudflare Access application's audience, issuer, settings and policies against what is expected.
doc.description: Reads an Access application by id, or by its domain (one two applications share is refused, naming both), its policies, and the issuer of the tokens Access signs for it (https:// and the account's team domain). Each field expect names is compared: audience, issuer and domain (domain and issuer without regard to case), type and session_duration. Policies are compared by name: a policy expected and absent is missing; one whose decision, precedence or include, exclude or require rules differ is changed, rules compared as JSON with their keys sorted; and with exact_policies one present and not expected is extra. The task fails listing every difference. It reads through Cloudflare's API with the cloudflare_account device's own token (stored with add-credential --token-stdin, sent only to its api_base, no redirect followed), follows every list page by page up to 50 pages, retries a rate limit or a server error twice, and changes nothing, so a check of it is the task itself. A token without the permission a read needs is refused by Cloudflare (403), and the error says so.

params.name: app
params.description: The application's id, or its domain.

params.name: expect
params.description: What the application must be: any of audience, issuer, domain, type, session_duration, and policies (a list of {name, decision, precedence, include, exclude, require}, each field optional but name).

params.name: exact_policies
params.description: Fail on a policy the application has and expect.policies does not name.

returns.name: id
returns.description: The application's id.

returns.name: domain
returns.description: Its domain.

returns.name: audience
returns.description: Its audience tag (aud), which an origin validating Access tokens must expect.

returns.name: issuer
returns.description: The issuer of its tokens.

returns.name: policies
returns.description: Each policy's name, decision and precedence.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: Every difference from what was expected; the task fails when there is one. A read that fails (a refused token, a name that resolves to nothing) fails the task before there are differences to list.

examples.name: Only staff reach the admin site
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Access
  edge.access:
    app: admin.example.com
    expect:
      audience: 2b1d0a9c5f3e8d7a6b4c1e0f9d8c7b6a5e4d3c2b1a0f9e8d7c6b5a4f3e2d1c0b
      issuer: https://example.cloudflareaccess.com
      policies:
        - name: staff
          decision: allow
          include: [{email_domain: {domain: example.com}}]
    exact_policies: true

doc.summary: Checks a DNS record set in a Cloudflare zone against what is expected.
doc.description: Reads a zone by id, or by name within the account (a zone of another account is refused, even where the token reaches it), and its records of one name and type. The set of contents is compared with expect.content, addresses in their canonical form and names in lower case without the final dot; proxied and ttl are compared on every record when expected; and absent requires there be none. With no expect, the task fails only when there is no such record. It reads through Cloudflare's API with the cloudflare_account device's own token (stored with add-credential --token-stdin, sent only to its api_base, no redirect followed), follows every list page by page up to 50 pages, retries a rate limit or a server error twice, and changes nothing, so a check of it is the task itself. A token without the permission a read needs is refused by Cloudflare (403), and the error says so.

params.name: zone
params.description: The zone's id, or its name.

params.name: name
params.description: The record's full name (www.example.com).

params.name: type
params.description: The record type.

params.name: expect
params.description: What the records must be: content (one value or a list, compared as a set), proxied, ttl (1 is automatic), or absent: true.

returns.name: zone
returns.description: The zone's name.

returns.name: records
returns.description: Each record's content, proxied and ttl.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: Every difference from what was expected; the task fails when there is one. A read that fails (a refused token, a name that resolves to nothing) fails the task before there are differences to list.

doc.summary: Checks a Cloudflare Tunnel's status and how many of its connectors are up.
doc.description: Reads a tunnel by id, or by name among the account's tunnels not deleted (a name two tunnels share is refused, naming both), and its connectors: each cloudflared process serving it, with its version, architecture and connections by colo. The task fails when the tunnel's status is not expect_status or fewer connectors than min_connectors have a live connection (one pending reconnect has dropped, and is only still tracked, so it does not count). It reads through Cloudflare's API with the cloudflare_account device's own token (stored with add-credential --token-stdin, sent only to its api_base, no redirect followed), follows every list page by page up to 50 pages, retries a rate limit or a server error twice, and changes nothing, so a check of it is the task itself. A token without the permission a read needs is refused by Cloudflare (403), and the error says so.

params.name: tunnel
params.description: The tunnel's id, or its name.

params.name: expect_status
params.description: The status the tunnel must have; any accepts every status.

params.name: min_connectors
params.description: The fewest connectors that must have a connection to Cloudflare's edge, 0 to 1000.

returns.name: id

returns.name: name

returns.name: connections

returns.name: differences

reversibility.notes: An arbitrary command's effect is unknown to this platform, so no undo can be derived from it. Pair the task with creates or removes to make re-running it safe, which is idempotence rather than rollback.

doc.summary: Runs one command directly, with no shell involved.
doc.description: Runs a single command on the target over SSH and reports its exit status, stdout and stderr. No shell interprets the command: a semicolon, pipe or dollar sign in an argument is passed through as text, so this cannot chain commands, expand a variable or redirect output. Use exec.shell when those are what you want. A command cannot be inspected, so this reports changed every time it runs; creates and removes are how a task says what its work having already happened looks like, and a run they short-circuit reports no change. Only a call with creates or removes can be checked: a check reads the guard's path and reports whether the command would run, running nothing. Any other call is named as unchecked, and check_mode on one is refused when the runbook is validated.

params.name: cmd
params.description: The command and its arguments as one string, split the way a shell splits a command line: whitespace separates arguments, and single quotes, double quotes and backslashes group them. Mutually exclusive with argv.

params.name: argv
params.description: The command and its arguments already split, one element each. Preferred when an argument contains characters whose quoting would be awkward to write. Mutually exclusive with cmd.

params.name: chdir
params.description: Change into this directory before running, and resolve a relative creates or removes against it too. The command does not run at all if the directory does not exist. Defaults to the device's own working directory, or to wherever the account lands on login.

params.name: creates
params.description: A path whose existence on the target means this work is already done. When it exists, the command does not run and the task reports no change. A relative path is resolved from chdir, the same directory the command itself runs in.

params.name: removes
params.description: A path whose absence on the target means this work is already done. When it is missing, the command does not run and the task reports no change. A relative path is resolved from chdir, the same directory the command itself runs in.

params.name: stdin
params.description: Text piped to the command's standard input.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: rc
returns.description: The command's exit status. Zero when it succeeded, and 0 for a run that creates or removes skipped.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: Everything the command wrote to standard output, with the trailing newline removed. A command that writes more than 64 MiB to either stream fails the task rather than returning part of it.

returns.name: stderr
returns.description: Everything the command wrote to standard error, with the trailing newline removed. A command that writes more than 64 MiB to either stream fails the task rather than returning part of it.

returns.name: cmd
returns.description: The exact command line sent to the device, empty for a skipped run.

returns.name: skipped
returns.description: True when creates or removes short-circuited this task, so no command ran.

returns.name: msg
returns.description: Why the task was skipped.

examples.name: Run a command and register its output
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the kernel version
  exec.command:
    cmd: uname -r
  register: kernel

- name: Unpack the release once

    chdir: /opt/app
    creates: /opt/app/VERSION

examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Write a literal value
  exec.command:
    argv:
      - /usr/bin/logger
      - "deployed $VERSION; done"

reversibility.notes: A shell command's effect is unknown to this platform, and a pipeline or redirect can touch things the command line does not name, so no undo can be derived from it. Pair the task with creates or removes to make re-running it safe, which is idempotence rather than rollback.

doc.summary: Runs a command through the target's shell, so pipes and redirects work.
doc.description: Runs a command line on the target through a real shell, which is what makes a pipe, a redirect, a variable expansion, a glob or a chain of commands behave the way they would if you typed them. That is also the whole risk: every one of those characters is syntax, so any runbook value interpolated into this command is code. Use exec.command when the command is a single program with arguments, which is most of the time. A command cannot be inspected, so this reports changed every time it runs; creates and removes are how a task says what its work having already happened looks like. Only a call with creates or removes can be checked: a check reads the guard's path and reports whether the line would run, running nothing. Any other call is named as unchecked, and check_mode on one is refused when the runbook is validated.

params.name: cmd
params.description: The command line, passed to the shell exactly as written. Pipes, redirects, globs, variable expansions and semicolons all work, because the shell sees them.

params.name: executable
params.description: The shell to run the command with, invoked as `<executable> -c <cmd>`. Defaults to the shell the device declares, or /bin/sh.

params.name: chdir
params.description: Change into this directory before running, and resolve a relative creates or removes against it too. The command does not run at all if the directory does not exist. Defaults to the device's own working directory, or to wherever the account lands on login.

params.name: creates
params.description: A path whose existence on the target means this work is already done. When it exists, the command does not run and the task reports no change. A relative path is resolved from chdir, the same directory the command itself runs in.

params.name: removes
params.description: A path whose absence on the target means this work is already done. When it is missing, the command does not run and the task reports no change. A relative path is resolved from chdir, the same directory the command itself runs in.

params.name: stdin
params.description: Text piped to the command's standard input.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: rc
returns.description: The command's exit status, which for a pipeline is the last command's. Zero when it succeeded, and 0 for a run that creates or removes skipped.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: Everything the command wrote to standard output, with the trailing newline removed. A command that writes more than 64 MiB to either stream fails the task rather than returning part of it.

returns.name: stderr
returns.description: Everything the command wrote to standard error, with the trailing newline removed. A command that writes more than 64 MiB to either stream fails the task rather than returning part of it.

returns.name: cmd
returns.description: The command line sent to the device, empty for a skipped run.

returns.name: skipped
returns.description: True when creates or removes short-circuited this task, so no command ran.

returns.name: msg
returns.description: Why the task was skipped.

- name: Count the failed units
  exec.shell:

  register: failed

  exec.shell:
    cmd: dpkg -l > /var/backups/packages.txt
    creates: /var/backups/packages.txt

examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Use a bash-only construct
  exec.shell:
    cmd: "[[ -f /etc/os-release ]] && echo present"

reversibility.notes: This platform cannot see what a script did, so it cannot say what would undo it. The same reasoning exec.command and exec.shell record: an arbitrary script's effect is opaque, and a guessed inverse is worse than none because a rollback would run it believing it was true. A task whose effect must be reversible should use a method that models the change it is making.

exec.winrm.shell.noCheckReason: a PowerShell or cmd script can change anything the account can reach, and what it changes is known only once it has run; this method has no creates or removes guard for a check to read

doc.summary: Runs a command on a Windows target through PowerShell, cmd.exe or no shell, over WinRM.
doc.description: Runs a command on a Windows host over WinRM, naming how it runs. This is exec.shell's Windows counterpart, and it is a separate FQCN for the same reason svc.systemd.start is separate from svc.start: the concrete method names the platform it actually speaks to. The task picks one of three modes. powershell runs a script through powershell.exe with -NoProfile and -NonInteractive, sent UTF-16LE and base64 encoded as -EncodedCommand requires, and keeps a failing native program's own exit code rather than flattening it to 1. cmd runs a one-line script through cmd.exe, which is the only way to reach a cmd builtin such as dir, set or %ERRORLEVEL%. none runs a Windows command line, reaching the program it names exactly as written, so that program parses its own arguments and nothing else acts on them. The WinRM service starts every command through cmd.exe and cannot be told not to, so every command line is escaped until that cmd.exe passes it through unchanged, and the parser that acts on the text is always the one the task named. Every mode shares cmd.exe's limit of 8191 characters, counted after escaping. Values the command needs go in env, never into its text. A command cannot be inspected, so this reports changed every time it runs.

params.name: command
params.description: The script to run, or with shell none the command line: a program and its arguments, quoted the way that program expects. It is passed on verbatim, so every metacharacter the named shell understands is syntax and any runbook value interpolated into it is code. Pass values in env instead.

params.name: shell
params.description: How the command runs: powershell, cmd or none. powershell and cmd name the interpreter that reads a script, and none runs a command line directly with no interpreter. Required rather than defaulted silently, because the three read the same text three different ways and a command written for one is not safe in another. Which programs run is the device's own setting (cmd_path, powershell_path).

params.name: env
params.description: Values the command reads, set as environment variables before it starts. Each name becomes PLEIADES_ followed by the name, read as $env:PLEIADES_NAME in PowerShell or !PLEIADES_NAME! in cmd, so a value never becomes part of the command text and needs no escaping for either shell. In cmd the %PLEIADES_NAME% form is refused, because cmd.exe expands it before it parses the line. Values must be strings, numbers or booleans. The environment is visible to other processes on the device, so a secret does not belong here.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait for the script to finish before giving up. This bounds the whole operation, including a device that accepts the connection and then never answers, which is what a host looks like after a script has reconfigured its own network. Raise it for an installer or an update run; the default is short because most work here is not.

params.name: expect_disconnect
params.description: Declare that this script is expected to destroy the connection carrying it, as an address change or a reboot does. The task then waits for the device to answer WinRM again instead of failing, and reports result_known false, because the script's exit status and output went down with the connection and are not recoverable. A device that never comes back is still a failure.

params.name: reconnect_timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait for the device to answer again after an expected disconnect. Only meaningful with expect_disconnect, and setting it without that is refused rather than silently ignored.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: Everything the script wrote to standard output.

returns.name: stderr
returns.description: Everything the script wrote to standard error. PowerShell progress output is suppressed before the script runs, so this carries real errors rather than progress records.

returns.name: exit_code
returns.description: The command's exit status. Under powershell a failing native program's own code survives, and a failed cmdlet reports 1. A non-zero status fails the task.

returns.name: result_known
returns.description: Whether this task actually saw the script finish. False only after an expected disconnect, where stdout, stderr and the exit status are all unavailable. Check this before trusting the other three: an unreceived result and a silent success are otherwise indistinguishable.

examples.name: Read a fact from a Windows host
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Report the OS caption
  exec.winrm.shell:
    shell: powershell
    command: (Get-CimInstance Win32_OperatingSystem).Caption
  register: os_caption

examples.name: Use a cmd builtin

  exec.winrm.shell:
    shell: powershell
    command: New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path $env:PLEIADES_DIR
    env:

examples.name: Run a program with no shell
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Query the time service
  exec.winrm.shell:
    shell: none
    command: w32tm /query /status

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing. This method runs uname and reads /etc/os-release and files under /proc, alters nothing on the device, and so has nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Gathers baseline system facts from the target (OS, kernel, distribution).
doc.description: Reads a small, fixed set of system facts over SSH and emits each one as a fact, so it is kept as drift data rather than as a value that expires at the end of the run. A fact the device cannot answer for is left out entirely: there is no guessed default and no empty string, so a condition reading ansible_distribution can tell "this device does not say" from "this device says nothing". Nothing is changed and no command is elevated, so this always reports no change. Three of ansible.builtin.setup's parameters are absent rather than accepted and ignored: gather_subset has nothing to select between at this size, gather_timeout is the task's own timeout here, and fact_path's local fact files are a separate feature this does not implement.

params.name: filter
params.description: Shell-style patterns, as ansible.builtin.setup takes them, narrowing which facts are gathered. A fact is gathered when its name matches any pattern, so ["ansible_distribution*"] gathers the distribution and its version and nothing else. Leaving this out gathers everything, and so does an empty list. A pattern set matching none of the facts this method knows about is refused rather than gathering nothing, since that is a typo far more often than an intention. Narrowing also skips the commands behind the facts it excludes, so it is a real saving rather than a filter on the way out.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: ansible_hostname
returns.description: The short host name, which is everything before the first dot of what uname reports.

returns.name: ansible_kernel
returns.description: The kernel release, as uname -r reports it.

returns.name: ansible_architecture
returns.description: The machine hardware name, as uname -m reports it, for example x86_64.

returns.name: ansible_distribution
returns.description: The distribution name, read from NAME in /etc/os-release, for example Ubuntu.

returns.name: ansible_distribution_version
returns.description: The distribution version, read from VERSION_ID in /etc/os-release. A rolling release that publishes no VERSION_ID reports no such fact.

returns.name: ansible_memtotal_mb
