returns.description: Total usable memory in megabytes, from MemTotal in /proc/meminfo, truncated the way Ansible truncates it.

returns.name: ansible_processor_count
returns.description: The number of physical processor packages, counted as the distinct physical id values in /proc/cpuinfo. An architecture whose /proc/cpuinfo carries no physical id field reports no such fact rather than a guessed 1.

returns.name: ansible_uptime_seconds
returns.description: How long the device has been up, in whole seconds, from the first field of /proc/uptime.

examples.name: Gather everything before deciding what to do
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Learn what this device is
  facts.gather:

examples.name: Gather only what a later condition reads
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Learn which distribution this is
  facts.gather:
    filter:
      - ansible_distribution*

reversibility.notes: Deleting text is usually the least reversible thing a method can do, and the markers are what make this the exception: they say exactly which lines belonged to the block, so the run that removes them captures the body and emits a file.block.set that writes it back. file.line is weaker because it identifies its target by a pattern rather than by a boundary, so it cannot be sure which of several matching lines it took away. What this still does not restore: a block that was in the MIDDLE of a file comes back at the END, because file.block.set appends, and the emitted inverse says so in its own description when that applies. Nor does it restore a final newline added to a file that had none. A run that found no block emits nothing, because undoing a run that changed nothing means doing nothing.

doc.summary: Removes a marked, multi-line block of text from a file.
doc.description: Takes away the region a file.block.set task left in a file, the two marker lines included, and leaves every other line alone. A file with no such markers is already in the state this asks for, so the task reports no change and writes nothing. The file must already exist, since a path that is not there is far more often a typo than a file whose block is missing; a symbolic link is refused, because writing the file back would replace the link with a regular file. Its mode, owner and group are put back after the rewrite. Markers that do not pair up (two end markers, or an end with no begin) are an error rather than a guess about which lines to delete, which matters more here than anywhere else in this namespace: the guess would be a deletion.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to edit. It must already exist.

params.name: marker
params.description: The template for both marker lines, which must be the one the block was written with. The {mark} placeholder is replaced by marker_begin on the line above the block and by marker_end on the line below it.

params.name: marker_begin
params.description: The word {mark} becomes on the line above the block.

params.name: marker_end
params.description: The word {mark} becomes on the line below the block.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task acted on.

returns.name: present
returns.description: Whether a marked block is in the file now, read back from the device. False after a successful run.

returns.name: block
returns.description: The text between the markers now, which is empty once the block is gone.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The before and after state of the marked region, each holding whether the block was present and what was between the markers. The before half is where the removed text is recorded. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

returns.name: inverse
returns.returned: when the run removed a block
returns.description: The task that undoes this run: a file.block.set carrying the body that was removed. A run that found no block records none, which is how the journal says undoing it means doing nothing.

examples.name: Stop managing a hosts file entry
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the cluster short names
  file.block.remove:
    path: /etc/hosts

examples.name: Remove a block written with its own marker
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Retire the hardening stanza
  file.block.remove:
    path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
    marker: "# {mark} PLEIADES HARDENING"

reversibility.notes: The strongest undo in the file namespace, and the markers are why: they delimit on the device the exact region this run replaced, so a run that changed a block emits an instruction restoring the previous body verbatim, and a run that added one emits a file.block.remove. file.line is weaker because it identifies its target by a pattern rather than by a boundary, so a later edit can make that pattern match a different line and its undo cannot promise the text lands where it came from. What this still does not restore: anything outside the markers, the file's mode and owner (which this method never changes, and puts back after each rewrite), and a final newline added to a file that had none, which the emitted inverse says in its own description. A converged run emits nothing, because undoing a run that changed nothing means doing nothing.

doc.summary: Ensures a marked, multi-line block of text is present in a file.
doc.description: Keeps a region of a text file, delimited by a begin and an end marker line, exactly as the runbook declares it. The markers are what make this safe to run twice: the region carries its own boundaries on the device, so a later run replaces the text between them in place rather than appending a second copy below the first. A file with no such markers gets the block, with its markers, appended at the end. A file whose block already matches is not written at all. The file must already exist, since file.touch and file.copy are what create; a symbolic link is refused, because writing the file back would replace the link with a regular file. Its mode, owner and group are put back after every rewrite, so managing a block in a file that services read does not quietly make it private. Markers that do not pair up (two begin markers, or a begin with no end) are an error rather than a guess about where the block stops.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to edit. It must already exist: this method edits a file rather than creating one.

params.name: block
params.description: The text to keep between the markers, usually written as a YAML block scalar. A trailing newline is not significant, so the same block written inline and as a block scalar produce the same region. It must not be empty and must not itself contain a marker line.

params.name: marker
params.description: The template for both marker lines. The {mark} placeholder is replaced by marker_begin on the line above the block and by marker_end on the line below it. Change it for a file whose comment character is not #, and keep it stable afterwards: a task that changes its marker stops finding the block it wrote last time and appends a second one.

params.name: marker_begin
params.description: The word {mark} becomes on the line above the block.

params.name: marker_end
params.description: The word {mark} becomes on the line below the block.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task acted on.

returns.name: present
returns.description: Whether a marked block is in the file now, read back from the device.

returns.name: block
returns.description: The text between the markers now, with no trailing newline.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The before and after state of the marked region, each holding whether the block was present and what was between the markers. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

returns.name: inverse
returns.returned: when the run changed the file
returns.description: The task that undoes this run: a file.block.set carrying the previous body, or a file.block.remove when the file carried no block before. A converged run records none, which is how the journal says undoing it means doing nothing.

examples.name: Manage a hosts file entry
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Keep the cluster's short names resolvable
  file.block.set:
    path: /etc/hosts
    block: |
      10.0.0.11 db1
      10.0.0.12 db2

examples.name: Use a marker a file's own syntax allows
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Manage the sshd hardening stanza
  file.block.set:
    path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
    marker: "# {mark} PLEIADES HARDENING"
    block: |
      PermitRootLogin no
      PasswordAuthentication no

examples.name: Keep two independent blocks in one file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Manage the proxy stanza only
  file.block.set:
    path: /etc/environment
    marker_begin: OPEN PROXY
    marker_end: CLOSE PROXY
    block: |
      http_proxy=http://proxy.internal:3128

reversibility.notes: A run that created the file emits a file.remove that deletes it again, which is a complete undo. A run that OVERWROTE an existing file emits a file.permissions restoring the mode, owner and group it found, and the previous CONTENT is not restored by it: those bytes are not read before the write and are not journaled anywhere, so once the new content lands the old content is gone. The emitted instruction says so in its own description rather than leaving a rollback to discover it. A run that changed nothing emits nothing.

doc.summary: Writes content, or a file from the project, to a file on the target, only when the bytes there differ.
doc.description: Writes content to a path on the device, comparing a SHA-256 of the content against a SHA-256 the device computes of what is already there, so a run that finds the same bytes sends no write at all and reports no change. A write that does happen goes to a temporary file in the destination's own directory, which is given the mode, owner and group the file is to have and only then renamed over it, so a reader of the path sees either the whole old file or the whole new one, and a write that cannot be finished leaves the destination as it was. The bytes are content, or src: a file in the project directory, read by the command line (pleiades run and adhoc), which holds the project. A Walk-tier Runner is a per-task container that cannot see the project, so there src is refused, naming content as the way to send the bytes. src is a path relative to the project directory that stays inside it, passes through no symbolic link, never reaches the project's .pleiades directory (its credentials and master key), and names a regular file of at most 64 MiB; it is read before anything is sent. Anything at dest that is not a regular file is refused rather than replaced. An existing file keeps the mode, owner and group it had unless the task names them. When the connecting account may not give a new file that owner or group (a login that is not root replacing a file another account owns), the bytes are copied into the existing file instead, which keeps everything it was, and the run warns that the write was not atomic; a file the account may not write is refused before anything changes. Ansible's atomic move would leave such a file owned by the connecting account: this method never changes an owner or group the task did not name. An owner or group the task names that the connecting account may not give is refused before anything is written, and a check refuses the same. A file this method creates and the task gave no mode gets 0600, which is a fixed, documentable default rather than Ansible's umask-derived one.

params.name: dest
params.description: The path to write on the device. Its parent directory must already exist: this method writes a file and never creates the directories above it, which is file.directory's job.

params.name: content
params.description: The bytes to write, used verbatim (set content or src, not both): nothing is appended, so a file that should end in a newline needs one in the value. An empty string is a real request and truncates the file to nothing. Quote a value YAML would otherwise read as a number or a boolean, since a non-string is refused rather than rendered.

params.name: src
params.description: A file in the project directory whose bytes the file should hold, as a path relative to that directory: it must stay inside it, pass through no symbolic link, not be in .pleiades, and be a regular file of at most 64 MiB. Read by the command line, which holds the project; refused on a Walk-tier Runner, which cannot see it, where content is the way. Set content or src, not both.

params.name: mode
params.description: The permission bits as one to four octal digits, quoted, for example "0644". Quote it: an unquoted 0644 is a number in YAML, not text. A symbolic mode such as u+x is refused, because it cannot be compared against the mode the device reports and the task would then report changed on every run. Left unset, an existing file keeps its mode and a newly created one gets 0600.

params.name: owner
params.description: The user name to give the file. A numeric id is refused: chown reads an all-digit argument as an id while the device reports names, so the two could never compare equal and the task would report changed forever. Left unset, an existing file keeps its owner and a new one belongs to the connecting account.

params.name: group
params.description: The group name to give the file, refused as a numeric id for the same reason owner is.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The path this task wrote.

returns.name: checksum
returns.description: The SHA-256 of the file's contents in hex, read back from the device after any write rather than computed from what was asked for. Ansible's copy reports a SHA-1 here; this reports SHA-256, which is the one hash this platform computes.

returns.name: mode
returns.description: The permission bits the file carries now, as four octal digits.

returns.name: owner
returns.description: The user name owning the file now.

returns.name: group
returns.description: The group owning the file now.

returns.name: size
returns.description: The file's size in bytes now.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The before and after state of the path, each holding its kind, mode, owner, group, size, modification time and the checksum of its contents. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

returns.name: warnings
returns.returned: when the write was not atomic
returns.description: Says the new bytes were copied into the existing file rather than renamed over it, because a new file could not be given its owner and group; a reader at that moment could have seen the file part written.

returns.name: inverse
returns.description: The concrete task that undoes this run: a file.remove when this run created the file, or a file.permissions restoring the attributes it found when the file already existed. Absent from a run that changed nothing, which is how the record says undoing it means doing nothing. When the previous content was overwritten, the description says plainly that those bytes are not restored.

examples.name: Write a configuration file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install the agent configuration
  file.copy:
    dest: /etc/pleiades/agent.yaml
    content: |
      endpoint: https://controller.internal:8443
      verify: true
    mode: "0644"

examples.name: Write a private file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the deploy token
  file.copy:
    dest: /etc/pleiades/token
    content: "{{ vars.deploy_token }}"
    mode: "0600"
    owner: pleiades
    group: pleiades

examples.name: Truncate a file to nothing
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Empty the local override file
  file.copy:
    dest: /etc/app/local.conf
    content: ""

reversibility.notes: A run that created the directory emits a file.remove naming it. That removal is deliberately not recursive, so it refuses rather than destroying anything put inside the directory after this task ran. A run that found the directory already there and only changed its mode, owner or group emits a file.permissions carrying the old ones, which puts the attributes back and never removes the directory. A converged run emits nothing at all. Parents a run created on the way to the directory are not removed by that undo.

doc.summary: Makes sure a directory exists on the target, with the mode, owner and group the task asks for.
doc.description: Ensures a directory exists at a path, creating any missing parents along the way exactly as mkdir -p does, and gives the directory, and every parent it creates, the mode, owner and group the task names, as Ansible does; a parent that already existed is never changed. This is ansible.builtin.file with state=directory; use file.remove to delete a directory and file.permissions to change attributes without creating anything. State is read before anything is written, so a run that finds the directory already correct reports no change, and only the attributes that actually differ are applied. If something that is not a directory already exists at the path, the task fails rather than replacing it: turning a file into a directory would destroy the file.

params.name: path
params.description: The directory to ensure exists. Missing parent directories are created too, the way mkdir -p does. Ansible creates parents implicitly and has no parameter for it, so neither does this.

params.name: mode
params.description: The permission bits in octal, written as a quoted string such as "0755". Quote it: an unquoted 0755 is read as a number by YAML and its leading zero is lost, so an unquoted value is refused rather than applied. A symbolic mode such as u+rwx is refused too, since it cannot be compared against the mode the device reports. Left unset, a new directory gets whatever the device's umask gives it and an existing one keeps the mode it has. Applies to the directory this task names and to every parent it creates on the way there, as ansible.builtin.file does, so a private tree is private all the way down; a parent that already existed keeps its mode.

params.name: owner
params.description: The user name that should own the directory. A name rather than a numeric id, because a name is what the device reports back and therefore the only form this method can compare against. Given to every parent this task creates too, as mode is. Left unset, ownership is not touched.

params.name: group
params.description: The group name that should own the directory, under the same rule as owner: a name, not a numeric id, and given to every parent this task creates. Left unset, the group is not touched.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The directory this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the path looked like before this task and what it looks like after, each holding exists, kind, mode, owner and group. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Create a directory tree
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure the release directory is there
  file.directory:
    path: /opt/app/releases/current

examples.name: Create it with a mode
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make a private directory
  file.directory:
    path: /var/lib/app/secrets
    mode: "0700"

examples.name: Hand it to a service account
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Own the data directory
  file.directory:
    path: /var/lib/app/data
    owner: app
    group: app
    mode: "0750"

reversibility.notes: A run that changed an existing file emits a file.copy writing back the whole text it held, with its mode, owner and group; that text is withheld from the journal, so a rollback replays it only from the task's own rollback: list. A run that created the file emits a file.remove. A run that changed nothing emits nothing. The modification time is not restored.

doc.summary: Sets, or removes, the value at a key path in a JSON file on the device, keeping the rest of the file.
doc.description: Reads the file (at most 4 MiB of UTF-8, refused when it holds a duplicate key, which two readers resolve differently) and sets the value at the key path, or removes it with state absent, keeping every other key in its place and every number and string exactly as written, so a 64-bit id or an escaped character survives. The file is written back at the indent unit it used (tabs, or a number of spaces, or on one line), one member per line, so a hand-aligned layout is normalized, and line endings are written as LF. A key already holding the value (by value, however it is spelled) is no change and nothing is written. The write keeps the file's owner, group and mode. The undo writes back the whole earlier text, withheld from the journal; a file the run created is removed. A check makes the same edit, reports the key's value before and after, and writes nothing.

params.name: path
params.description: The JSON file on the device, an absolute path.

params.name: key
params.description: The key path: dotted (server.port, items.0.name, a whole number indexing a list), or a list of segments ([server, "a.b", 0]) for a key holding a dot. A missing key is created, with a mapping for each missing step; an index one past a list's end appends.

params.name: value
params.description: The value to set, any YAML value (a mapping, a list, a scalar, null). Required with state present.

params.name: state
params.description: present sets the value; absent removes the key, which is no change when it is not there.

params.name: create
params.description: Start from an empty document when the file does not exist; without it a missing file is refused. A file it creates is mode 0644, owned by the account the device is reached as (file.attrs changes either).

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file.

returns.name: key
returns.description: The key path, dotted.

returns.name: created
returns.description: Whether the run created the file (or, in a check, would).

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The key's value before and after, as the format writes it; empty where there is none. Masked as every diff is.

examples.name: Move the service to another port
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Port
  file.json:
    path: /etc/app/config.json
    key: server.port
    value: 8443

examples.name: Drop a deprecated setting
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remove the old flag
  file.json:
    path: /etc/app/config.json
    key: [features, "legacy.mode"]
    state: absent

reversibility.notes: A run that removed something emits a file.copy carrying the whole text the file held beforehand, with its mode, owner and group. The whole file, because this can take several lines from several places and putting them back with file.line.set would pile them all at the end instead. That makes the record as large as the file. A run that found nothing to remove emits nothing, and so does a run against a file that was not there. The modification time is not restored, and file.copy itself is declared rather than implemented today.

doc.summary: Ensures no line matching a pattern remains in a file.
doc.description: Makes sure no line matching a pattern remains in a text file, which is ansible.builtin.lineinfile with state: absent. The whole file is read, the surviving lines are worked out locally, and the file is written back only when the bytes really differ, so a run that finds nothing to remove sends no write at all. Every matching line goes, not only the first. A file that is not there is already in the wanted state, so the task reports no change instead of failing, which is what lets one runbook strip a setting from a fleet where not every host has the file. Three differences from Ansible are deliberate: setting both regexp and line is refused rather than silently preferring regexp, insertafter and insertbefore are refused rather than accepted and ignored, and a file that ends without a newline keeps ending without one. Patterns are Go's RE2, which has no backreferences and no lookaround; search_string, backup and validate are not implemented. Lines are split on the newline byte alone, so a file with Windows endings carries its carriage return as part of each line's text and a pattern meant to match one has to say so.

params.name: path
params.description: The text file to edit. A file that is not there is reported as no change rather than as an error, since it holds no lines to remove. A symbolic link is refused rather than followed, because writing replaces the path and would leave a regular file where the link was.

params.name: regexp
params.description: Remove every line this pattern matches. Matched anywhere in a line unless anchored with ^ or $. Cannot be combined with line, and one of the two is required.

params.name: line
params.description: Remove every line whose text is exactly this. It may not contain a newline, since a line is matched whole. Cannot be combined with regexp, and one of the two is required.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task acted on.

returns.name: found
returns.description: How many lines were removed. Zero when the file held none matching, and zero when the file was not there at all.

returns.name: msg
returns.description: What happened, in lineinfile's own words: "3 line(s) removed", "file not present", or empty when the file held nothing to remove.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The file's state before and after, each holding exists and kind, plus mode, owner, group, size, mtime and the file's whole text when it is there. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

examples.name: Drop a package source by pattern
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the retired package mirror
  file.line.remove:
    path: /etc/apt/sources.list
    regexp: '^deb .*mirror\.old\.example\.com'

examples.name: Drop one exact entry
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remove the decommissioned host entry
  file.line.remove:
    path: /etc/hosts
    line: 10.0.4.9 registry.internal

examples.name: Act only when something was really removed
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Strip every commented out override
  file.line.remove:
    path: /etc/app/app.conf
    regexp: '^#\s*override'
  register: overrides

- name: Reload the service that read them
  exec.command:
    cmd: systemctl reload app
  when_cel: result.overrides.found > 0

reversibility.notes: A run that changed the file emits a file.copy carrying the whole text the file held beforehand, with its mode, owner and group. The whole file, because a line edit is not reliably undone by another line edit: a replacement has already thrown the old line away, and an anchored insert cannot be located again. That makes the record as large as the file. A converged run emits nothing, since undoing a change that was never made means doing nothing, and a run that fails partway emits nothing either. The modification time is not restored, and file.copy itself is declared rather than implemented today.

doc.summary: Ensures one line matching a pattern is present in a file, replacing or appending it.
doc.description: Makes sure one line is present in a text file, which is ansible.builtin.lineinfile with state: present. The whole file is read, the new text is worked out locally, and the file is written back only when the bytes really differ, so a run that finds the line already in place sends no write at all. When regexp is set, the last line it matches is replaced; when it is not set, a line already exactly equal to line means the task is done. A line that has to be added goes at the end of the file unless insertafter or insertbefore names a pattern to place it against. The file has to exist already, since Ansible's create is not implemented, so file.touch or file.copy is what makes one. Two differences from Ansible are deliberate and worth knowing. A regexp that does not match the line being placed is refused, because such a task adds the line again on every single run and never settles. And a file that ends without a newline keeps ending without one, where Ansible would add it. Patterns are Go's RE2, which has no backreferences and no lookaround; backrefs, search_string, firstmatch, create, backup and validate are not implemented. Lines are split on the newline byte alone, so a file with Windows endings carries its carriage return as part of each line's text and a pattern meant to match one has to say so.

params.name: path
params.description: The text file to edit. It has to exist already and it has to be a regular file. A symbolic link is refused rather than followed, because writing replaces the path and would leave a regular file where the link was.

params.name: line
params.description: The exact text of the line to make sure is present, written verbatim, so leading whitespace is part of the line. It may not contain a newline: this method places one line, and file.block.set is what places several.

params.name: regexp
params.description: A pattern naming the line to replace. The last line it matches is replaced by line, and if nothing matches then line is added. It has to match line itself, and is refused when it does not, because otherwise no run would ever find the line it just added and the file would grow forever. Matched anywhere in a line unless anchored with ^ or $.

params.name: insertafter
params.description: Where to put the line when it has to be added: a pattern, and the line goes after the last line matching it. The value EOF means the end of the file, which is also what happens when this is left out and when the pattern matches nothing. Cannot be combined with insertbefore.

params.name: insertbefore
params.description: Where to put the line when it has to be added: a pattern, and the line goes before the last line matching it. The value BOF means the start of the file. A pattern matching nothing puts the line at the end, which is Ansible's own behavior. Cannot be combined with insertafter.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task edited.

returns.name: msg
returns.description: What happened, in lineinfile's own words: "line added", "line replaced", or empty when the file was already correct.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The file's state before and after, each holding exists, kind, mode, owner, group, size, mtime and the file's whole text. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

examples.name: Correct a setting whether or not it is commented out
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Turn off root login over SSH
  file.line.set:
    path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
    regexp: '^#?PermitRootLogin'
    line: PermitRootLogin no

examples.name: Append an entry that is either there or not
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Add the internal registry to the hosts file
  file.line.set:
    path: /etc/hosts
    line: 10.0.4.12 registry.internal

examples.name: Place a line against an anchor
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Put the include ahead of the defaults section
  file.line.set:
    path: /etc/app/app.conf
    line: include /etc/app/conf.d/all.conf
    insertbefore: '^\[defaults\]'

reversibility.notes: A run that changed something emits a file.permissions carrying the mode, owner and group the path had before, which restores it exactly. A converged run emits nothing, because undoing a change that was never made means doing nothing. A run that fails partway emits nothing either, so whatever it applied before failing stays applied and has to be re-run rather than undone.

doc.summary: Sets a file's owner, group, and mode on the target.
doc.description: Sets the mode, owner and group of a path that already exists, changing only the ones that differ from what the device reports. A path that is absent is a refusal rather than a create, since making a file exist is file.touch's job and making a directory exist is file.directory's; that keeps a typo in a path from silently producing an empty file. A symbolic link is refused too, because chmod and chown follow a link while a stat of the link reports the link itself, so such a task would change one path while comparing against another and could never report converged. At least one of mode, owner and group must be given: a task that asks for nothing is a runbook mistake, not a no-op.

params.name: path
params.description: The path to change. It must already exist: this method changes a path rather than creating one.

params.name: mode
params.description: The permission bits as one to four octal digits, quoted, for example "0644". Quote it: an unquoted 0644 is a number in YAML, not text. A symbolic mode such as u+x is refused, because it cannot be compared against the mode the device reports and the task would then report changed on every run.

params.name: owner
params.description: The user name to give the path. A numeric id is refused: chown reads an all-digit argument as an id while the device reports names, so the two could never compare equal and the task would report changed forever.

params.name: group
params.description: The group name to give the path, refused as a numeric id for the same reason owner is.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The path this task acted on.

returns.name: mode
returns.description: The permission bits the path carries now, as four octal digits.

returns.name: owner
returns.description: The user name owning the path now.

returns.name: group
returns.description: The group owning the path now.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The before and after state of the path, each holding its kind, mode, owner, group, size and modification time. Recorded even when nothing changed, in which case the two halves are identical.

examples.name: Lock down a key file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Keep the deploy key private
  file.permissions:
    path: /etc/pleiades/deploy.key
    mode: "0600"
    owner: pleiades
    group: pleiades

examples.name: Make a script executable
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Allow the rotation script to run
  file.permissions:
    path: /usr/local/bin/rotate-logs
    mode: "0755"

examples.name: Hand a directory to a service account
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Give the cache directory to the service
  file.permissions:
    path: /var/cache/pleiades
    owner: pleiades

reversibility.notes: What this removes is gone. The content is not journaled anywhere, not the bytes of a file, not the tree under a directory, not what a symbolic link pointed at, so nothing on this platform can put it back and no run of this method emits an inverse. The recorded diff still describes what was there, so a rollback can report precisely what it cannot restore, which is the honest answer. Emitting an inverse that recreated the path would be worse than emitting none: it would leave an empty file where a full one had been and call that a restore.

doc.summary: Removes a file or directory from the target.
doc.description: Ensures nothing exists at a path, which is ansible.builtin.file with state=absent. It reads the path first, so a path that is already gone reports no change and sends no removal command at all, and a symbolic link is removed as the link rather than followed to whatever it points at. It diverges from Ansible in exactly one place, deliberately: Ansible deletes a non-empty directory without being asked, and this refuses unless the task sets recurse, because a recursive delete is the most destructive thing in this namespace and should be readable in the runbook that asks for it. Nothing this method removes can be restored by this platform.

params.name: path
params.description: The path that must not exist when this task finishes. A symbolic link is removed as the link, so whatever it points at is left alone.

params.name: recurse
params.description: Permit removing a directory that is not empty, and everything inside it. Without it, a non-empty directory is refused rather than emptied. Ansible's state=absent recurses without asking; this does not.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What was at the path before this task and what is there after, under before and after. The before half carries exists, kind, mode, owner, group and size, which is everything a rollback can report about what it cannot restore. On a path that was already absent the two halves are identical, which is how a reader tells "nothing to do" from "never ran".

examples.name: Remove a file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the leftover lock file
  file.remove:
    path: /var/run/deploy.lock

examples.name: Remove an empty directory
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the empty spool directory
  file.remove:
    path: /var/spool/old-queue

examples.name: Remove a directory and everything in it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the previous release
  file.remove:
    path: /opt/app/releases/2024-11-02
    recurse: true

reversibility.notes: It only reads what is at a path; nothing on the device changes, so there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Reports what is at a path on the target, and changes nothing.
doc.description: Reads what is at a path and reports it: whether anything is there, what it is (a file, a directory, a symlink or something else), its mode, owner and group, a symlink's target, its size and its modification time. This is ansible.builtin.stat. It only reads, so it never reports a change, records no undo, and its check is the same read. An absent path is an answer (exists is false), not a failure. Use it to look at a path before or after a change instead of a shell command, which reports changed on every run because it cannot tell what its command did.

params.name: path
params.description: The path to look at. A symlink is reported as the link itself, with its target, not as what it points to.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The path this task looked at.

returns.name: exists
returns.description: Whether anything is at the path.

returns.name: kind
returns.description: What is there: file, directory, symlink, other, or absent.

returns.name: mode
returns.description: The permission bits in octal, such as 0755, with the setuid, setgid and sticky digit when one is set.

returns.name: owner
returns.description: The owning user's name.

returns.name: group
returns.description: The owning group's name.

returns.name: size
returns.description: The size in bytes.

returns.name: mtime
returns.description: The modification time, as a Unix timestamp.

returns.name: target
returns.description: Where the symlink points.

examples.name: Look at a directory before changing it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: See what is at the app directory
  file.stat:
    path: /srv/app
  register: app_dir

reversibility.notes: A run that created the link emits a file.remove naming it, which deletes the link and never what it points at. A run that found a link already there and repointed it emits a file.symlink pointing back at the target it had, because removing that link would delete something the run never created. A converged run emits nothing, since it sent no command at all.

doc.summary: Makes a path a symbolic link pointing at a target, and refuses to replace a real file or directory.
doc.description: Makes path be a symbolic link pointing at src, which is ansible.builtin.file with state=link. It reads the path before it acts and only sends a command when the answer differs, so a run that finds the link already pointing at src reports no change and sends no ln at all. A link pointing somewhere else is repointed. A path with nothing at it gets a new link. Anything else already there, a regular file, a directory, a socket, is refused rather than replaced, because ln would delete it and this method could not put it back; Ansible's force parameter is deliberately not implemented for that reason. src does not have to exist, which is ln's own behavior: a link to a path that is not there yet is a dangling link, and creating one is a real change like any other.

params.name: src
params.description: The path the link points AT, written into the link exactly as given. It does not have to exist. A relative value is stored verbatim and is resolved by the system against the directory holding the link, not against the directory this task runs in.

params.name: path
params.description: The link itself, the path this task creates or repoints. Its parent directory must already exist: this method creates a link, never the directories above it. Ansible's alias dest is accepted for this too.

params.name: dest
params.description: Ansible's own alias for path, accepted so a converted playbook needs no renaming. Setting both of them to different paths is refused rather than guessed at.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The path's state before and after, each carrying exists and kind, plus target when it is a link. It is recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because 'it was already like this' is exactly what tells a rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Point a stable name at a versioned release
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Point current at the new release
  file.symlink:
    src: /opt/app/releases/1.4.2
    path: /opt/app/current

examples.name: Repoint a link that already exists
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Select the staging configuration
  file.symlink:
    src: /etc/app/config.staging.yaml
    path: /etc/app/config.yaml

examples.name: Use dest, the way a converted playbook writes it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Link the vendor binary onto the path
  file.symlink:
    src: /opt/vendor/bin/tool
    dest: /usr/local/bin/tool

doc.summary: Renders a template and writes the result to the target.

reversibility.notes: A run that created the file emits a file.remove naming it. A run that found the file already there and also changed its mode, owner or group emits a file.permissions carrying the old ones, which is a partial undo: the modification time this method moves on every run is NOT restored, because no method in this catalog can set one. A run that found the file already there and only re-stamped it emits nothing at all, since the modification time is then the single thing that moved and nothing here can put it back.

doc.summary: Creates an empty file on the target, or updates its modification time.
doc.description: Makes sure a regular file exists at a path, creating it empty when nothing is there and updating its modification time when it already is. This is ansible.builtin.file with state: touch, and it reports changed on every run for the same reason that module does: moving a modification time is a real change to the device, so a run that claimed otherwise would be wrong rather than tidy. The two kinds of change are told apart in the recorded diff, where a created file reads exists false then true and a re-stamped one reads true then true. Anything at the path that is not a regular file is refused rather than replaced.

params.name: path
params.description: The full path to the file. It is created empty when nothing is there, and left alone apart from its modification time when a regular file already is. A directory, a symbolic link or anything else at the path is refused.

params.name: mode
params.description: The permission bits as one to four octal digits, quoted, for example "0644". Quote it: an unquoted 0644 is a number in YAML, not text, and is refused rather than silently ignored. A symbolic mode such as u+x is refused too, because it cannot be compared against the mode the device reports. Sent to the device only when it differs from what is already there, so a converged file is not re-chmodded. Left alone when not set.

params.name: owner
params.description: The user that should own the file, by name. A numeric id is refused: chown reads an all-digit argument as an id while the device reports names back, so the two would compare unequal on every run. Sent only when it differs. Left alone when not set.

params.name: group
params.description: The group that should own the file, by name. A numeric id is refused, for the same reason it is on owner. Sent only when it differs, and in one chown alongside owner when both are set. Left alone when not set.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The path this touched, exactly as the task named it.

returns.name: created
returns.description: True when nothing was at the path and an empty file was made. False when a file was already there and only its modification time moved.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The before and after state of the path, each holding exists, kind, and for a path that is there its mode, owner, group, size and mtime. This is the record a rollback reads, so it is written even though this method always reports changed.

examples.name: Create a marker file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Mark the host as provisioned
  file.touch:
    path: /var/lib/pleiades/provisioned

examples.name: Create a log file with an owner and a mode
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make the log file the service will append to
  file.touch:
    path: /var/log/app/app.log
    owner: app
    group: app
    mode: "0640"

examples.name: Act only when the file had to be created
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Create the seed file
  file.touch:
    path: /opt/app/seed
  register: seed

- name: Seed the database the first time only
  exec.command:
    cmd: /opt/app/bin/seed
  when_cel: result.seed.created

reversibility.notes: A run that changed an existing file emits a file.copy writing back the whole text it held, with its mode, owner and group; that text is withheld from the journal, so a rollback replays it only from the task's own rollback: list. A run that created the file emits a file.remove. A run that changed nothing emits nothing. The modification time is not restored.

doc.summary: Sets, or removes, the value at a key path in a YAML file on the device, keeping its comments and the rest of the file.
doc.description: Reads the file (at most 4 MiB of UTF-8, one document; refused when it holds a duplicate key) and sets the value at the key path, or removes it with state absent, keeping comments and key order, and a replaced value's own comments. The rest of the document is written back in go.yaml.in/yaml/v3's style at the indent the file used, so quoting and spacing may be normalized; it is not a byte-for-byte edit. A path through an alias is refused, since one edit would change every place the alias is used. A key already holding the value is no change and nothing is written. The write keeps the file's owner, group and mode. The undo writes back the whole earlier text, withheld from the journal; a file the run created is removed. A check makes the same edit, reports the key's value before and after, and writes nothing.

params.name: path
params.description: The YAML file on the device, an absolute path.

params.name: key
params.description: The key path: dotted (server.port, items.0.name, a whole number indexing a list), or a list of segments ([server, "a.b", 0]) for a key holding a dot. A missing key is created, with a mapping for each missing step; an index one past a list's end appends.

params.name: value
params.description: The value to set, any YAML value (a mapping, a list, a scalar, null). Required with state present.

params.name: state
params.description: present sets the value; absent removes the key, which is no change when it is not there.

params.name: create
params.description: Start from an empty document when the file does not exist; without it a missing file is refused. A file it creates is mode 0644, owned by the account the device is reached as (file.attrs changes either).

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file.

returns.name: key
returns.description: The key path, dotted.

returns.name: created
returns.description: Whether the run created the file (or, in a check, would).

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The key's value before and after, as the format writes it; empty where there is none. Masked as every diff is.

examples.name: Raise the replica count
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Replicas
  file.yaml:
    path: /srv/app/values.yaml
    key: web.replicas
    value: 3

reversibility.notes: A run that mounted an absent path emits an fs.unmount naming it, which also strips the fstab entry this run added, if any. A run that found the path already mounted and only added or updated its fstab entry emits no inverse: undoing that without also unmounting a mount this task did not create needs a capability this namespace does not expose. A run that found everything already as requested emits nothing.

doc.summary: Mounts a filesystem on the target, and optionally persists it to fstab.
doc.description: Makes sure path is mounted from src, creating the mount if it is not already there. This is close to ansible.builtin.mount with state=mounted, split so that persisting to fstab (see the persist parameter) is independent of mounting: either can be true without the other. Mount state is read from findmnt before anything is sent, so a path already mounted from src with a matching fstype reports no change; a path already mounted from a different src or fstype is refused rather than silently remounted, since that is not something this method can do without first unmounting it. opts is compared only when the task actually names it: a path already mounted with different options than an unspecified opts is left alone rather than treated as drift. A check reads findmnt and fstab, mounts nothing and writes nothing, and leaves a new mount's options out of its prediction, since the kernel rewrites them.

params.name: path
params.description: The mountpoint to mount onto.

params.name: src
params.description: The device, share or filesystem source to mount.

params.name: fstype
params.description: The filesystem type, as mount's own -t takes it (e.g. ext4, nfs, xfs).

params.name: opts
params.description: Mount options, as mount's own -o takes them. Defaults to "defaults" for a fresh mount and a fresh fstab entry; an existing mount or fstab entry is only compared or rewritten against this when the task actually sets it.

params.name: persist
params.description: Also make sure path has a matching entry in fstab, so it mounts again on the next boot.

params.name: fstab
params.description: The fstab-format file to read and, if persist is true, write.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The mountpoint this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What findmnt and the fstab file reported about path before this task and after it, each holding mounted, source, fstype, options and persisted. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Mount and persist a data volume
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Mount the data volume
  fs.mount:
    path: /data
    src: /dev/sdb1
    fstype: ext4

examples.name: Mount without touching fstab
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Mount a scratch volume for this run only
  fs.mount:
    path: /mnt/scratch
    src: /dev/sdb2
    fstype: ext4
    persist: false

reversibility.notes: A run that unmounted a mounted path emits an fs.mount pinned to the exact src, fstype and opts this run captured before unmounting, which is a real, restorable inverse. If this run also removed the path's fstab entry, the inverse asks fs.mount to persist it again. A run that found the path already unmounted and only removed a stale fstab entry emits no inverse: undoing that without also mounting something this task did not mount needs a capability this namespace does not expose. A run that found everything already absent emits nothing.

doc.summary: Unmounts a filesystem on the target, and optionally removes it from fstab.
doc.description: Makes sure path is not mounted, unmounting it if it is. This is close to ansible.builtin.mount with state=unmounted, split so that removing the fstab entry (see the persist parameter) is independent of unmounting: either can happen without the other. Mount state is read from findmnt before anything is sent, so a path already unmounted reports no change from the unmount itself.

params.name: path
params.description: The mountpoint to unmount.

params.name: persist
params.description: Also remove any matching entry from fstab, so it does not mount again on the next boot.

params.name: fstab
params.description: The fstab-format file to read and, if persist is true, write.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The mountpoint this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What findmnt and the fstab file reported about path before this task and after it, each holding mounted, source, fstype, options and persisted. After always reports mounted: false on a successful unmount.

examples.name: Unmount and forget a volume
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Unmount the old data volume
  fs.unmount:
    path: /data

examples.name: Unmount but leave the fstab entry
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Unmount temporarily for maintenance
  fs.unmount:
    path: /data
    persist: false

reversibility.notes: A run that allowed the permanent configuration, the runtime one, or both emits an fw.firewalld.deny naming the same port or service and zone, with permanent and immediate set to match exactly which half this run actually changed. A run that found everything already allowed emits nothing.

doc.summary: Opens a port or service in firewalld.
doc.description: Makes sure a port or service is allowed through firewalld in the given zone. This is close to community.general.firewalld with state=enabled, except permanent and immediate are decided independently rather than as one of firewalld's own permanent/runtime toggle: either can be true without the other. Both configurations are read before anything is sent, so a half already allowing the rule is left alone and reports no change from that half.

params.name: port
params.description: The port to allow. Exactly one of port or service is required.

params.name: protocol
params.description: The protocol for port (tcp or udp). Ignored when service is given.

params.name: service
params.description: The firewalld service name to allow, e.g. http. Exactly one of port or service is required.

params.name: zone
params.description: The firewalld zone to allow the rule in.

params.name: permanent
params.description: Also add the rule to the permanent configuration, so it survives a reload.

params.name: immediate
params.description: Also add the rule to the runtime configuration, so it takes effect now.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: zone
returns.description: The zone this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether the rule was allowed in the permanent configuration and in the runtime one, before this task and after it. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Open a port
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Allow HTTPS
  fw.firewalld.allow:
    port: 443

examples.name: Allow a service immediately without persisting it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Temporarily allow SSH from a maintenance zone
  fw.firewalld.allow:
    service: ssh
    zone: maintenance
    permanent: false

reversibility.notes: A run that removed the rule from the permanent configuration, the runtime one, or both emits an fw.firewalld.allow naming the same port or service and zone, with permanent and immediate set to match exactly which half this run actually changed. A run that found everything already denied emits nothing.

doc.summary: Closes a port or service in firewalld.
doc.description: Makes sure a port or service is not allowed through firewalld in the given zone. This is close to community.general.firewalld with state=disabled, except permanent and immediate are decided independently rather than as one of firewalld's own permanent/runtime toggle: either can be true without the other. Both configurations are read before anything is sent, so a half already denying the rule is left alone and reports no change from that half.

params.name: port
params.description: The port to deny. Exactly one of port or service is required.

params.name: protocol
params.description: The protocol for port (tcp or udp). Ignored when service is given.

params.name: service
params.description: The firewalld service name to deny, e.g. http. Exactly one of port or service is required.

params.name: zone
params.description: The firewalld zone to remove the rule from.

params.name: permanent
params.description: Also remove the rule from the permanent configuration.

params.name: immediate
params.description: Also remove the rule from the runtime configuration, so it takes effect now.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: zone
returns.description: The zone this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether the rule was allowed in the permanent configuration and in the runtime one, before this task and after it. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Close a port
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Deny telnet
  fw.firewalld.deny:
    port: 23

reversibility.notes: A reload applies the permanent configuration to the runtime one, and there is no instruction that un-applies it. Undoing whatever permanent rules were added or removed is the task that changed them, not this one.

doc.summary: Reloads firewalld to apply pending rule changes.
doc.description: Runs firewall-cmd --reload, which applies the permanent configuration to the runtime one and is what makes an fw.firewalld.allow or fw.firewalld.deny run with permanent: true, immediate: false visible without a full firewalld restart. This is ansible.posix.firewalld's own no-op-detecting reload, except firewall-cmd exposes no way to ask whether a reload would have made any difference, so this always reports changed the same way svc.systemd.daemon_reload does for the identical reason.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

examples.name: Persist a rule and apply it now
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Allow HTTPS permanently
  fw.firewalld.allow:
    port: 443
    immediate: false

- name: Apply it
  fw.firewalld.reload: {}

reversibility.notes: It reads the manifest and runs nothing, so there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Validates a project's gate manifest on the device and lists how each check is classified, running nothing.
doc.description: Reads and validates the same manifest gate.run reads, under the same rules, and reports each check's name, kind, whether it is heavy or serial, its timeout, where it would run (a directory on the device or an image), its preconditions, and whether the task's selection would run it, with the reason when it would not. A check that needs a container engine on a device with none onboarded is reported as not runnable. Nothing in the manifest runs, so a check of this task is the task itself.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The gate manifest's path on the device.

params.name: kinds
params.description: Mark as selected only checks of these kinds, as gate.run would select them.

params.name: checks
params.description: Mark as selected only these checks, by name.

params.name: heavy
params.description: include, exclude or only, as for gate.run.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: checks
returns.description: One entry per check: name, kind, heavy, serial, timeout_s, runs ("dir <path>" or "image <reference>"), requires (the preconditions, as written), selected, reason (why it is not selected), and runnable (false, with the reason in reason, for a check the device cannot run).

returns.name: kinds
returns.description: Every kind the manifest may use: name, builtin and description.

returns.name: selected
returns.description: How many checks the selection would run.

examples.name: Show how a project's checks are classified
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: List the gate
  gate.list:
    manifest: /srv/app/gates.yaml
  register: gates

reversibility.notes: It runs the project's own checks and changes nothing of its own; what a check writes is that check's doing, which this platform cannot see to undo. It is not declared read-only, since a check is a command.

doc.summary: Runs a project's gate manifest of named checks on the device and reports PASS, FAIL or SKIP for each.
doc.description: Reads a gate manifest (YAML, at most 1 MiB, decoded strictly) from the device and runs the checks the task selects, one result per check. A check runs its command in a directory on the device over SSH, or in a fresh container from a digest-pinned image on the device's container engine, with no network unless it names one, a read-only root with a writable /tmp unless it says writable, and no new privileges; the image is pulled only when the check says pull. Every check has a timeout, its own or the manifest's default, and there is no implicit one; a directory check's is enforced on the device with the timeout command, which the device must have, and an image check's by killing its container. Checks run one at a time unless the manifest's defaults.parallelism or the task's parallelism raises it, at most one heavy check runs at a time, and a serial check runs with nothing else. A check skips, rather than runs to fail, when a precondition it declares is not met (a command on the PATH, an environment variable set, a file, the operating system, the container engine, a TCP endpoint the device reaches), or when it exits with a code its skip_exit lists; a check the task did not select, or that the task's deadline or a cancellation reached before it started, is skipped too, saying why. No exit code means skipped unless a check declares it, and a SKIP is never counted as a PASS. Any FAIL fails the task, and with fail_on_skip so does any SKIP. A failed task's error carries each failing check's reason and the end of its output, and its returns are reported with the failure too. The output kept is the last 40 lines and 8 KiB of a failing or skipping check, with anything a terminal would act on escaped. The manifest is refused whole, before anything runs, for a check with no kind, a kind neither built in (pure, db, network, model) nor declared, a check with no timeout, an image not pinned by digest, and every other rule it breaks. A check gets no environment and no credential from the platform. A check is not checkable: whether it passes is known only by running it, so a check of this task reads and validates the manifest and the selection, then reports the task unchecked.

params.name: manifest
params.description: The gate manifest's path on the device. A check's dir is relative to the manifest's own directory.

params.name: kinds
params.description: Run only checks of these kinds. Every kind when absent. A kind the manifest does not have is refused.

params.name: checks
params.description: Run only these checks, by name, among those the kinds select. A name the manifest does not have is refused.

params.name: heavy
params.description: include runs heavy checks with the rest, exclude leaves them out, only runs nothing else. A selection that runs no check at all is refused, since it would read as a pass.

params.name: parallelism
params.description: How many checks run at once, overriding the manifest's defaults.parallelism; 1 when neither sets it, at most 16. Heavy checks still run one at a time and serial checks alone.

params.name: fail_on_skip
params.description: Fail the task when any check is skipped, for a gate whose every check must run.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: checks
returns.description: One entry per check in the manifest, in its order: name, kind, status (PASS, FAIL or SKIP), reason, duration_ms, exit_code (-1 when it did not run to an exit status) and tail (the end of a failing or skipping check's output).

returns.name: passed
returns.description: How many checks passed.

returns.name: failed
returns.description: How many checks failed, which is zero for a task that succeeded.

returns.name: skipped
returns.description: How many checks were skipped, for any reason.

returns.name: summary
returns.description: The counts for a person, for example "12 passed, 0 failed, 3 skipped".

returns.name: ledger
returns.description: The skipped checks grouped by reason, largest group first.

examples.name: Run a project's pure and db checks
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Gate the release
  gate.run:
    manifest: /srv/app/gates.yaml
    kinds: [pure, db]

examples.name: Run only the heavy checks, two at a time
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Run the slow suites
  gate.run:
    manifest: /srv/app/gates.yaml
    heavy: only
    parallelism: 2

reversibility.notes: It sends a GET or a HEAD, which HTTP defines as safe, and changes nothing a later task could undo.

doc.summary: Checks that a URL answers with the expected status, and optionally body, without ever returning or logging the body.
doc.description: Sends a GET (or a HEAD) to the URL, following at most max_redirects redirects and refusing one from https to http, since the check would then vouch for a page anyone on the path could have served. It fails when the status is not one of status_code, or when the body does not contain body_contains or match body_matches (RE2). The body is read, at most 4 MiB, only to match it: what is returned is the status, the final URL and each redirect (scheme, host and path, never a query or fragment, which can carry a token), the time taken, and the body's size and SHA-256, and a failure names the same. A URL carrying a user name or password is refused. Certificates are verified unless validate_certs is false, which is per task and loud. It only reads, so a check of it is the task itself, and it runs once with no target device.

params.name: url
params.description: The http or https URL to request.

params.name: status_code
params.description: The status, or statuses, that pass.

params.name: body_contains
params.description: Text the body must contain.

params.name: body_matches
params.description: A regular expression (RE2, at most 1024 bytes) the body must match. One of body_contains and body_matches.

params.name: method
params.description: GET, or HEAD for the status alone.

params.name: max_redirects
params.description: How many redirects to follow, 0 to 10. A redirect past them is the answer checked, so max_redirects: 0 with status_code: 301 checks a redirect itself.

params.name: timeout
params.description: Seconds the whole check may take, redirects included.

params.name: validate_certs
params.description: Verify the server's certificate. False is set per task, never by a setting, and is visible in the runbook that sets it.

returns.name: status
returns.description: The final answer's status.

returns.name: final_url
returns.description: The URL that answered last, without query or fragment.

returns.name: redirects
returns.description: Each redirect followed, in order, without query or fragment.

returns.name: elapsed_ms
returns.description: How long the check took, in milliseconds.

returns.name: body_bytes
returns.description: How many bytes of body were read, at most 4 MiB.

returns.name: body_sha256
returns.description: The SHA-256 of the bytes read, in hex.

returns.name: body_over_limit
returns.description: Whether the body was longer than 4 MiB.

returns.name: matched
returns.description: Whether the body matched.

examples.name: The release answers healthy
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Health
  http.check:
    url: https://app.example.com/healthz
    body_contains: "\"status\":\"ok\""

reversibility.notes: One answer has to cover every verb, and no verb can produce an inverse. A read-only request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) changed nothing, so there is nothing to undo. A writing request changed something inside a remote system this platform never observes: it cannot read what the state was before, cannot tell what the call altered, and cannot know which call would put it back, so any inverse would be a guess dressed as an instruction.

doc.summary: Makes an HTTP request and reports its status code and body.
doc.description: Calls a URL from wherever the task runs, not from the target device, and records the status, body and response headers. A response whose status is not one of the expected ones fails the task, after recording what came back, since the body is usually the only thing that explains the failure. Certificates are verified unless a task says otherwise in its own text. Reporting changed follows the verb: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are read-only by HTTP's own definition and report no change, while any other verb reports a change, because what it did to the far side cannot be inspected from here. That is a deliberate difference from ansible.builtin.uri, which never reports changed at all. Four of that module's parameters are absent rather than accepted and ignored: body_format (the body is sent exactly as written, so set Content-Type in headers), return_content (the body is always recorded), follow_redirects (redirects are always followed), and the url_username and url_password pair (a credential belongs in the credential store, not in a runbook file). Only a request in a safe method (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS or TRACE) can be checked, and a check sends it for real, since reading is all it does. Any other method may change something on the server, so such a call is named as unchecked and sends nothing, and check_mode on one is refused when the runbook is validated.

params.name: url
params.description: The URL to call. It must be http or https: any other scheme is refused rather than attempted, since this method speaks one protocol and a file or ftp URL is a mistake in the runbook rather than a request this could make. A path beginning with one / instead calls the target device's own API: it is joined to the base URL of a generic_http device that onboarding proved (HTTPAPICapable), and only such a request carries a credential, the device's own from the credential store, sent as its http_auth property says. It cannot leave that origin: a scheme, a host, a second leading / and a .. segment are refused, a redirect elsewhere is not followed, and the task may set neither Authorization nor Host. It speaks the device's own TLS (its pinned authority, its client certificate, and any weakening its record allows, reported as a warning), so validate_certs false is refused for it.

params.name: method
params.description: The HTTP method. It is upper-cased before being sent, because HTTP method names are case sensitive and a server given get will answer 501 rather than doing what the author meant.

params.name: body
params.description: The request body, sent exactly as written. Set its Content-Type through headers: nothing here inspects the body or guesses a type for it.

params.name: headers
params.description: Request headers as a mapping of name to value. Every value must be text, so a numeric one is quoted in the runbook. A Host header is honored as the request's real Host rather than added as an ordinary header, which is what makes name-based routing testable against an address.

params.name: status_code
params.description: The status code, or codes, that count as success. Anything else fails the task. Written as one number or a list of them, so an endpoint answering 200 or 201 depending on whether it created something can be accepted without a follow-up condition.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long to wait, in seconds, for the whole request including reading the body. Fractions are allowed, unlike Ansible's whole-second version, since a health check with a half-second budget is a real thing to want. Zero and negative values are refused: neither is a wait.

params.name: validate_certs
params.description: Verify the server's TLS certificate. Setting it false accepts any certificate, including one an attacker in the middle presents, so it belongs only on a target you have decided does not need it. There is no setting anywhere that changes the default: turning verification off is written in the task it applies to.

returns.name: status
returns.description: The status code the server answered with, recorded even when it is not one of the expected ones.

returns.name: content
returns.description: The whole response body as text. Held in memory, so this method is for calling an API rather than for fetching a large file: a body over 16 MiB fails the task.

returns.name: headers
returns.description: The response headers, names lower-cased, with a header sent more than once joined by a comma and a space.

returns.name: url
returns.description: The URL the response actually came from, which differs from the one asked for when redirects were followed.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How long the request took, in seconds, with its fraction kept. Ansible reports whole seconds here, which is zero for every call that went well.

returns.name: msg
returns.description: The status line, for example "404 Not Found", for a person reading a run log.

returns.name: json
returns.description: A JSON response body, decoded, so a later task can read one field of it (Ansible uri's own key). Recorded only when the response says its content is JSON (application/json, or a type ending in +json), the body parses as JSON and it is at most 1 MiB; otherwise the key is left out and content still holds the text.

examples.name: Check that a service answers
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the health endpoint
  http.request:
    url: https://api.example.com/healthz
    timeout: 5

examples.name: Post JSON to an API
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Register the release
  http.request:
    url: https://api.example.com/releases
    method: POST
    body: '{"version": "1.4.0"}'
    headers:
      Content-Type: application/json
    status_code:
      - 200
      - 201

examples.name: Call a device's own API with its stored credential
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the device's interfaces
  http.request:
    url: /interfaces

reversibility.notes: It sends a GET or a HEAD, which HTTP defines as safe, and changes nothing a later task could undo.

http.wait.noCheckReason: what a wait waits for is usually an earlier task's change, which a check never makes, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits, from the machine pleiades runs on, until a URL answers with the expected status, and optionally body.
doc.description: Repeats http.check's request and its tests until they pass: the status is one of status_code, and the body contains body_contains or matches body_matches. A refused connection, a timeout or an answer that does not pass all mean not yet. It runs once with no target device, from the machine pleiades runs on, so it waits for a service published there (a container's port on 127.0.0.1) that wait.port, which looks from a device over SSH, cannot see. Each attempt is bounded by 10 seconds or by what is left of the timeout, and running out of time fails the task naming the last answer, or the last error. What it returns is http.check's, never the body: the last answer's status and final URL, how many attempts were made and how long the wait took.
