A URL carrying a user name or password is refused, a redirect from https to http is not followed, and certificates are verified unless validate_certs is false.

params.name: url
params.description: The http or https URL to request.

params.name: status_code
params.description: The status, or statuses, that pass.

params.name: body_contains
params.description: Text the body must contain.

params.name: body_matches
params.description: A regular expression (RE2, at most 1024 bytes) the body must match. One of body_contains and body_matches.

params.name: method
params.description: GET, or HEAD for the status alone.

params.name: max_redirects
params.description: How many redirects to follow, 0 to 10.

params.name: validate_certs
params.description: Verify the server's certificate. False is set per task, never by a setting, and is visible in the runbook that sets it.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait in total before giving up, counted from the start of the task, so the delay comes out of it. Must be more than 0, and at most 86400.

params.name: delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait before the first request. Must be shorter than the timeout, which it is spent out of.

params.name: sleep
params.description: How many seconds to wait between requests. Must be more than 0.

returns.name: status
returns.description: The last answer's status.

returns.name: final_url
returns.description: The URL that answered last, without query or fragment.

returns.name: attempts
returns.description: How many requests were made.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How many whole seconds the task waited, including the delay.

examples.name: Wait for a service this machine runs to answer
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for Batfish's API
  http.wait:
    url: http://127.0.0.1:9996/v2/version
    timeout: 180
    sleep: 3

reversibility.notes: A run that created an absent group emits an identity.group.remove naming it. A run that found the group already present but converged its gid emits an identity.group.modify pinned to the old gid, which is a real, restorable inverse. A run that found the group already at the requested gid emits nothing.

doc.summary: Makes sure a POSIX group exists on the target.
doc.description: Makes sure a group is present on the target, creating it if absent. This is ansible.builtin.group with state=present. Group state is read from getent before anything is sent, so a group already present at the requested gid (or present with none requested) reports no change and no command reaches the device; a group present at a different gid than requested is converged with groupmod rather than recreated.

params.name: name
params.description: The group name to create or converge.

params.name: gid
params.description: The numeric group ID to assign. An existing group with a different gid is converged to this one.

params.name: system
params.description: Create the group as a system group (groupadd -r). Ignored when the group already exists.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The group this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the group before this task and after it, each holding exists and gid. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Create a plain group
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure admins exists
  identity.group.create:
    name: admins

examples.name: Pin a gid
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Create a service group
  identity.group.create:
    name: appsvc
    gid: 5000
    system: true

reversibility.notes: A run that converged the gid emits an identity.group.modify pinned to the old gid, which is a real, restorable inverse. A run that found the gid already matching emits nothing.

doc.summary: Changes the gid of an existing POSIX group on the target.
doc.description: Converges an existing group's gid, refusing outright if the group does not exist rather than creating one (use identity.group.create for that). A POSIX group has no other mutable attribute this platform manages: renaming is not something groupmod supports and ansible.builtin.group does not offer it either, and membership is identity.user.*'s own concern. Group state is read from getent before anything is sent, so a gid already matching what was requested reports no change and no command reaches the device.

params.name: name
params.description: The group to modify. Must already exist.

params.name: gid
params.description: Converge the group to this numeric gid.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The group this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the group before this task and after it, each holding exists and gid.

examples.name: Change a group's gid
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Renumber admins
  identity.group.modify:
    name: admins
    gid: 6000

reversibility.notes: A run that removed a present group emits an identity.group.create pinned to the exact gid this run captured before removing it, which is a real, restorable inverse. A run that found the group already absent emits nothing. What the inverse cannot restore is any user's primary or supplementary membership in the group at the moment it was removed.

doc.summary: Removes a POSIX group from the target.
doc.description: Makes sure a group is absent from the target, removing it if present. This is ansible.builtin.group with state=absent. Group state is read from getent before anything is sent, so a group already absent reports no change and no command reaches the device. groupdel itself refuses to remove a group that is still any user's primary group; that refusal surfaces here as a plain task failure naming what groupdel said, not something this method works around.

params.name: name
params.description: The group name to remove.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The group this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the group before this task and after it. After always reports exists: false on a successful run.

examples.name: Remove a group
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure the old admins group is gone
  identity.group.remove:
    name: admins

reversibility.notes: A run that created an absent account emits an identity.user.remove naming it, which also removes the home directory the run made (none was there before) while that still holds only what useradd copied into it; a home in use since is kept, and the undo says so. A run that found the account already present but converged one or more attributes (uid, group, shell, home or comment) emits an identity.user.modify pinned to exactly the old values of the attributes it changed, which is a real, restorable inverse. A run that found the account already exactly as requested emits nothing. What no inverse here can restore is the account's password, or anything a login shell or profile script did while the account existed.

doc.summary: Makes sure a POSIX user account exists on the target.
doc.description: Makes sure a user account is present on the target, creating it if absent. This is ansible.builtin.user with state=present. Account state is read from getent before anything is sent, so an account already present with every requested attribute already matching reports no change and no command reaches the device; an account present with a different uid, group, shell, home or comment than requested is converged with usermod rather than recreated. Supplementary group membership and the account password are not managed by this method.

params.name: name
params.description: The account name to create or converge.

params.name: uid
params.description: The numeric user ID to assign. An existing account with a different uid is converged to this one.

params.name: group
params.description: The primary group, by name or numeric gid. An existing account with a different primary group is converged to this one.

params.name: shell
params.description: The login shell, such as /bin/bash. An existing account with a different shell is converged to this one.

params.name: home
params.description: The home directory path. An existing account with a different home is converged to this one; its contents are not moved.

params.name: comment
params.description: The GECOS comment field, typically the account's full name.

params.name: create_home
params.description: Create the home directory when the account is created. Ignored when the account already exists.

params.name: system
params.description: Create the account as a system account (useradd -r). Ignored when the account already exists.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The account this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the account before this task and after it, each holding exists, uid, gid, comment, home and shell. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

doc.summary: Changes attributes of an existing POSIX user account on the target.

params.name: name

params.name: uid

params.name: group

params.name: shell

params.name: home

params.description: Converge the account's GECOS comment field.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The account this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the account before this task and after it, each holding exists, uid, gid, comment, home and shell.

reversibility.notes: A run that removed a present account emits an identity.user.create pinned to the exact uid, group, shell, home and comment this run captured before removing it, which is a real, restorable inverse for the account's identity attributes. A run that found the account already absent emits nothing. What the inverse cannot restore is the account's password (never captured by this platform), or the home directory's contents once remove=true has asked userdel to delete them.

doc.summary: Removes a POSIX user account from the target.
doc.description: Makes sure a user account is absent from the target, removing it if present. This is ansible.builtin.user with state=absent. Account state is read from getent before anything is sent, so an account already absent reports no change and no command reaches the device.

params.name: name
params.description: The account name to remove.

params.name: remove
params.description: Also delete the home directory and mail spool (userdel -r). Left false, they are left on disk.

params.name: remove_home_if_unchanged

params.name: created_home
params.description: With remove_home_if_unchanged, the home the account was made with: the home is deleted only while the account's home is still this path, so a home moved since (identity.user.modify) is never judged in its place. identity.user.create's undo sets it.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The account this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What getent reported about the account before this task and after it. After always reports exists: false on a successful run.

examples.name: Remove an account
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure the old deploy account is gone
  identity.user.remove:
    name: deploy

- name: Remove deploy entirely
  identity.user.remove:
    name: deploy

reversibility.notes: It asks Batfish about configurations and changes no device; the snapshot it uploads is removed when the task ends.

doc.summary: Checks configurations against Batfish's model of the network before any of them is applied, and fails closed.
doc.description: Builds a snapshot from each device's whole configuration (config, or src: a file in the project), its secrets masked before anything is sent (equal secrets alike, so key mismatches still show), asks Batfish to parse it, and holds the model to the assertions given: OSPF sessions established, a route present (through the next hops named) or absent, a flow delivered or not and through or around the nodes named, and a node's modelled routes equal to the routes net.frr.facts read from it live. Each scenario forks the snapshot with interfaces or nodes down and holds it to its own assertions, so a link failure is checked before it happens. Its target is the batfish device. FRR configurations go to Batfish in the layout it reads FRR in, with each ip ospf passive moved under router ospf; Cisco IOS ones go as they are. It fails closed: an assertion that does not hold, a file Batfish could not parse, a question it could not answer, a convert error Batfish reports (part of a device missing from the model), or a line it did not recognise that the task does not accept by name with a reason (lines with no meaning of their own, exit, end and !, need none). Recognising a line is not modelling it, so a feature measured to be parsed and then ignored (on Cisco IOS: GLBP, IP SLA, SLA tracking, BFD) is refused the same way until accepted by name: the model cannot predict its failover, and a passing gate must not imply that it did. The result reports three things apart: whether the model parsed (each file's status and every unrecognised line), whether it agrees (each assertion), and what it does not model (the lines accepted). It returns the SHA-256 of each configuration as given, for net.frr.config's expect_sha256, so the change applied is the one checked. It changes nothing on any device; Batfish keeps the snapshot in a network of the run's own, removed when the task ends. A model that agrees is evidence, not proof: rehearse on the same OS image, and verify the change live.

params.name: devices
params.description: Each device's whole configuration: name (the node's name, which a Cisco configuration's hostname must match), format (frr, the default, or cisco_ios), and config (the text, e.g. a registered net.frr.facts result's running_config) or src (a file in the project, read by the command line only).

params.name: assertions
params.description: What must hold of the configurations as given, each one of: ospf_established: true (every OSPF session Batfish finds is established, and there is one); bgp_established: true (the same for BGP); route: {node, prefix, next_hops, protocol}; no_route: {node, prefix}; reach: {from (node or node[interface]), dst (an address), delivered (default true), through (nodes), avoids (nodes), accepted_by (the node that must answer dst, such as an HSRP or VRRP group's elected owner of a virtual address)}; routes_match: {node, routes (net.frr.facts' routes for that node), ignore (prefixes the configurations do not hold, such as a management network)}, comparing connected, static, OSPF, BGP, IS-IS, EIGRP and RIP routes by prefix, protocol and next hop; question: {name (any Batfish question, e.g. hsrpProperties, filterLineReachability), variables, where (column: value), min_rows (default 1), max_rows}, the rows matching where counted.

params.name: scenarios

doc.summary: Runs one show/exec-mode command against a network device's CLI.
doc.description: Opens an interactive session over SSH (or over Telnet, with insecure_telnet) and runs one command, matched against the device's own declared cli_prompt property (a generic Dialect, built by netcli.FromPrompt, with no vendor-specific paging, configuration-mode or error convention of its own). Reports the command's own output, with its echoed input line and the trailing prompt both stripped. A command cannot be inspected, so this reports changed every time it reaches the device without error, the same convention exec.command established: pair it with when/when_or/when_cel when idempotence matters. Refuses outright when the target device's cli_prompt property is unset, rather than guessing at a prompt shape. Because this method has no known paging convention for a generic device, a command whose output is longer than the device's own terminal length can pause on a pager prompt this method cannot answer (verified directly against a real device); each command is bounded to 30 seconds so that failure is a clear, timely error rather than an indefinite hang. Pipe a long-output command through the device's own output filter (e.g. "show running-config | include hostname") to avoid triggering it, or use net.ios.config, whose vendor-specific dialect disables paging for real. A command that asks questions before it finishes is answered from prompts, each answer written in the task, and a question nobody listed can go to a model with ask, which picks one of the task's own choices by id or refuses; expect_disconnect counts the device closing the session after an answer as success. The 30 seconds cover the whole command, its questions included.

params.name: command
params.description: The single CLI line to run, e.g. "show version".

params.name: prompts
params.description: Questions the command may ask, each {match, answer} or {match, refuse: true}. match is RE2 found on the line the device waits on (case-sensitive unless it starts with (?i)); answer is typed and then Enter, "" being Enter alone; refuse closes the session, which abandons the command, and fails the task. The first unanswered entry matching is used and each answers once, so a question the device asks again after its answer fails the task; list it twice to answer it twice. Text is never sent to a question asking for a password, passphrase or secret.

params.name: ask
params.description: A model for questions no prompts entry matches, on the Crawl tier: choices, a list of {id, answer, means} the model picks from by id (it never types its own answer, and may refuse, which fails the task, or say the line was no question); max, how many it may answer (1 to 10, default 3); shape, the RE2 a waiting line must match to be asked about (default: ending in ?, ] or ]:); and ai.chat's own provider, model, residency, prompt or prompt_file (a built-in prompt when neither), signing, review, usage_sink and call options. Its provider is resolved before the device is reached. A held answer fails the task as held, which abandons the command; decided with pleiades ai review, running again reuses the decision for that same question.

params.name: expect_disconnect
params.description: Count the device closing the session after at least one answer as success, which is how a reload ends. A close before any answer still fails.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: Everything the device printed in response to the command, its questions and the echo of each answer included, with the echoed command line and the trailing prompt removed.

returns.name: exchanges
returns.returned: when prompts, ask or expect_disconnect is set
returns.description: Each question the device asked and what was typed: question and answer, with prompt (the entry's index) or, for the model, choice, reason, provider, model, confidence, usage and review.

returns.name: disconnected
returns.returned: when prompts, ask or expect_disconnect is set
returns.description: Whether the device closed the session after an answer (expect_disconnect).

Each line is bounded to 30 seconds for the same reason net.cli.command's own line is: a generic device has no known paging convention, so an unexpectedly long response can pause on a pager prompt this method cannot answer, and a bounded, clear error is preferable to an indefinite hang.

doc.summary: Makes an FRRouting router run exactly the configuration given, and saves what it ran before so the change can be undone.
doc.description: Takes the whole intended configuration (config, or src: a file in the project) and applies only what differs, through FRR's own frr-reload.py. The candidate is first checked with vtysh -m -f, and a line vtysh refuses fails the task before anything reaches the router: frr-reload reads a file vtysh cannot parse as an empty configuration and would delete everything. The difference comes from frr-reload.py --test; an empty one is no change, and a check returns it as the prediction. A real run saves the running configuration to a file on the router (0600, under the connecting account's ~/.pleiades-frr), reloads, confirms the running configuration now matches the candidate, and saves the result beside the backup. Its undo names only that backup, so no configuration text, and no secret in one, reaches the journal; the undo restores exactly the configuration that was running, and refuses when the router no longer runs what this change left, unless its step names force. The undo is recorded before the reload and kept if the reload then fails, since restoring a backup when nothing changed is itself no change. With save, the running configuration is also written to frr.conf, keeping that file's owner and mode, so it survives a restart; the backup then keeps frr.conf as it was too, and the undo puts it back (where there was none, the undo writes the configuration it restores). expect_sha256 refuses a candidate whose bytes are not the ones a model check analysed.

params.name: config
params.description: The whole intended configuration, as frr.conf text. Set config or src, not both. Lines not in it are removed from the running configuration.

params.name: src
params.description: A file in the project directory holding the whole intended configuration, read by the command line; refused on a Walk-tier Runner, where config is the way. Set config or src, not both.

params.name: save
params.description: Also write the configuration to frr.conf (keeping that file's owner and mode), so it survives a restart. The undo puts frr.conf back as it was, or, where there was none, writes the configuration it restores.

params.name: expect_sha256
params.description: Refuse unless the candidate's SHA-256 is this, in hex: the digest net.batfish.check returned for the bytes it analysed, so the change applied is the change checked.

params.name: restore
params.description: Restore the configuration this method saved before an earlier change, by the path its undo recorded. Set by an undo; with restore, config and src are not given.

params.name: force
params.description: With restore, restore even though the router no longer runs what the earlier change left (someone changed it since).

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: lines_added
returns.description: The configuration lines frr-reload added, as it reported them.

returns.name: lines_deleted
returns.description: The configuration lines frr-reload removed.

returns.name: sha256
returns.description: The SHA-256 of the configuration applied, in hex.

returns.name: backup
returns.description: The path of the running configuration saved before the change, on the router.

returns.name: inverse
returns.description: The undo: this method with restore set to backup (and save when the change saved), held whole in the journal.

doc.summary: Applies configuration lines to a Cisco IOS device, keeping a checkpoint of the configuration before them so the change can be undone exactly.
doc.description: Opens an interactive session over SSH (or over Telnet, with insecure_telnet), using netcli.IOS's own paging, configuration-mode and error conventions, and applies lines as a batch: "configure terminal", each line in order, then "end". Aborts on the first line the device rejects (an IOS "% ..." error), still leaving configuration mode before returning that error. Before the lines, it copies the running configuration to a checkpoint file on the device (its default writable disk or flash, such as unix: or flash:), and after them the device's own show archive config differences says what changed: no difference reports unchanged and deletes the checkpoint, so a second run of the same lines changes nothing. A change copies the configuration it left to a second checkpoint and records its undo as net.ios.replace naming both files, which returns the device exactly to the first (configure replace) and refuses if the device no longer matches the second. The files stay on the device until that undo runs. A device with no writable file system, or no configure replace, records no undo, with a warning: the configuration lines that would undo the change, written from its configuration read before and after it (the negation of each added line, each removed line put back), are reported under undo_lines, masked, for the task's rollback: list, since lines read off a device never reach the journal. A change inside an access list, a banner or a certificate has no such lines. checkpoint: false does the same on any device. The differences this reports are masked as net.batfish.check masks a candidate.

params.name: lines
params.description: The configuration lines to apply, in order, WITHOUT "configure terminal" or "end": this method supplies both itself.

params.name: checkpoint
params.description: Keep a checkpoint of the running configuration on the device before the change, which its undo returns to exactly. false records no undo, and reports the lines that would undo the change for the task's rollback: list.

params.name: backup
params.description: Capture the device's running-config with "show running-config" before applying any line, recorded under the backup stat.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: checkpoint
returns.returned: when a checkpoint was kept and the lines changed the configuration
returns.description: The checkpoint file on the device holding the configuration before the change, which the undo returns to.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: The device's own contextual differences the change made (+ added, - removed), masked.

returns.name: undo_lines
returns.returned: when no checkpoint was kept and the lines changed the configuration
returns.description: The configuration lines that would undo the change, masked; copy them into the task's rollback: list, putting each masked secret back.

returns.name: backup
returns.description: The device's full running-config, captured immediately before this task's own lines were applied. Not sanitized: it genuinely contains this device's own enable secret, enable password, local user password hashes, and any TACACS+/RADIUS shared key in whatever strength (or weakness -- IOS's own "type 7" is trivially reversible) encoding the device applies. Mask it with "register_mask: backup" on this task.

examples.name: Create a loopback interface, undoable by pleiades rollback
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Add a loopback interface
  net.ios.config:
    lines:
      - interface Loopback0
      - description managed by pleiades

reversibility.notes: A read-only fact gatherer changes nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Gathers structured facts from a Cisco IOS device over its CLI.
doc.description: Closes a real gap: facts.gather requires FactGathererCapable, which no Cisco device type declares, so before this method a Cisco device could be commanded and configured but never described. Opens an interactive PTY session over SSH using netcli.IOS's own paging and prompt conventions, runs the read-only show commands the requested subsets need, and emits what it parses through EmitFact rather than SetStat, the same choice facts.gather and net.catalyst.device_facts both make: a fact is long-lived drift data worth comparing across weeks, and a software version recorded as a stat answers nothing next month. Every parser in this method was written against output captured from a real Cisco IOS XE device rather than from documentation or memory. A field the device does not report is left out entirely rather than emitted as an empty string, so a condition can tell "this device does not say" from "this device says nothing". Nothing is changed, so this always reports no change. Two of cisco.ios.ios_facts's own subsets are deliberately absent rather than accepted and ignored: config, because net.ios.config's own backup parameter already captures a running-config and doing it twice invites two answers, and hardware, because the memory and flash figures IOS reports vary enough by platform that parsing them generically would be a guess.

params.name: gather_subset
params.description: Which subsets to gather: "min" (hostname, version, model, serial number, image, uptime, from "show version" and "show inventory"), "interfaces" (from "show ip interface brief"), or "all" for both. An unrecognized subset is refused rather than skipped.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: ansible_net_hostname
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: The device's own hostname, read from the "<hostname> uptime is ..." line of "show version".

returns.name: ansible_net_version
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: The IOS XE version string, e.g. "17.15.04c".

returns.name: ansible_net_model
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: The platform model, e.g. "C8000V".

returns.name: ansible_net_serialnum
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: The chassis serial number, preferring "show inventory"'s Chassis SN and falling back to "show version"'s Processor board ID.

returns.name: ansible_net_image
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: The running system image file, e.g. "bootflash:packages.conf".

returns.name: ansible_net_uptime
returns.returned: when the min subset is gathered and the device reports it
returns.description: Uptime exactly as the device words it, e.g. "1 hour, 32 minutes". Not converted to seconds: IOS reports a rounded phrase, and parsing it into a precise number would invent precision the device never gave.

returns.name: ansible_net_interfaces
returns.returned: when the interfaces subset is gathered
returns.description: One entry per interface: name, ip_address (omitted when the device says "unassigned"), status, and protocol. Status is taken whole, so "administratively down" is reported as written rather than truncated at the first space.

returns.name: ansible_net_gather_subset
returns.description: The subsets actually gathered, after "all" is expanded.

examples.name: Gather a device's identity before deciding anything
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Learn what this router is
  net.ios.facts:
  register: device

examples.name: Gather interfaces as well
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Learn the interface list too
  net.ios.facts:
    gather_subset:
      - all

reversibility.notes: It runs one show command and changes nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Runs a show command on a Cisco IOS or IOS XE device and returns its output parsed into Genie's schema.
doc.description: Runs one show command over the same session net.ios.command opens and parses its output with a parser ported from Cisco's Genie (genieparser, Apache License 2.0), returning the same nested structure Genie returns for that command, so Genie's own schema documentation describes the result and a later task can compare two reads field by field, such as the state before a change and after its rollback. Each parser is held to every one of genieparser's own recorded device outputs and expected results for the command forms it covers. Output in which the parser finds nothing (no OSPF neighbors yet) is an empty result with empty true, not a failure, so a before and after can compare it; a command the device refuses (% BGP not active) fails the task. A command no parser covers is refused before the device is reached, naming the commands that are covered. It only reads, so it reports unchanged, and a check runs it as a real run does.

params.name: command
params.description: The show command to run and parse, one of the commands a parser covers (pleiades doc net.ios.parse lists them), for example "show ip interface brief" or "show ip route". IOS's abbreviations are not accepted: write the command in full.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: parsed
returns.description: The command's output in Genie's schema for it: for show ip interface brief, interface, keyed by interface name, each with ip_address, interface_is_ok, method, status and protocol.

returns.name: parser
returns.description: The Genie parser class whose port parsed it, such as ShowIpInterfaceBrief.

returns.name: empty
returns.description: Whether the parser found nothing in the output, parsed then being empty.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: The command's output as the device printed it, except that the secrets in show archive config differences (a password, secret, key or SNMP community) are masked, as net.ios.replace masks them, before it is parsed or recorded.

examples.name: Read the interfaces before a change, to compare after its rollback
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the interfaces
  net.ios.parse:
    command: show ip interface brief
  register: interfaces_before

reversibility.notes: A ping is read-only: it sends echoes and reports what came back, changing nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Runs a ping from a Cisco IOS device and reports the result.
doc.description: Answers a different question from net.ssh.ping, and the difference is the point: net.ssh.ping proves this platform can reach the device, while this method proves the DEVICE can reach somewhere else, which is the question that actually matters when a routing or ACL change is under review. Runs IOS's own ping from an interactive PTY session and parses its "Success rate is N percent (rx/tx)" line, including the trailing "round-trip min/avg/max = a/b/c ms" clause that IOS omits entirely when nothing came back. Nothing is changed on the device, so this always reports no change. Use state to turn the result into a gate: state present (the default) fails the task when every packet is lost, and state absent fails it when anything answers, so a runbook can assert reachability or its absence without a separate condition.

params.name: dest
params.description: The address or hostname to ping from the device.

params.name: count
params.description: How many echoes to send, passed to IOS as "repeat".

params.name: source
params.description: Source address or interface for the ping, passed to IOS as "source".

params.name: vrf
params.description: VRF to ping from, passed to IOS as "vrf".

params.name: state
params.description: "present" fails the task if the destination is unreachable (0 percent success); "absent" fails it if the destination answers at all. Set neither expectation by using a when condition on the returned facts instead.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: packet_loss
returns.description: Percentage of packets lost, as a string with a trailing percent sign, e.g. "0%".

returns.name: packets_tx
returns.description: How many echoes the device sent.

returns.name: packets_rx
returns.description: How many replies the device received.

returns.name: rtt
returns.returned: when at least one packet returned
returns.description: Round-trip times in milliseconds: min, avg, max. Absent entirely when every packet was lost, because IOS prints no round-trip clause in that case.

examples.name: Assert the device can still reach its gateway
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Confirm the upstream gateway answers
  net.ios.ping:
    dest: 192.0.2.1

examples.name: Record reachability without failing the run
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Measure reachability to a peer
  net.ios.ping:
    dest: 198.51.100.10
    count: 10
    state: absent
  register: peer

reversibility.notes: It is the undo net.ios.config records; what it removes is the change that checkpoint was kept before, which running that change again puts back.

doc.summary: Replaces a Cisco IOS device's running configuration with a checkpoint file on the device.
doc.description: Runs IOS's configure replace with a checkpoint file the device holds (net.ios.config writes one before each change and records this method as its undo), so the device itself puts back exactly the configuration the checkpoint holds: lines a change added are removed and lines it replaced or removed come back, with no inverse line written by anyone. When expect names a second checkpoint (the one net.ios.config writes after its change), the device must still match it, by the device's own show archive config differences, or this refuses before replacing anything, unless force is true: configure replace returns the whole configuration to the checkpoint, so a change someone made since would be undone with it. After the replace, the device must report no differences from the checkpoint, or the task fails. The checkpoint files net.ios.config made (named pleiades-<id>.cfg) are deleted afterwards unless keep is true; any other file, such as nvram:startup-config or a configuration kept on flash:, is never deleted. A check reports what the replace would change, from the same comparison, and changes nothing. The configuration lines this reports are masked as net.batfish.check masks a candidate: a password, secret or key is never shown.

params.name: checkpoint
params.description: The checkpoint to return to, a file on the device such as unix:pleiades-3f2a.cfg or flash:pleiades-3f2a.cfg.

params.name: expect
params.description: A checkpoint the running configuration must still match before anything is replaced, refusing otherwise: the configuration as the change left it.

params.name: force
params.description: Replace even when the running configuration no longer matches expect, undoing whatever changed since along with the change.

params.name: keep
params.description: Keep the checkpoint files net.ios.config made on the device after a replace that leaves no differences, rather than deleting them. A file it did not make is never deleted.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: The device's own contextual differences between the running configuration and the checkpoint before the replace, masked: what the replace changes, or would change in a check.

examples.name: Return a device to a checkpoint a change left
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Undo the loopback change
  net.ios.replace:
    checkpoint: unix:pleiades-3f2a.cfg
    expect: unix:pleiades-3f2a-after.cfg

reversibility.notes: Saving overwrites startup-config with running-config, and the device keeps no copy of what startup-config held beforehand, so this platform cannot reconstruct an inverse. Capture the prior configuration first (net.ios.config's backup parameter) if a rollback target is needed.

doc.summary: Saves a Cisco IOS device's running configuration to startup.
doc.description: Runs IOS's "write memory", copying running-config over startup-config so the current configuration survives a reload. This is the step that makes every earlier net.ios.config task permanent, and it is deliberately a separate method rather than a parameter on net.ios.config: persisting configuration is a decision about blast radius, not a detail of applying a line, and a runbook that applies several changes should be able to decide once, at the end, whether any of them should outlive the next reload. Reports changed whenever the save completes, since IOS gives no way to know whether startup-config already matched. Aborts on a real IOS "% ..." error rather than reporting a save that did not happen. A check opens the session a real run opens and predicts the change, since a save always reports one, without sending write memory.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

params.name: insecure_telnet
params.description: Reach a device that has no SSH over bare Telnet, answering its login with the task's credential. Telnet carries everything, the login included, in cleartext, so set this only for a device on a network you trust.

returns.name: stdout
returns.description: Whatever the device printed in response to "write memory", typically a "Building configuration..." line followed by "[OK]".

examples.name: Persist a change after verifying it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Save the running configuration
  net.ios.save:

doc.summary: Applies configuration to a Juniper Junos device.

reversibility.notes: An edit-config merge has no reliable inverse: deleting what was added is not the same as restoring what was replaced, and this method cannot know which of the two a given element did. Set backup: true to capture the prior configuration for a human-directed rollback. Note that rollback-on-error, which this method requests whenever the device supports it, covers a DIFFERENT case: it undoes a partially applied edit that the device itself rejected, not one that succeeded and was later regretted.

net.netconf.config.noCheckReason: only applying the document says what the device makes of it: the running datastore has no staging area, and a check through the candidate datastore would stage the document on the device, which a check promises not to do

doc.summary: Applies a configuration document to a device over NETCONF, with an optional pre-change backup.
doc.description: Opens an RFC 6241 NETCONF session over the SSH "netconf" subsystem and applies content to the chosen datastore with edit-config. Parameter names are ansible.netcommon.netconf_config's own, with its target parameter under its own alias, datastore, since target names the device a task runs on. The session negotiates RFC 6242 chunked framing whenever the device offers base:1.1, and requests rollback-on-error whenever the device advertises it, so a rejected document leaves the device unchanged rather than half configured; that matters most on a device offering only writable-running, which is what Cisco IOS XE offers, because such a device has no staging area and every element lands on the live configuration as it is applied. A datastore the device never advertised support for is refused when the session opens rather than at the first write, naming the missing capability. Unlike the net.cli.* and net.ios.config methods, a rejected element comes back as a structured error carrying the device's own error-tag and the XPath of the element it objected to. Reports changed whenever the document reaches the device and the device answers ok.

params.name: content
params.description: The configuration document to apply, as the XML that goes inside edit-config's <config> element. Per-element operations are expressed the standard way, with an nc:operation attribute; pair that with default_operation: none so the device changes only what the document explicitly names.

params.name: datastore
params.description: The datastore to configure: running, candidate or startup. A datastore the device does not advertise support for is refused before anything is applied. Cisco IOS XE offers only running.

params.name: default_operation
params.description: What the device does with elements carrying no explicit operation attribute: merge, replace or none. RFC 6241 defines no "delete" here; express a delete with an nc:operation attribute in content.

params.name: error_option
params.default: rollback-on-error when the device supports it, otherwise the device's own stop-on-error default
params.description: How the device handles a rejected element: stop-on-error, continue-on-error or rollback-on-error. Left unset this method asks for rollback-on-error whenever the device advertises the capability, because stop-on-error leaves a rejected document half applied.

params.name: lock
params.description: Whether to lock the datastore for the duration: never, always, or if_supported. Locking prevents another client changing the datastore mid-edit; it also blocks every other client, which matters on a shared device.

params.name: commit
params.description: Commit after a successful edit. Only meaningful when datastore is candidate, since a running-datastore edit is already live; ignored otherwise.

params.name: backup
params.description: Capture the datastore's full contents with get-config before applying anything, recorded under the backup stat.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: backup
returns.description: The datastore's full contents as XML, captured immediately before this task's own document was applied. Not sanitized: a device's configuration genuinely contains its enable secret, local user password hashes, and any TACACS+/RADIUS shared key, in whatever strength of encoding the device applies. Mask it with "register_mask: backup" on this task.

examples.name: Set a device's hostname over NETCONF
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Set the hostname
  net.netconf.config:
    content: |
      <native xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-native">
        <hostname>edge-01</hostname>
      </native>
    backup: true
  register_mask: backup

examples.name: Remove an interface, changing nothing else
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remove the loopback
  net.netconf.config:
    default_operation: none
    content: |
      <native xmlns="http://cisco.com/ns/yang/Cisco-IOS-XE-native">
        <interface>
          <Loopback xmlns:nc="urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:netconf:base:1.0" nc:operation="delete">
            <name>8990</name>
          </Loopback>
        </interface>
      </native>

reversibility.notes: Its undo puts back what it found: a created bridge is removed, a changed datapath set back, and a removed bridge recreated without its ports or settings such as a fail mode or a controller, which that undo says by being partial.

doc.summary: Makes an Open vSwitch bridge exist with the datapath given, or not exist.
doc.description: Reads the bridge through ovs-vsctl and changes only what differs. Its undo puts back what it found: a bridge it created is removed, a datapath it changed is set back. Removing a bridge also removes its ports, which its undo does not recreate, so that undo is partial and says so.

params.name: name
params.description: The bridge.

params.name: state
params.description: present or absent.

params.name: datapath_type
params.description: system (the kernel datapath) or netdev (userspace). Left unset, an existing bridge keeps its own and a new one gets Open vSwitch's default.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: exists
returns.description: Whether the bridge exists now.

returns.name: datapath_type
returns.description: Its datapath now.

returns.name: inverse
returns.description: The undo.

examples.name: A userspace bridge
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: br0 exists
  net.ovs.bridge:
    name: br0
    datapath_type: netdev

reversibility.notes: Its undo puts back what it found: an added port is removed, a removed one added back on its bridge with its tag (partial when it carried more, such as an interface type or trunks), a moved one moved back, and a changed tag set back.

doc.summary: Makes a port exist on an Open vSwitch bridge with the VLAN tag given, or not exist.
doc.description: Reads the port through ovs-vsctl and changes only what differs. Its undo puts back what it found: a port it added is removed, one it removed is added back on the bridge it was on, and a tag it changed is set back.

params.name: bridge
params.description: The bridge the port belongs on.

params.name: name
params.description: The port, usually an interface name (eth1).

params.name: state
params.description: present or absent.

params.name: tag
params.description: An access VLAN, 1 to 4094; 0 removes the tag. Left unset, an existing port keeps its own.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: exists
returns.description: Whether the port exists now.

returns.name: tag
returns.description: Its access VLAN now, 0 for none.

returns.name: inverse
returns.description: The undo.

examples.name: A port on br0
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: h1's port is on br0
  net.ovs.port:
    bridge: br0
    name: eth2

reversibility.notes: This method opens a connection and echoes a value back. It changes nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo; that is the same fact that makes it report changed: false.

doc.summary: Opens a real SSH connection to the target and echoes a value back, to prove reachability.
doc.description: Dials the device's SSHTransportCapable host and port, authenticates with the credential the Controller attached to this dispatch, and runs a trivial, read-only remote command that echoes params.data (default "pong") back. Never reports changed: a connectivity check does not alter device state.

returns.name: reply
returns.description: The trimmed value the remote command echoed back.

examples.name: Check a device is reachable over SSH
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Ping the device
  net.ssh.ping:
  register: reachability

reversibility.notes: It sends probes and reads their answers, changing nothing.

doc.summary: Traces the path to an address from a Linux device or a container on a container host, and fails when it is not the path expected.
doc.description: Runs tracepath, which needs no raw socket and so no privilege, and returns each hop's address. Without container it runs on the device, a Linux machine reached over SSH. With container it runs inside that container on the device, a container host, through the engine's own exec as container.exec does, so a lab host with no SSH of its own (a containerlab end host) can be traced from; the container needs tracepath (iputils) and /bin/sh. pleiades validate refuses a call whose device cannot take the shape it chose: container on a device that is not a container host, or none on one that is not a Linux SSH device. With expect, it fails the task when the destination was not reached, or a hop named in includes is missing, or one named in avoids is on the path. It changes nothing.

params.name: dest
params.description: The address to trace to.

params.name: max_hops
params.description: The most hops to try.

params.name: expect
params.description: reached (bool), includes (list of addresses that must be hops) and avoids (list that must not be).

params.name: container
params.description: Trace from this container on the device, a container host, rather than from the device itself. The device then needs a container engine, not SSH and Linux. An empty value is refused rather than read as none: leave container out to trace from the device.

params.name: engine
params.description: With container, the engine on a device that runs both Docker and Podman: docker or podman. Never inferred.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: hops
returns.description: Each hop's address, in order, the destination last when reached.

returns.name: reached
returns.description: Whether the destination answered.

examples.name: Expect a path through r2
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: h1's LAN reaches h2 through r2
  net.trace:
    dest: 10.3.3.10
    expect:
      reached: true
      includes: [10.0.12.1]

examples.name: Trace from a lab host container
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: h1 reaches h2 through r1
  net.trace:
    target: dockerhost
    container: clab-routing-h1
    dest: 10.3.3.10
    expect:
      reached: true
      includes: [10.1.1.1]

reversibility.notes: A run that installed an absent package emits a pkg.apt.remove naming it and the packages the install pulled in with it (dependencies), which the remove takes too while nothing else needs them and removing them takes nothing else with them; any it keeps it names. An install that pulled in more than 128 packages, or whose installed set could not be read afterwards, names the package alone and says so, leaving the rest to apt-get autoremove. A run that found it already present, even at a different version than requested, emits nothing: reinstalling over an existing package is not something removing it would undo correctly, since the version that was already there before this task ran would be lost along with the one this task left. What the inverse cannot restore is anything the package's install scripts did: a service they started, a user they created, a config file they wrote outside dpkg's own tracking.

doc.summary: Makes sure a package is installed via APT.
doc.description: Makes sure a package is present on a Debian-family host, installing it if it is absent. This is ansible.builtin.apt with state=present. Installed state is read from dpkg before anything is sent, so a package that is already present at the requested version (or present at any version, when none is requested) reports no change and no command reaches the device. version pins to an exact version string, the same way apt-get install name=version does; leave it unset to mean whatever apt-get would install unpinned.

params.name: name
params.description: The APT package name to install, such as curl or nginx.

params.name: version
params.description: Install exactly this version rather than whatever is current. A package already installed at a different version is upgraded or downgraded to match.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The package this task acted on.

returns.name: version
returns.description: The version left installed after this task.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What dpkg reported about the package before this task and after it, each holding installed and version. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Install a package
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure curl is installed
  pkg.apt.install:
    name: curl

examples.name: Pin an exact version
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install a specific nginx build
  pkg.apt.install:
    name: nginx
    version: 1.24.0-2ubuntu7

reversibility.notes: A run that removed a present package emits a pkg.apt.install pinned to the exact version this run captured before removing it, which is a real, restorable inverse: reinstalling that version undoes exactly what this run did to the package database. A run that found the package already absent emits nothing. Reinstalling brings back the dependencies it removed with the package, at whatever version APT then picks. What the inverse cannot restore is anything the removal's own maintainer scripts did beyond deleting the package's files.

doc.summary: Removes a package via APT.
doc.description: Makes sure a package is absent from a Debian-family host, removing it if it is present. This is ansible.builtin.apt with state=absent. Installed state is read from dpkg before anything is sent, so a package that is already absent reports no change and no command reaches the device. This removes the package but does not purge it (apt-get remove, not apt-get purge), so its configuration files are left on disk; there is no separate purge parameter today.

params.name: name
params.description: The APT package name to remove.

params.name: dependencies
params.description: Packages installing this one pulled in, as pkg.apt.install's undo names them. Each is removed with the package only while it is still installed, APT would remove it as no longer needed, and removing them takes nothing else with them; any other is kept and named in a warning.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The package this task acted on.

returns.name: version
returns.description: Always empty after a successful run: a removed package has no installed version, and a package that was already absent had none either.

returns.name: dependencies_removed
returns.returned: when dependencies names one the run removes
returns.description: The dependencies removed with the package, or that a check predicts would be.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What dpkg reported about the package before this task and after it, each holding installed and version.

examples.name: Remove a package
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure telnet is not installed
  pkg.apt.remove:
    name: telnet

reversibility.notes: Downgrading a package is not something apt-get reliably supports once the previous version has left the local cache and the repository's own metadata (a mirror generally keeps only the latest build of a package), so no safe inverse can be promised here. This mirrors exec.command's own reasoning for why it cannot be undone: the platform does not control whether the information an undo would need still exists anywhere reachable.

doc.summary: Makes sure a package is at its newest available version via APT.
doc.description: Makes sure one named package is at the newest version APT knows about, upgrading it if a newer one is available. This is ansible.builtin.apt with state=latest for a single package, not apt-get upgrade or apt-get dist-upgrade: it never touches any package other than the one named. A package that is absent is installed fresh, since there is no "current" version to upgrade from. A package that is already at the newest candidate version reports no change and no command reaches the device.

params.name: name
params.description: The APT package to keep current.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The package this task acted on.

returns.name: version
returns.description: The version left installed after this task.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What dpkg reported about the package before this task and after it, each holding installed and version.

examples.name: Keep a package at its newest available version
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Keep openssl current
  pkg.apt.upgrade:
    name: openssl

reversibility.notes: A run that installed an absent package emits a pkg.dnf.remove naming it. A run that found it already present, even at a different version than requested, emits nothing, for the same reason pkg.apt.install's inverse does not fire on a version change: the version already there before this task ran is gone the moment dnf replaces it, so removing afterward would not restore it. What the inverse cannot restore is anything the package's scriptlets did beyond placing its own files.

returns.name: diff

reversibility.notes: The inverse is whatever the concrete method records, so on an APT host a run that installed an absent package emits a pkg.apt.remove and a run that found it already present emits nothing. The instruction names the concrete method rather than pkg.remove, which is deliberate: by the time an undo runs, the device that was resolved is the device that must be undone.

doc.summary: Makes sure a package is present, whichever package manager the device runs.
doc.description: Makes sure a package is installed, without caring which package manager the device uses. This is ansible.builtin.package with state=present: it resolves the device's package manager and hands the call to that manager's concrete method, so on an APT host it runs pkg.apt.install and behaves exactly as that method does, including reporting no change when the package is already present at the requested version. Use the concrete method instead when a runbook is written for one platform and should say so.

params.name: name
params.description: The package to act on. This is passed straight through to the concrete method for the device's package manager, so it means whatever that manager means by a package name: an APT package name on a Debian-family host, an RPM package name on a Red Hat-family one.

params.name: version
params.description: Pin to this exact version instead of whatever the package manager considers current. Passed straight through to the concrete method; leave unset to mean "whatever version is current."

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The package this task acted on, as recorded by the concrete method that ran.

returns.name: version
returns.description: The version left installed after this task, empty when the package is absent afterward. The exact value comes from the concrete method that ran.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the package manager reported before this task and after it. The exact keys come from the concrete method that ran, since what there is to say about a package differs between package managers.
