reversibility.notes: It changes nothing on the device: it closes the platform's own connection, and the next task opens a new one, so the device is as it would have been had the task never run and there is nothing to undo.

doc.summary: Closes the SSH connection kept open to the device, so its next task logs in again.
doc.description: A run keeps one SSH connection per device open between tasks unless persist_connections is turned off. A login made before a change to the account it logs in as does not see that change: a group the account was just added to, a new shell, a changed limit. The identity methods close the connection themselves after they run, so this is for the change they cannot see, such as a group membership edited by exec.command. It is Ansible's meta: reset_connection, and migrate-playbook converts that to it. It touches nothing on the device, so it never reports changed, and a check runs it as it is. Where connections do not persist it does nothing, since every task already logs in afresh.

examples.name: Pick up a group membership in the next task
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Add deploy to the docker group
  exec.command:
    cmd: usermod -aG docker deploy
- name: Log in again, so the new group applies
  pleiades.builtin.connection.reset: {}
- name: Use docker as deploy
  exec.command:
    cmd: docker ps

reversibility.notes: It overwrites a file in the project, whose earlier content is never journaled: the journal keeps names and counts, never file content. The project is the author's own working copy, kept under version control, which is where an earlier version comes back from.

doc.summary: Writes text a run produced, such as a router's running configuration, to a file in the project.
doc.description: Writes content to path, a file in the project directory, so a value a task read (a registered result's running_config) can be kept, edited and used as a candidate: net.frr.config's src and net.batfish.check's src read such a file. The path is held to the rules a method reading the project is held to: relative, never leaving the project, never through a symbolic link, never into the project's .pleiades directory (matched by the directory itself, not only its name), and a regular file or none yet. It also never replaces the project's inventory (inventory.yaml and its generated state file), or an external Collections directory or anything in one (its programs and its approval list). The path is the author's choice: an expression in it may read only vars, never a registered result, so a device's output cannot choose which file is replaced. A missing directory on the way is created inside the project. The file is written whole to a temporary file beside it and renamed over it, so it is never seen half written, and the task reports changed only when the bytes or the mode differ. A check reads the file and predicts the same answer. It runs on the command line only (pleiades run and adhoc), which holds the project; a Walk-tier Runner refuses it. It acts on no device and needs no hosts. A configuration read by net.frr.facts or net.ios.* is masked: each secret in it is a pleiades-masked- placeholder, and net.frr.config refuses a candidate holding one, so put each secret back before applying the file. It cannot be undone by a rollback: the file's earlier content is never journaled, since the project is the author's working copy, kept under version control.

params.name: path
params.description: The file to write, a slash-separated path relative to the project directory, such as configs/r3.running.frr.conf. An expression in it may read only vars, such as configs/{{ vars.site }}.conf, never nodes, result or error.

params.name: content
params.description: The text to write, usually rendered from a registered result, such as "{{ result.r3.running_config }}". An empty string writes an empty file.

params.name: mode
params.description: The file's permission bits as a quoted octal string, such as "0640". Only the owner can read the default, since a configuration can hold more than its masked secrets. An execute bit is refused: the file holds text a run read, which is never made a program.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file written, as given.

returns.name: sha256
returns.description: The SHA-256 of the content, in hex: the digest net.batfish.check reports for the same bytes.

returns.name: size
returns.description: The content's length in bytes.

examples.name: Keep r3's running configuration as a candidate file
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read r3 as it runs
  net.frr.facts:
    target: r3
    include_config: true
  register: r3
- name: Keep it in the project, to edit into a candidate
  pleiades.builtin.project.write:
    path: configs/r3.running.frr.conf
    content: "{{ result.r3.running_config }}"

reversibility.notes: This method only observes: it opens a TCP connection from the device and reports whether it succeeded, so the device is in exactly the state it would have been in had the task never run. There is nothing to undo, and an inverse that waited again would be work the forward run never did.

pleiades.builtin.wait.port.noCheckReason: what a wait waits for is usually an earlier task's change, which a check never makes, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits for a TCP port on the target to start (or stop) accepting connections.
doc.description: Holds the runbook until a TCP port accepts a connection, or until it stops accepting one. The check runs ON THE DEVICE, over the SSH connection the task already holds, which is where Ansible's wait_for runs it and is the only place it answers the useful question: a service bound to 127.0.0.1 is invisible from the runner, and a firewall between the runner and the device would report on the path rather than on the service. Running there costs a prerequisite, stated rather than assumed: the device needs python3 or bash, checked once before polling starts and refused by name when neither is present. python3 is preferred because its exit status is this method's own to define; bash is the fallback because it needs no package installed, using its /dev/tcp redirection, and a bash built without that feature is detected and reported rather than mistaken for a closed port. nc is deliberately not used: its flags and exit statuses differ between the openbsd, traditional and busybox builds, so a wrong answer from it could not be told apart from a real one. Never reports changed: waiting observes, it does not act.

params.name: port
params.description: The TCP port to wait on, 1 to 65535. Write it unquoted: a quoted "8080" is text rather than a number and is refused by name.

params.name: host
params.description: The address to connect to, resolved and dialed ON THE DEVICE. The default is loopback, which means the device itself, and is what makes this method see a service bound only to 127.0.0.1.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait in total before giving up, at most 86400. Measured from the start of the task, so delay, the SSH connection and the tool check all come out of this budget, exactly as Ansible measures it. Running out is an error, not a quiet pass.

params.name: delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait before the first check, at most 86400. Useful when a service is known to accept connections briefly before it is really ready.

params.name: sleep
params.description: How many seconds to wait between checks, at least 1 and at most 86400. The sleep happens on the runner, not on the device, so it costs the device nothing. Zero is refused because it would open SSH sessions in a tight loop.

params.name: state
params.description: Wait for the port to start accepting connections, or to stop. Ansible's present and absent describe a path and its drained describes connection counts, so all three are refused here rather than silently read as started.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: Whole seconds spent waiting, including the delay. Recorded on a timeout too, so a failed task still says how long it held.

returns.name: port
returns.description: The port that was waited on.

returns.name: host
returns.description: The address that was dialed from the device, filled in with the default when the task did not name one.

returns.name: state
returns.description: The state that was waited for, either started or stopped.

examples.name: Wait for a database to come back after a restart
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for postgres to accept connections
  pleiades.builtin.wait.port:
    port: 5432
    timeout: 120

examples.name: Wait for a port to be released before rebinding it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the old listener to go away
  pleiades.builtin.wait.port:
    port: 8080
    state: stopped
    timeout: 60

examples.name: Give a service a head start, then poll slowly
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the API on its private address
  pleiades.builtin.wait.port:
    host: 10.0.0.7
    port: 443
    delay: 10
    sleep: 5

reversibility.notes: Its undo removes the directory it created; it never writes into an existing one, so nothing else is lost.

doc.summary: Writes an SPDX 2.3 SBOM of an image archive or a directory, held to the NTIA minimum elements, with its SHA256SUMS.
doc.description: Runs Syft over an image archive or a directory on the device with no network, names the SBOM's subject with the task's name and version, records the task's supplier on the subject alone (never on a dependency, whose supplier the operator does not speak for), and holds the result to the NTIA minimum elements: the document's author, timestamp and namespace, a subject it describes that is a package it holds, and every component's name, version, purl or CPE and a dependency relationship. An SBOM holding no component but its subject fails unless allow_empty. A dependency's supplier, which a generator rarely knows, is counted and warned about, and fails the task only with strict_suppliers. The SBOM (sbom.spdx.json) and a SHA256SUMS in sha256sum's format are written into dest, a new directory, so sha256sum -c verifies it anywhere; the undo removes the directory. A check generates and validates the SBOM as a run does, and writes and pulls nothing: without the scanner's image, the check says it cannot check. The scanner runs in a fresh container on the device's own engine, from an image pinned here by its multi-platform index digest, so nothing is installed on the device and every run uses the scanner this release was tested with; what it scans is mounted read-only, its root is read-only, it runs with no-new-privileges and is removed afterwards. Paths are the engine host's, which is the device's for an engine reached over SSH or its local socket.

params.name: dir
params.description: A directory on the device to describe. One of dir and image_archive.

params.name: image_archive
params.description: An image archive on the device, as docker save or podman save writes one.

params.name: dest
params.description: The directory to write, which must not exist, in one that does.

params.name: name
params.description: The subject's name: what is being shipped.

params.name: version
params.description: The subject's version.

params.name: supplier
params.description: Who supplies the subject, as SPDX writes it: "Organization: name" or "Person: name".

params.name: strict_suppliers
params.description: Fail when a dependency has no supplier, rather than counting it.

params.name: allow_empty
params.description: Write, with a warning, an SBOM holding no component but its subject. Without it that fails the task, since an SBOM of nothing (a wrong path, or files Syft could not read) meets every element and says nothing.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long the scanner may run, up to 2h, after which its container is killed and removed.

params.name: pull
params.description: Pull the scanner's pinned image when the engine does not have it, in a run: a check never pulls, and says it cannot check without the image. The image is pinned by digest, so a pull cannot substitute another; a device that cannot pull needs the image on its engine under that digest first.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The directory written.

returns.name: sbom
returns.description: The SBOM's path on the device.

returns.name: sha256
returns.description: The SBOM's SHA-256 in hex, as SHA256SUMS records it.

returns.name: components
returns.description: How many components the SBOM holds, the subject included.

returns.name: missing_supplier
returns.description: How many dependencies have no supplier.

returns.name: scanner
returns.description: The scanner's image, pinned by digest.

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: Ignore entries expired or unused, and anything else the run must say.

examples.name: Describe a release's image
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: SBOM
  scan.sbom:
    image_archive: /srv/release/app.tar
    dest: /srv/release/sbom-2.4.1
    name: app
    version: 2.4.1
    supplier: "Organization: Example Co"

reversibility.notes: It reads the tree, mounted read-only into the scanner's container, and writes nothing.

doc.summary: Finds credentials leaked into a directory, naming each by file, line and rule, never by its value.
doc.description: Runs Gitleaks over a directory on the device with its default rules and no network, and fails on every finding an ignore entry does not suppress, each named by its file (relative to dir), line, rule and fingerprint (file:rule:line, the id an ignore entry names). Gitleaks runs with --redact, so no value is in its report, and this reads only a finding's file, line and rule, so no value could be kept even if one were. A finding means rotating the credential, not only removing it. A file or directory Gitleaks could not read, which it skips with only a warning, fails the scan, named: what was not read was not scanned. A .gitleaks.toml or .gitleaksignore at the directory's root, which Gitleaks would read as its own rules or ignores, refuses the scan, and an inline gitleaks:allow comment suppresses nothing: what is scanned never decides what is reported. It only reads, so a check is the scan a run makes, except that a check never pulls the scanner's image: without it, the check says it cannot check. The scanner runs in a fresh container on the device's own engine, from an image pinned here by its multi-platform index digest, so nothing is installed on the device and every run uses the scanner this release was tested with; what it scans is mounted read-only, its root is read-only, it runs with no-new-privileges and is removed afterwards. Paths are the engine host's, which is the device's for an engine reached over SSH or its local socket.

params.name: dir
params.description: The directory on the device to scan.

params.name: ignore
params.description: An ignore file on the device: a YAML list of {id, reason, until}, every field required, until a date (YYYY-MM-DD, in UTC) no more than 366 days after the day of the run, since an end years away is no end. An entry suppresses its finding through its until day; past it, it suppresses nothing and the run warns, and an entry that matched nothing is warned about so the file shrinks as fixes land.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long the scanner may run, up to 2h, after which its container is killed and removed.

params.name: pull
params.description: Pull the scanner's pinned image when the engine does not have it, in a run: a check never pulls, and says it cannot check without the image. The image is pinned by digest, so a pull cannot substitute another; a device that cannot pull needs the image on its engine under that digest first.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: findings
returns.description: Up to 1000 findings: file, line, rule, fingerprint, and ignored (the reason) when an ignore entry suppressed it.

returns.name: failing
returns.description: How many findings no ignore entry suppressed, which is zero for a task that succeeded.

returns.name: scanner
returns.description: The scanner's image, pinned by digest.

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: Ignore entries expired or unused, and anything else the run must say.

doc.summary: Lists the known vulnerabilities in an image archive, a directory or lockfiles, and fails at a severity.
doc.description: Runs OSV-Scanner over an image archive (docker save), a directory (recursively, every lockfile and manifest it recognizes) or named lockfiles on the device, and reports each package exposed to each group of aliased advisories: its severity from the highest CVSS score (critical from 9.0, high from 7.0, medium from 4.0, low below), and the versions that fix it. A vulnerability at or above fail_on fails the task, and with fixable_only only one a fixed version exists for; one with no score is gated as high, since an advisory nobody has scored is not evidence it is harmless. Online, the scanner joins the engine's default network and sends osv.dev the names and versions of the packages it found; with offline_db it joins none and reads OSV-Scanner's local databases from the device. A directory holding an osv-scanner.toml at any depth, which OSV-Scanner would read as a list of vulnerabilities to ignore with no reason or end, refuses the scan, and none is read in any mode; a directory the search cannot read whole is refused too. A lockfile OSV-Scanner could not read or extract, which it leaves out with only a line on its standard error, fails the scan, named: what was not read was not scanned. It only reads, so a check is the scan a run makes and sends what a run sends (give offline_db for one that sends nothing), except that a check never pulls the scanner's image: without it, the check says it cannot check. The scanner runs in a fresh container on the device's own engine, from an image pinned here by its multi-platform index digest, so nothing is installed on the device and every run uses the scanner this release was tested with; what it scans is mounted read-only, its root is read-only, it runs with no-new-privileges and is removed afterwards. Paths are the engine host's, which is the device's for an engine reached over SSH or its local socket.

params.name: dir
params.description: A directory on the device to scan, recursively, whatever its .gitignore files list (see respect_gitignore). One of dir, image_archive and lockfiles.

params.name: image_archive
params.description: An image archive on the device, as docker save or podman save writes one.

params.name: lockfiles
params.description: Lockfiles on the device to scan, each recognized by its name (package-lock.json, Cargo.lock, go.mod, requirements.txt and the rest OSV-Scanner reads).

params.name: fail_on
params.description: The least severity that fails the task: critical, high, medium, low, or any (every finding, scored or not).

params.name: fixable_only
params.description: Fail only on vulnerabilities a fixed version exists for; the rest are still reported.

params.name: respect_gitignore
params.description: Let the .gitignore files in dir narrow the scan, as git sees the tree. By default they do not: the runbook decides what is scanned, never the tree, so a directory a .gitignore lists (a vendored tree, a build output) is scanned all the same. OSV-Scanner itself never reads lockfiles inside node_modules either way, since the root lockfile already lists what npm installed there. Only with dir.

params.name: allow_empty
params.description: Pass, with a warning, when OSV-Scanner finds no package to check. Without it that fails the task, since a scan that saw nothing (a wrong path, or files the scanner could not read) is no evidence of no vulnerability.

params.name: offline_db
params.description: A directory on the device holding OSV-Scanner's local databases (osv-scalibr/<ecosystem>/all.zip, as osv-scanner --download-offline-databases writes them); the scan then joins no network, and refuses an ecosystem it has no database for.

params.name: ignore
params.description: An ignore file on the device: a YAML list of {id, reason, until}, every field required, until a date (YYYY-MM-DD, in UTC) no more than 366 days after the day of the run, since an end years away is no end. An entry suppresses its finding through its until day; past it, it suppresses nothing and the run warns, and an entry that matched nothing is warned about so the file shrinks as fixes land.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How long the scanner may run, up to 2h, after which its container is killed and removed.

params.name: pull
params.description: Pull the scanner's pinned image when the engine does not have it, in a run: a check never pulls, and says it cannot check without the image. The image is pinned by digest, so a pull cannot substitute another; a device that cannot pull needs the image on its engine under that digest first.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: findings
returns.description: Up to 1000 findings: package, version, ecosystem, id, aliases, severity, score, fixed, source (the file on the device it was found in), and ignored (the reason) when an ignore entry suppressed it.

returns.name: failing
returns.description: How many findings fail the gate, which is zero for a task that succeeded.

returns.name: counts
returns.description: How many findings at each severity.

returns.name: scanner
returns.description: The scanner's image, pinned by digest.

returns.name: warnings
returns.description: Ignore entries expired or unused, and anything else the run must say.

- name: Known vulnerabilities
  scan.vuln:

reversibility.notes: Re-reading unit files has no prior state to restore. What systemd held before the reload was a view of unit files that have since changed on disk, and nothing can ask it to go back to believing the old contents. Undoing whatever wrote those files is that task's inverse, not this one's.

doc.summary: Makes systemd re-read every unit file on disk.
doc.description: Runs systemctl daemon-reload, which makes systemd pick up unit files that were written, changed or removed since it last read them. This is ansible.builtin.systemd with daemon_reload=yes on its own. It is the step that makes a unit file an earlier task wrote visible to systemd at all: without it, svc.systemd.start on a brand new unit fails with the unit not found, which reads as a broken unit file rather than as a stale view. It takes no unit name, because it is not about one unit, and it always reports changed: systemd exposes no way to ask whether a reload would have made any difference, so claiming otherwise would be a guess.

    dest: /etc/systemd/system/app.service
    mode: "0644"

- name: Make systemd re-read its unit files
  svc.systemd.daemon_reload: {}

- name: Start the new service
  svc.systemd.start:
    name: app

A run that changed a start type of Manual to Disabled emits no inverse at all, deliberately: this namespace's enable only sets Automatic, which is not what Manual was, and emitting an instruction that would over-correct is worse than emitting none. The undo restores the boot-time setting only; it never starts a service, because disabling never stopped one running right now.

doc.summary: Stops a Windows service starting at boot, without stopping it now.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows service's start type is Disabled, refusing it from starting at all until this is undone. This is ansible.windows.win_service with start_mode=disabled, and it leaves the running system alone: a service disabled by this task keeps running until svc.windows.stop also runs or it is stopped some other way. State is read before anything is sent, so a service whose start type is already Disabled reports no change. Windows recognizes a third start type, Manual, that neither this method nor svc.windows.enable targets: a service found Manual becomes Disabled, and running svc.windows.enable afterward would leave it Automatic rather than back at Manual, which is why that specific transition records no inverse instruction rather than a wrong one.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows service to act on, its short service name (not its display name), such as Spooler rather than "Print Spooler". The service must already exist: a name the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as already stopped, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The service this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the Service Control Manager reported about the service before this task and after it, each holding exists, running, status and start_type. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

reversibility.notes: A run that enabled a service whose start type was Disabled emits an svc.windows.disable naming it. A run that found the start type already Automatic emits nothing. A run that changed a start type of Manual to Automatic emits no inverse at all, deliberately: this namespace's disable only sets Disabled, which is a stronger claim than restoring Manual, and emitting an instruction that would over-correct is worse than emitting none. The undo restores the boot-time setting only; it never stops a service that is running, because enabling never started one.

doc.summary: Makes a Windows service start at boot, without starting it now.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows service's start type is Automatic. This is ansible.windows.win_service with start_mode=auto, and it is deliberately not also start: a service enabled by this task is not running until svc.windows.start runs or the device reboots. State is read before anything is sent, so a service whose start type is already Automatic reports no change. Windows recognizes a third start type, Manual, that neither this method nor svc.windows.disable targets: a service found Manual becomes Automatic, and running svc.windows.disable afterward would leave it Disabled rather than back at Manual, which is why that specific transition records no inverse instruction rather than a wrong one.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows service to act on, its short service name (not its display name), such as Spooler rather than "Print Spooler". The service must already exist: a name the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as already stopped, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The service this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the Service Control Manager reported about the service before this task and after it, each holding exists, running, status and start_type. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

reversibility.notes: A restart's effect is the interruption itself, and there is no instruction that un-interrupts a service. Restarting it a second time would run this method again rather than reverse it. The service's state is still recorded under diff, so a rollback reaching this task can see the service was running before and after and decide for itself, but this method emits no instruction because none would be true.

doc.summary: Restarts a Windows service, starting it if it was not running.
doc.description: Restarts a Windows service. This is ansible.windows.win_service with state=restarted, and like that module it starts a service that was not running rather than failing. It is the one method in this namespace that is never converged: restarting a running service is the point, not a no-op, so this always sends the command and always reports changed. That makes it the method most worth putting behind a when condition or a handler, so a service is only bounced when something it reads actually changed. A service the Service Control Manager does not know is refused, and a service whose start type is Disabled is refused with that named.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows service to act on, its short service name (not its display name), such as Spooler rather than "Print Spooler". The service must already exist: a name the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as already stopped, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The service this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the Service Control Manager reported about the service before this task and after it, each holding exists, running, status and start_type. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Restart after a config change
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Write the app's config
  win.file.copy:
    src: app.config
    path: C:\Program Files\App\app.config
  register: app_config

- name: Restart the app service only if the config actually changed
  svc.windows.restart:
    name: AppService
  when:
    - result.app_config.diff.before != result.app_config.diff.after

reversibility.notes: A run that started a stopped service emits an svc.windows.stop naming it. A run that found it already running emits nothing. What the inverse cannot restore is anything the service did while it was up: connections it accepted, files it wrote, messages it consumed. Stopping it again returns the service to where it was, not the system.

doc.summary: Starts a Windows service now, without changing its start type.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows service is running right now. This is ansible.windows.win_service with state=started, and it is deliberately not also enable: starting and setting the start type are separate in the Service Control Manager and separate here, so a task that wants both says both. State is read before anything is sent, so a service that is already running reports no change and no command reaches the device. A service the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as started, and a service whose start type is Disabled is refused with that named, since Windows itself refuses to start one and its own error describes a generic failure rather than the cause.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows service to act on, its short service name (not its display name), such as Spooler rather than "Print Spooler". The service must already exist: a name the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as already stopped, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The service this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the Service Control Manager reported about the service before this task and after it, each holding exists, running, status and start_type. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Start a service

examples.runbookYaml:

reversibility.notes: A run that stopped a running service emits an svc.windows.start naming it. A run that found it already stopped emits nothing. Starting it again returns the service to running, but nothing can restore what it missed while it was down: requests that were refused, queues that backed up, timers that did not fire.

doc.summary: Stops a Windows service now, without changing its start type.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows service is not running right now. This is ansible.windows.win_service with state=stopped, and it leaves the start type alone: a service stopped by this task still starts at the next reboot unless svc.windows.disable is also run. State is read before anything is sent, so a service that is already stopped reports no change. A service the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as stopped, since a typo in the name should not read as success.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows service to act on, its short service name (not its display name), such as Spooler rather than "Print Spooler". The service must already exist: a name the Service Control Manager does not know is refused rather than reported as already stopped, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The service this task acted on.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the Service Control Manager reported about the service before this task and after it, each holding exists, running, status and start_type. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

reversibility.notes: A run that made a lab emits virt.cml.lab.delete naming its id, so a rollback removes exactly that lab and whatever was later built in it.

doc.summary: Creates an empty CML lab with a title.
doc.description: Makes a lab with no nodes. A title a lab already has is refused, since CML lets two labs share one and every later task names its lab by title; a second run of the same task is therefore a refusal, not a second lab. Its undo is virt.cml.lab.delete of the lab's id, so a rollback removes exactly the lab this task made. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check reads whether the title is free and changes nothing.

params.name: title
params.description: The new lab's title.

returns.name: id
returns.description: The new lab's id.

doc.summary: Stops, wipes and deletes a CML lab.
doc.description: Stops every node, wipes every node's disks and removes the lab. A lab that does not exist is unchanged. It cannot be undone: every node's disk and configuration is gone, which is why it is a method of its own and never part of another. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check reads whether the lab exists and changes nothing.

params.name: lab
params.description: The lab, by id or by title. A title two labs share is refused, naming both ids; an undo always names the id.

returns.name: lab_id
returns.description: The id of the lab removed.

examples.name: Remove a lab

reversibility.notes: It only reads the controller.

doc.summary: Reports one CML lab: its nodes, their interfaces and its links.
doc.description: Reads one lab and changes nothing. A lab that does not exist is not a failure: exists is false and nothing else is reported, so a later task can decide what to do. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check is the same read.

params.name: lab
params.description: The lab, by id or by title. A title two labs share is refused, naming both ids; an undo always names the id.

doc.summary: Lists the labs on a CML controller.

returns.name: labs

examples.name: List the labs

reversibility.notes: A run that started nodes emits virt.cml.lab.stop naming exactly those nodes, kept when the wait for them to boot fails, so a rollback never stops a node someone else started. Stopping them does not undo what they did while they ran.

doc.summary: Starts a CML lab's nodes and waits until they boot.
doc.description: Starts each of the lab's nodes (or those nodes names) that is not running, then waits until every one of them reports BOOTED, up to timeout. A node already running is left alone, and a lab whose nodes all run is unchanged. Its undo is virt.cml.lab.stop of exactly the nodes this task started, so a rollback never stops a node someone else started. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check reads which nodes it would start and changes nothing.

params.name: lab
params.description: The lab, by id or by title. A title two labs share is refused, naming both ids; an undo always names the id.

params.name: nodes
params.description: The nodes to act on, by label or id; every node of the lab when empty. A rollback sets it to exactly the nodes the run changed.

params.name: timeout
params.description: Seconds to wait for every node started to report BOOTED.

returns.name: started

returns.name: lab_id

examples.name: Start a lab

- name: Start the CVD lab
  virt.cml.lab.start:

reversibility.notes: A run that stopped nodes emits virt.cml.lab.start naming exactly those nodes, kept when a stop fails partway, so a rollback starts only what this task stopped.

doc.summary: Stops a CML lab's nodes.
doc.description: Stops each of the lab's nodes (or those nodes names) that is running, keeping their disks. A node already stopped is left alone. Its undo is virt.cml.lab.start of exactly the nodes this task stopped. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check reads which nodes it would stop and changes nothing.

params.name: lab
params.description: The lab, by id or by title. A title two labs share is refused, naming both ids; an undo always names the id.

params.name: nodes

doc.summary: Links two nodes' interfaces in a CML lab.
doc.description: Links interface a_interface of node a to interface b_interface of node b. The same link already there is unchanged; an interface already linked to anything else is refused. Its undo is virt.cml.link.delete of the link's id. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. params.description: Its interface, by label.

reversibility.notes: A run that made a node emits virt.cml.node.delete naming its lab's id and its own, so a rollback removes exactly that node.

doc.summary: Creates a node in a CML lab, optionally seeded with an inventory device's login and address.
doc.description: Makes a node from a node definition, with the definition's interfaces, stopped. With device, the node stands for that inventory device (a cisco_router or cisco_switch; only an IOS or IOS XE definition): its day-0 configuration sets the hostname to the label, puts the device's host on management_interface in the Mgmt-intf VRF with a default route to management_gateway, enables SSH, and creates the device's login as "username <user> privilege 15 secret 9 <hash>" (and "enable secret 9" when the credential has an enable password), from the device's stored credential. The passwords never reach the runbook, the task's output or the controller: the method is handed type 9 hashes only. configuration adds lines after those. A label the lab already uses is refused, so a second run is a refusal rather than a second node. Its undo is virt.cml.node.delete of the node's id. The task's target is a cml_controller device (its api_base, TLS settings and its own credential, stored with add-credential --password-stdin); the method runs on this machine and talks to the controller's REST API. A check reads the lab, the definition and the label and changes nothing.

params.name: lab
params.description: The lab, by id or by title. A title two labs share is refused, naming both ids; an undo always names the id.

params.name: label
params.description: The node's label in the lab, also its hostname when device is set.

params.name: definition
params.description: The node definition's id, e.g. iol-xe.

params.name: device

params.name: management_prefix

params.name: management_gateway
params.description: The management network's gateway, the Mgmt-intf VRF's default route. Required with device.

params.name: configuration
params.description: Day-0 configuration lines added after the seeded ones, or the whole day-0 configuration without device. Never put a password here: use device.

params.name: x
params.description: The node's place on the lab's canvas, left to right.

params.name: y
params.description: The node's place on the lab's canvas, top to bottom.

returns.name: id
returns.description: The new node's id.

returns.name: interfaces
returns.description: Its interfaces' labels, in slot order.

returns.name: management_address
returns.description: The address the node's management interface was given.

doc.summary: Deletes a snapshot of a VirtualBox VM.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM has no snapshot with this name. None under the name reports no change. The snapshot's saved state is merged away and cannot be brought back, so this cannot be undone. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing.

params.name: vm
params.description: The VM whose snapshot this is, named as for virt.vbox.vm.start.

params.name: name
params.description: The snapshot's name, under the same rule as a VM's. VirtualBox lets two snapshots share a name; virt.vbox.snapshot.take never makes a second, and the methods that find a snapshot by name refuse one that matches more than one unless uuid says which.

params.name: uuid
params.description: The snapshot's UUID, needed only when more than one snapshot of the VM has this name (which only VirtualBox itself, or a tool other than this one, makes). It must be one of them.

returns.name: uuid
returns.description: The snapshot deleted.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a snapshot under the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Drop a snapshot
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Drop the old baseline
  virt.vbox.snapshot.delete:
    vm: ubuntu-lab
    name: clean

reversibility.notes: Restoring discards everything the VM did since the snapshot, and nothing keeps what was discarded, so there is no state an undo could put back. Take a snapshot first to keep it.

doc.summary: Puts a VirtualBox VM back to a snapshot, discarding its current state.
doc.description: Restores a VM to a snapshot. Everything the VM did since that snapshot is discarded, so this always reports a change and cannot be undone. A running VM is refused: stop it first with virt.vbox.vm.stop, so that discarding a running machine is a decision a runbook states rather than a side effect. A snapshot that does not exist is refused. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing.

params.name: vm
params.description: The VM whose snapshot this is, named as for virt.vbox.vm.start.

params.name: name
params.description: The snapshot's name, under the same rule as a VM's. VirtualBox lets two snapshots share a name; virt.vbox.snapshot.take never makes a second, and the methods that find a snapshot by name refuse one that matches more than one unless uuid says which.

params.name: uuid
params.description: The snapshot's UUID, needed only when more than one snapshot of the VM has this name (which only VirtualBox itself, or a tool other than this one, makes). It must be one of them.

returns.name: uuid
returns.description: The snapshot restored.

examples.name: Reset to a clean install

- name: Stop the lab VM
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    mode: poweroff

- name: Back to the clean install
  virt.vbox.snapshot.restore:
    vm: ubuntu-lab
    name: clean

- name: Start it again
  virt.vbox.vm.start:
    name: ubuntu-lab

reversibility.notes: A run that took a snapshot emits virt.vbox.snapshot.delete naming it by UUID, so the undo deletes that snapshot and no other of the same name; one that found a snapshot under the name emits nothing.

doc.summary: Takes a snapshot of a VirtualBox VM under a name no other snapshot of it has.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM has a snapshot with this name. A snapshot already under the name reports no change and takes no second one, although VirtualBox itself would. A running VM can be snapshotted; a snapshot of a running VM holds its memory too. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing.

params.name: vm
params.description: The VM whose snapshot this is, named as for virt.vbox.vm.start.

params.name: name
params.description: The snapshot's name, under the same rule as a VM's. VirtualBox lets two snapshots share a name; virt.vbox.snapshot.take never makes a second, and the methods that find a snapshot by name refuse one that matches more than one unless uuid says which.

params.name: description
params.description: Text stored with the snapshot, at most 200 characters on one line.

returns.name: uuid

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a snapshot under the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Snapshot a clean install
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Keep the clean install
  virt.vbox.snapshot.take:
    vm: ubuntu-lab
    name: clean
    description: fresh install, before any test

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this reads the VM and the host's DHCP leases and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Reports the addresses a VM's host-only adapters were given, from VirtualBox's DHCP server and from virt.vbox.vm.clone.
doc.description: Reports each address a VM's host-only adapters have: the leases VirtualBox's own DHCP server handed them (read from the leases file it keeps for the host's account), and the fixed address virt.vbox.vm.clone gave the VM (the extradata pleiades/address). A VM whose first boot did not apply its fixed address shows the address DHCP gave it too, which is how to reach it anyway. A NAT adapter's address is private to the VM and is not reported. Nothing is changed. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the same as a run.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

returns.name: addresses
returns.description: Each address as nic (the adapter's number), mac, adapter (the host's), address, source (dhcp or fixed), and for a DHCP lease its state (acked while held, expired after), issued and expires.

returns.name: address
returns.description: The address to reach the VM at: the fixed one, or else a held DHCP lease's. A first boot that applied its fixed address leaves the lease it took before then marked held for a while, so a VM whose fixed address was never applied is known by that lease being the only one it answers at.

examples.name: Find a VM's address
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Where the lab VM answers
  virt.vbox.vm.addresses:
    name: win-lab
  register: found

reversibility.notes: A run that made a VM emits virt.vbox.vm.delete naming it and pinning its UUID, so a VM made later under the name is refused rather than deleted; one that found a VM under the name emits nothing.

doc.summary: Makes a VM as a linked clone of another's snapshot, seeded with a device's login by cloud-init or a Windows answer file.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM of this name exists, creating it as a linked clone of a snapshot of another VM, so it takes little space and starts from that snapshot's disk. A VM already under the name reports no change and is not reconfigured or reseeded; when its CPUs or memory are not those asked for, the task says so in a warning, and virt.vbox.vm.resize changes them. The new VM gets the size asked for, or the memory and CPUs, and one larger than the host is refused: more CPUs than it has processors online, or more memory than it has. It also gets a NAT adapter for the internet, a host-only adapter at a fixed address, a serial console written to console.log in its folder (virt.vbox.vm.host_keys reads a Linux VM's SSH host keys from there), and a seed on its DVD drive: a cloud-init NoCloud seed, or for a VM of a Windows OS type a Windows answer file (Autounattend.xml). The seed is built by Pleiades, not on the host, and reaches the host on the command's standard input, never on a command line. For a Linux VM it carries login's user name, the public half of its key and a salted hash of its password, taken from the vault by pleiades add-credential login --generate; never the key or the password. SSH then admits the key only; the password is for the VM's console. A login of root may log in by key; any other user gets passwordless sudo. A Windows VM is reached over WinRM by the built-in Administrator's password, and an answer file can hold nothing else, so for one the login must be a device reached over WinRM whose credential names Administrator, and the answer file carries that password itself, beside the computer name, the fixed address and the first-boot screens it skips. Windows reads that answer file at first boot only from a base virt.vbox.vm.install made, which points it at the clone's one DVD (D:); a clone of another generalized image, such as Microsoft's evaluation VHDX, stops at its first-boot screens. A Windows VM given no size is small rather than xsmall. The seed stays in the VM's folder until virt.vbox.vm.eject_seed or virt.vbox.vm.delete removes it: eject it once the first boot has read it. The address and login are recorded on the VM as VirtualBox extradata (pleiades/address, pleiades/device), which virt.vbox.vm.list reports, since VirtualBox cannot know a guest's address without its Guest Additions. The VM is not started. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the host's VMs and the snapshot, and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: from
params.description: The VM to clone, named as name is.

params.name: snapshot
params.description: The snapshot of from to clone. Exactly one of from's snapshots may have this name.

params.name: login
params.description: The inventory device whose stored login the VM is seeded with, usually the device that stands for this VM. For a Linux VM, one reached over SSH: its user name, its key's public half and a hash of its password. For a Windows VM, one reached over WinRM whose credential names Administrator: its password.

params.name: address
params.description: The host-only adapter's address with its prefix, as 192.168.56.10/24. Keep it out of the host-only DHCP server's range.

params.name: hostname
params.description: The VM's host name, or a Windows VM's computer name, which is at most 15 letters, digits and hyphens. Defaults to name, which must then be a valid one.

params.name: size
params.description: The VM's size, a T-shirt size, which sets its CPUs and memory together as a cloud's instance type does: xsmall is 1 CPU and 1024 MB, small 1 CPU and 2048 MB, medium 2 CPUs and 4096 MB, large 4 CPUs and 8192 MB, and xlarge 8 CPUs and 16384 MB. Give size, or memory_mb and cpus, not both; with none of the three, the VM is xsmall, or small for a Windows VM.

params.name: memory_mb
params.description: Its memory, in megabytes, when size is not given.

params.name: cpus
params.description: Its virtual CPU count, when size is not given.

params.name: paravirt_provider
params.description: The paravirtualization interface the guest is offered, as VBoxManage modifyvm --paravirt-provider takes it: default picks one by the guest's OS type (kvm for Linux, hyperv for Windows), and none offers nothing, so the guest keeps time by its own clocks. Left out, the VM keeps from's.

params.name: host_only_adapter
params.description: The host's host-only adapter, as VBoxManage list hostonlyifs names it.

params.name: packages
params.description: Packages a Linux or FreeBSD VM's first boot installs as root, from the guest's own repositories over its NAT adapter: cloud-init's packages list, which FreeBSD's nuageinit reads too, bootstrapping pkg first. Each is a package name of letters, digits and . + _ -, at most 64 of them. On FreeBSD, whose base system has no sudo, listing sudo is what gives a login other than root the passwordless sudo the seed grants it. Refused for a Windows VM, whose answer file installs nothing. Like the rest of the seed, it is read at the first boot only, so a VM already under the name is not changed.

returns.name: uuid
returns.returned: when not a check that would clone
returns.description: The VM's UUID, which is also a Linux VM's cloud-init instance ID.

returns.name: address
returns.description: The host-only address the VM was given, without its prefix.

returns.name: size
returns.description: The VM's T-shirt size, read from its CPUs and memory (those asked for, in a check that would clone), or empty when they are not exactly one size's.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a VM of the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Clone and start a lab VM
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make the lab VM from the base's clean snapshot
  virt.vbox.vm.clone:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    from: ubuntu-2404-base
    snapshot: base
    login: ubuntu-lab
    address: 192.168.56.10/24
    size: small

- name: Start it
  virt.vbox.vm.start:
    name: ubuntu-lab

examples.name: Clone a Windows VM
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make a Windows lab VM, seeded with win-lab's Administrator password
  virt.vbox.vm.clone:
    name: win-lab
    from: ws2025-base
    snapshot: base
    login: win-lab
    address: 192.168.56.30/24
    size: medium

reversibility.notes: Deleting a VM deletes its disks, and nothing keeps what was on them, so there is no VM an undo could bring back. Take a snapshot and keep the base it was cloned from to make it again.

doc.summary: Deletes a stopped VirtualBox VM and its disks.
doc.description: Makes sure no VM of this name exists. None reports no change. A running or paused VM is refused: stop it first with virt.vbox.vm.stop. A saved VM's state (virt.vbox.vm.stop's mode save) is discarded first, since VirtualBox will not detach media from a saved VM and the delete throws that memory away anyway. The VM is unregistered and its disks deleted, along with a seed ISO or console log virt.vbox.vm.clone put in its folder and a screenshot virt.vbox.vm.install saved there; install media attached from anywhere else (a shared ISO) is detached, never deleted. A VM that others were linked-cloned from is refused by VirtualBox while they exist. This cannot be undone. A VM VirtualBox lists as <inaccessible> (its folder deleted or unreadable) is named by the UUID list vms shows for it, and is only unregistered: nothing is deleted, since VirtualBox cannot read where its disks are. Left registered, such a VM makes VirtualBox 7.2's autostart service refuse to start any of the account's VMs. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing, and reports a running or paused VM as not checkable, since an earlier task in the same run may stop it.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: uuid
params.description: When set, the VM under name must be this one, by its VirtualBox UUID, or the task is refused and nothing is deleted. A rollback sets it, so undoing the task that made a VM never deletes a different VM made later under the same name.

returns.name: uuid
returns.description: The VM deleted.

returns.name: inaccessible
returns.description: The VM was a registration VirtualBox could not read; it was unregistered and nothing was deleted.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a VM of the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Throw a lab VM away
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Power the lab VM off
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    mode: poweroff

- name: Delete it
  virt.vbox.vm.delete:
    name: ubuntu-lab

reversibility.notes: The seed file is deleted, and nothing keeps what it held (a hash of the login's password, or a Windows VM's Administrator password), so it cannot be put back; a VM that needs seeding again is made again with virt.vbox.vm.clone.

doc.summary: Takes a VM's seed out of its DVD drive and deletes it, once its first boot has read it.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM virt.vbox.vm.clone made no longer holds its seed: the cloud-init seed or Windows answer file clone put on its DVD drive and in its folder, which holds a hash of the login's password or, for Windows, the Administrator's password itself. The drive is emptied at once, even while the VM runs and even when the guest has locked it, so the guest can never read the seed again. The seed file is then deleted; but VirtualBox keeps an image locked for as long as the VM that held it runs (measured on the lab host), so on a running VM the file stays until the VM is stopped, the task says so in a warning and reports deleted false, and running it again once the VM is stopped deletes it. Run it once the first boot has read the seed: after virt.vbox.vm.host_keys finds a Linux VM's keys, or after wait.connection reaches a Windows VM. A VM holding no seed, in a drive or on the host, reports no change. The seed cannot be put back. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

returns.name: ejected
returns.description: Whether a seed was taken out, or would be, in a check.

returns.name: deleted
returns.returned: when a seed was taken out
returns.description: Whether the seed file was deleted from the host: false while the VM runs, which keeps it locked.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether the VM held its seed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Delete a Windows VM's answer file after its first boot
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Take the lab VM's answer file out, now that it has booted
  virt.vbox.vm.eject_seed:
    name: win-lab

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this reads the VM's console log and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Reads a VM's SSH host keys from what cloud-init printed on its serial console.
doc.description: Waits for cloud-init to print the VM's SSH host keys on its serial console, which virt.vbox.vm.clone logs to a file on the host, and reports them. They are read over the host's own authenticated connection, not from the network the VM answers SSH on, so they are what a known_hosts file can trust before the first SSH connection: pleiades trust-host <device> --from-console <host> writes them there. The newest complete block is the one read. Nothing is changed. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the console once, without waiting.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait for the keys.

returns.name: ssh_host_keys
returns.description: Each key as algorithm and base64, the form a known_hosts line holds after its host names. Empty in a check that found none yet.

examples.name: Wait for a new VM's host keys
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the lab VM's first boot
  virt.vbox.vm.host_keys:
    name: ubuntu-lab
  register: keys

reversibility.notes: A run that made a VM emits virt.vbox.vm.delete naming it and pinning its UUID, which deletes the copied disk with it; the image copied from is never changed. One that found a VM under the name emits nothing.

doc.summary: Makes a VirtualBox VM from a disk image on the host, such as Microsoft's Windows Server evaluation VHDX.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM of this name exists, creating it from a disk image already on the host: a VHDX, VHD, VMDK or VDI file, such as the evaluation VHDX Microsoft publishes for Windows Server. The image is copied into the VM's folder as a VDI that grows as the guest writes to it, and the image itself is left as it was, so one image can make many VMs. The copy is the VM's disk, and virt.vbox.vm.delete removes it with the VM. The VM gets os_type; a SATA controller holding the disk and an IDE controller for the DVD a clone's seed goes in; network cards Windows has a driver for, with nothing attached; and the firmware the disk boots with, read from its first sectors: EFI for a GUID partition table, BIOS for a master boot record. A VM already under the name reports no change and is not compared with the image. The VM is not started, and is meant as a base to snapshot and clone. For Windows the image must be generalized (by sysprep), and virt.vbox.vm.clone then gives each clone its own name, address and password on a DVD. Microsoft's Windows Server evaluation VHDX is generalized but never reads that DVD at its first boot (measured on the lab host), so its clones stop at the first-boot screens; virt.vbox.vm.install makes a Windows base whose clones read theirs. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the host's VMs and sends nothing; it does not read the disk, so it reports the firmware only when firmware names one.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: path
params.description: The disk image's absolute path on the host. It may not hold a quote, a wildcard or a control character.

params.name: os_type
params.description: The VM's guest OS type, as VBoxManage list ostypes names it: Windows2025_64 for Windows Server 2025, Windows2022_64 for 2022, Ubuntu_64 for Ubuntu. VirtualBox tunes the VM to it, and virt.vbox.vm.clone seeds a clone of a Windows type with a Windows answer file.

params.name: firmware
params.description: What the VM boots with. auto reads the disk's first sectors: EFI for a GUID partition table, BIOS for a master boot record.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds the copy may take. A disk of many gigabytes takes minutes.

returns.name: uuid
returns.returned: when not a check that would import
returns.description: The VM's UUID.

returns.name: firmware
returns.returned: when not a check with firmware auto
returns.description: What the VM boots with: bios or efi.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a VM of the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Make a Windows Server base from Microsoft's VHDX
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make a Windows Server 2025 base from the evaluation VHDX
  virt.vbox.vm.import_disk:
    name: ws2025-base
    path: G:\iso\server-2025-datacenter-eval.vhdx
    os_type: Windows2025_64

- name: Snapshot it, never booted
  virt.vbox.snapshot.take:
    vm: ws2025-base
    name: base

reversibility.notes: A run that imported a VM emits virt.vbox.vm.delete naming it and pinning its UUID, so a VM made later under the name is refused rather than deleted; one that found a VM under the name emits nothing.

doc.summary: Imports an OVA appliance on a VirtualBox host as a VM, with no network adapter.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM of this name exists, importing it from an OVA file already on the host (win.file.download fetches one) into the host's vm_folder. A VM already under the name reports no change, and is not compared with the file. The imported VM is left with no network adapter, whatever the appliance asked for: Ubuntu's cloud image asks for a bridged one, which would put the VM on the host's own network. A VM made from it (virt.vbox.vm.clone) is given the networks it is meant to have. The VM is not started, and is meant as a base to snapshot and clone rather than to boot. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the host's VMs and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: path
params.description: The OVA file's absolute path on the host. It may not hold a quote, a wildcard or a control character.

returns.name: uuid
returns.returned: when not a check that would import
returns.description: The VM's UUID.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a VM of the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Import the Ubuntu cloud image
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Import the Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image as a base
  virt.vbox.vm.import_ova:
    name: ubuntu-2404-base
    path: G:\PleiadesLab\ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.ova

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this runs VBoxManage showvminfo and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Reports a VirtualBox VM's state, hardware and snapshots.
doc.description: Reads a VM on a VirtualBox host with VBoxManage showvminfo and changes nothing. A VM that does not exist is not a failure: exists is false and nothing else is reported, so a later task can decide what to do. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check is the same read.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

returns.name: exists
returns.description: Whether a VM with this name is registered on the host.

returns.name: uuid
returns.description: The VM's UUID.

returns.name: state
returns.description: VirtualBox's state for it: poweroff, running, saved, paused, aborted, or another VirtualBox reports.

returns.name: memory_mb
returns.description: Its memory, in megabytes.

returns.name: cpus
returns.description: Its virtual CPU count.

returns.name: size
returns.description: Its T-shirt size, read from its CPUs and memory: xsmall, small, medium, large or xlarge, or empty when they are not exactly one size's.

returns.name: autostart_enabled
returns.description: Whether it is marked to start with the host account's autostart service. virt.vbox.vm.start sets this on a Windows host and virt.vbox.vm.stop clears it.

returns.name: snapshots
returns.description: Each snapshot as name, uuid and description, a parent before its children.

returns.name: current_snapshot_uuid
returns.description: The snapshot the VM's state descends from, or empty when it has none.

examples.name: Read a VM
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the lab VM
  virt.vbox.vm.info:
    name: ubuntu-lab
  register: vm

reversibility.notes: A run that installed a VM emits virt.vbox.vm.delete naming it and pinning its UUID, which deletes its disk with it; the ISO is never changed. One that found an installed VM under the name emits nothing.

doc.summary: Makes a Windows or FreeBSD VM by installing it from its installation ISO, unattended, as a base to clone.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM of this name exists, creating it by installing an operating system from an installation ISO already on the host, with no one at the keyboard. installer says which: windows or freebsd, declared by the task rather than read from os_type. The VM gets a new disk of disk_gb, BIOS firmware, the size asked for, os_type, and no network adapter, so the install downloads nothing. Its DVD drives hold the ISO and an answer medium Pleiades builds. For windows it is an answer file (Autounattend.xml), which partitions the disk, installs image and accepts its license, then takes the new Windows through audit mode, where it deletes the two copies of itself Windows cached, points the registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\Setup, UnattendFile) at D:\Autounattend.xml, and runs sysprep to generalize the installation and shut it down. A generalized Windows looks for its answer file at first boot only there and in its own folders, never on a DVD, so the pointer is how a clone reads its seed. The answer file holds a password only for audit mode's sign-in, made at random for this install and kept nowhere by Pleiades; Windows keeps it, not blanked, in one of the two copies it caches, which is why audit mode deletes both, and a clone's seed sets a password of its own. For freebsd it is bsdinstall's script (installerconfig), which a released DVD cannot hold, so Pleiades watches the VM's screen for the installer's Welcome dialog, chooses its shell, and types the command that mounts the script's DVD and runs it. The command first says so on the VM's serial console, which is written to console.log in its folder, then copies the installer's log there, so the console shows how far an install got; running the task again resumes an install that stopped before or after the command, and never types it twice. The script installs the kernel and base system from the DVD onto the first disk with bsdinstall's default partitioning, enables sshd, and prepares the system for its clones' first boot: nuageinit reads each clone's seed, the serial console stays on, and the SSH host keys are printed on it between the lines cloud-init uses, which virt.vbox.vm.host_keys reads. Then the VM powers off; a script that fails leaves it running at a shell. The task waits for the power-off: about six to eight minutes for Windows on the lab host. When the VM is off, both DVDs are taken out, the answer medium is deleted, and the VM is marked installed (the extradata pleiades/installed). The VM is meant as a base to snapshot and clone: virt.vbox.vm.clone gives each clone its own name, address and login. A VM already under the name reports no change when it is marked installed, and is refused when it is not, since an install that did not finish is no base: delete it with virt.vbox.vm.delete and run again. An install still running at the timeout is left running, with a picture of its screen saved in its folder to show where it stopped. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the host's VMs and memory, and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: installer
params.description: The operating system the ISO installs, which sets how: windows reads an answer file by itself, and freebsd is started from its installer's Welcome dialog. Declared here, never inferred from os_type.

params.name: iso
params.description: The installation ISO's absolute path on the host, such as Microsoft's Windows Server evaluation ISO or FreeBSD's dvd1 ISO. It is attached and then taken out again, never changed or deleted.

params.name: image
params.description: windows only, and required with it. The edition to install: its name in the ISO's install.wim, such as Windows Server 2025 Standard Evaluation, which is Server Core, or Windows Server 2025 Datacenter Evaluation (Desktop Experience); or its index there, 1 for the first.

params.name: os_type
params.description: The VM's guest OS type, as VBoxManage list ostypes names it: Windows2025_64 for Windows Server 2025, Windows2022_64 for 2022, Ubuntu_64 for Ubuntu. VirtualBox tunes the VM to it, and virt.vbox.vm.clone seeds a clone of a Windows type with a Windows answer file.

params.name: disk_gb
params.description: The size of the VM's new disk, in gigabytes, at least 32 for windows and 8 for freebsd. It grows on the host as the guest writes to it.

params.name: size
params.description: The VM's size while it installs, a T-shirt size, which sets its CPUs and memory together as a cloud's instance type does: xsmall is 1 CPU and 1024 MB, small 1 CPU and 2048 MB, medium 2 CPUs and 4096 MB, large 4 CPUs and 8192 MB, and xlarge 8 CPUs and 16384 MB. Windows Server needs at least small.

params.name: language
params.description: windows only. The installation's language and locale, as a tag such as en-US. The ISO must hold it.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait for the install to finish and the VM to power itself off.

returns.name: uuid
returns.returned: when not a check that would install
returns.description: The VM's UUID.

returns.name: size
returns.description: The VM's T-shirt size, or empty when its CPUs and memory are not exactly one size's.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether a VM of the name existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Install Windows Server Core as a base
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install Windows Server 2025 Core from the evaluation ISO
  virt.vbox.vm.install:
    name: ws2025-core-base
    installer: windows
    iso: G:\iso\server-2025-eval.iso
    image: Windows Server 2025 Standard Evaluation
    os_type: Windows2025_64

- name: Snapshot the generalized install
  virt.vbox.snapshot.take:
    vm: ws2025-core-base
    name: base

examples.name: Install FreeBSD as a base
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install FreeBSD 15.1 from its DVD
  virt.vbox.vm.install:
    name: freebsd-base
    installer: freebsd
    iso: G:\iso\FreeBSD-15.1-RELEASE-amd64-dvd1.iso
    os_type: FreeBSD_64
    size: small
    disk_gb: 16

- name: Snapshot the installed base
  virt.vbox.snapshot.take:
    vm: freebsd-base
    name: base

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this lists VMs and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Lists the VMs on a VirtualBox host, with their state and the address Pleiades gave them.
doc.description: Reports every VM registered on the host for the account Pleiades reaches it as: its name, UUID, state, memory, CPUs and autostart mark, and, for a VM virt.vbox.vm.clone made, the host-only address it was given and the inventory device whose login it was seeded with. VirtualBox keeps a separate list of VMs for each Windows account, so these are not the VMs a person sees in their own VirtualBox Manager, and theirs are not listed here. Nothing is changed. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check is the same read.

returns.name: vms
returns.description: Each VM as name, uuid, state, memory_mb, cpus, autostart_enabled, size when its CPUs and memory are one T-shirt size's, and address and device when Pleiades made it, in the order VirtualBox lists them.

examples.name: List the lab's VMs
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: What runs on the lab host
  virt.vbox.vm.list: {}

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this reads the VM's log and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Reads the end of a VM's VirtualBox log, optionally only the lines matching a pattern.
doc.description: Reads the end of the log VirtualBox writes for a VM's current or last run (VBox.log in its folder's Logs), and reports its last lines, or its last lines matching pattern. The log says what the VM's firmware and VirtualBox did: where a boot stopped, which hypervisor interface the guest used, and why a VM aborted. Nothing is changed. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the log as a run does.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: lines
params.description: How many lines to report, from the end: 1 to 2000.

params.name: pattern
params.description: Report only lines matching this Go RE2 regular expression, such as EFI|GIM|fatal.

returns.name: lines
returns.description: The log's last lines, or its last lines matching pattern, oldest first. Empty when the VM has never run.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The log file's path on the host.

examples.name: See where a VM's firmware stopped
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the lab VM's firmware lines
  virt.vbox.vm.log:
    name: win-lab
    pattern: "EFI|debug point"
    lines: 20

reversibility.notes: A run that changed the VM emits virt.vbox.vm.resize back to the memory and CPUs it had; one that found them already right emits nothing.

doc.summary: Changes a stopped VirtualBox VM's CPUs and memory, by T-shirt size or by count.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM has the CPUs and memory asked for: a size, or memory_mb and cpus, either of which alone leaves the other as it is. A VM that has them already reports no change. VirtualBox changes them only while a VM is powered off, so a running, paused or saved VM is refused: stop it first with virt.vbox.vm.stop. A size larger than the host is refused: more CPUs than it has processors online, or more memory than it has. The guest sees the change at its next boot. A run that changed the VM emits virt.vbox.vm.resize back to the CPUs and memory it had. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and the host, and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: size
