params.description: The size to give the VM, a T-shirt size, which sets its CPUs and memory together as a cloud's instance type does: xsmall is 1 CPU and 1024 MB, small 1 CPU and 2048 MB, medium 2 CPUs and 4096 MB, large 4 CPUs and 8192 MB, and xlarge 8 CPUs and 16384 MB. Give size, or memory_mb, cpus or both, not size with either.

params.name: memory_mb
params.description: The memory to give it, in megabytes.

params.name: cpus
params.description: The virtual CPU count to give it.

returns.name: memory_mb
returns.description: Its memory after this task, in megabytes (predicted, in a check).

returns.name: cpus
returns.description: Its virtual CPU count after this task (predicted, in a check).

returns.name: size
returns.description: Its T-shirt size after this task, or empty when its CPUs and memory are not exactly one size's.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Its memory_mb, cpus and size before this task and after it.

examples.name: Make a lab VM bigger
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Shut the lab VM down
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab

- name: Make it medium
  virt.vbox.vm.resize:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    size: medium

- name: Start it again
  virt.vbox.vm.start:
    name: ubuntu-lab

examples.name: Give a VM more memory only
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Double the build VM's memory
  virt.vbox.vm.resize:
    name: build-vm
    memory_mb: 8192

reversibility.notes: The VM is not changed; the file at dest is replaced by the picture, and what it held before is not kept.

doc.summary: Saves a picture of a running VM's screen as a PNG file on the machine running Pleiades.
doc.description: Takes a picture of a running VM's screen on the host, brings it back over the host's own connection, and writes it to dest on the machine running this task, as Ansible's fetch brings a file back; the host keeps no copy. It is how to see a VM with no window, such as one stopped at a first-boot screen or an installer's error. A VM that has not set a display mode yet (still in its firmware, or stopped before it drew anything) has no picture to take, and says so. The VM is not changed; dest is replaced when it exists. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM, takes no picture and writes nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: dest
params.description: Where to write the PNG on the machine running this task. Its folder must exist.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: Where the picture was written, or would be, in a check.

returns.name: width
returns.description: The picture's width, in pixels.

returns.name: height
returns.description: The picture's height, in pixels.

returns.name: bytes
returns.description: The PNG file's size.

examples.name: See where a Windows VM's first boot stopped
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Save a picture of the lab VM's screen
  virt.vbox.vm.screenshot:
    name: win-lab
    dest: ./win-lab.png

reversibility.notes: What was typed was acted on by the guest, and no key undoes that in general.

doc.summary: Types into a running VM's console, as its keyboard would.
doc.description: Types keys into a running VM's console, written as Packer's boot_command writes them: text as it is, a named key between angle brackets (<enter>, <tab>, <esc>, <bs>, <del>, <spacebar>, <up>, <down>, <left>, <right>, <home>, <end>, <pageup>, <pagedown>, <insert>, <f1> to <f12>), and <wait> or <wait5> for a pause of one or five seconds (at most 60). Text is typed with a US keyboard layout and may hold only printable ASCII. It is for a VM with no other way in yet, such as one at a first-boot screen; see what it shows with virt.vbox.vm.screenshot. Never type a secret: text travels on the host's VBoxManage command line, where any process on the host can read it. This cannot be undone. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and the keys, and types nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: keys
params.description: What to type, as Packer's boot_command writes it, such as <tab><tab><enter>.

returns.name: strokes
returns.description: How many steps were typed, or would be, in a check: each run of text, named key and pause is one.

examples.name: Accept a first-boot screen
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Move to the Accept button and press it
  virt.vbox.vm.send_keys:
    name: win-lab
    keys: <tab><tab><enter>

reversibility.notes: A run that started a stopped VM emits virt.vbox.vm.stop naming it; one that found it running emits nothing. Stopping it does not undo what the guest did while it ran.

doc.summary: Starts a VirtualBox VM with no window.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM is running, started headless. A VM that is already running reports no change. A saved VM (virt.vbox.vm.stop's mode save) resumes where it was, with no boot. A paused VM is refused, since starting is not resuming. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. On a Windows host, a VM cannot start from the WinRM logon this task uses: Windows' catalog signature check fails for a non-administrator logon that is not interactive, and VirtualBox's hardening then refuses the hypervisor (VirtualBox ticket 20341). So when none of the account's VMs is running, the VM is marked for autostart and started by the account's VirtualBox autostart service, which runs under a service logon; examples/windows_lab/winrm-cert-setup.ps1 -VirtualBoxAutostart installs it. While any of the account's VMs runs, a plain start works, because every client is then handed the VirtualBox server that VM keeps alive. The autostart mark stays on while the VM runs, since VirtualBox refuses to change a running VM's settings, so a host restart in that time starts it again; virt.vbox.vm.stop clears it. A VM with more memory than the host has free, less 1024 MB kept for the host itself, is refused rather than started, since the host would page to find it; the host's free memory is read at the start. A check reads the VM and the host and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

returns.name: state
returns.description: The VM's state after this task, read back from the host.

returns.name: via_autostart_service
returns.description: Whether the start went through the account's autostart service. False when nothing was started.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The VM's state before this task and after it.

examples.name: Start a VM
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Start the lab VM
  virt.vbox.vm.start:
    name: ubuntu-lab

reversibility.notes: A run that stopped a running VM emits virt.vbox.vm.start naming it; one that found it stopped emits nothing. Starting it again does not bring back what a power cut lost.

doc.summary: Stops a VirtualBox VM, by its power button or by cutting its power.
doc.description: Makes sure a VM is not running. A VM that is already off, saved or aborted reports no change. mode acpi presses the VM's power button, and again every 30 seconds while it waits (an idle Windows guest spends a press waking its display), for the guest to shut itself down, failing, rather than cutting the power, if it has not within timeout; mode poweroff stops it at once, as pulling its plug would, and loses whatever the guest had not written; mode save writes the VM's memory to disk and stops it, so the host has the memory back and virt.vbox.vm.start resumes the guest where it was, with no boot. Once the VM is off, its autostart mark is cleared, which virt.vbox.vm.start sets on a Windows host. The task's target is the VirtualBox host (a device with virtualbox: true), not the VM, which is a resource on it. A check reads the VM and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The VM's name on the host. It must start with a letter or digit and hold only letters, digits, '.', '_' and '-', at most 63 characters; any other name is refused rather than quoted.

params.name: mode
params.description: acpi asks the guest to shut down; poweroff cuts its power; save keeps its state for virt.vbox.vm.start to resume.

params.name: timeout
params.description: With mode acpi, how many seconds to wait for the guest to shut down before failing.

returns.name: state
returns.description: The VM's state after this task, read back from the host.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The VM's state before this task and after it.

examples.name: Shut a VM down
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Shut the lab VM down
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab

examples.name: Cut a VM's power
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Power the lab VM off now
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    mode: poweroff

examples.name: Put a VM away until it is next needed
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Save the lab VM's state and free its memory
  virt.vbox.vm.stop:
    name: ubuntu-lab
    mode: save

reversibility.notes: This method waits for a device to answer and changes nothing on it, so there is nothing to undo.

wait.connection.noCheckReason: what it waits for is usually a machine an earlier task starts or restarts, which a check never does, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits until the target answers a command over its own connection, SSH or WinRM.
doc.description: Tries the device over the connection its other tasks use (WinRM for a device reached that way, such as a Windows server, and SSH for any other) until a command runs there, and fails when the timeout runs out first. It is Ansible's wait_for_connection: the task to put after one that starts or restarts a machine, before the tasks that need it. Each try logs in afresh with the device's credential and runs a command that does nothing, so a machine whose port answers before its account can log in is not taken for ready, and a session kept open from an earlier task is never taken for a login. A network device's CLI is not a shell with a command that does nothing, so for one that declares CiscoIOSCapable, or a cli_prompt, a try opens its terminal and waits for its prompt instead. A failed try is not an error, since it is what the task waits to see stop; the last one is quoted when the timeout ends the wait. The delay is spent out of the timeout rather than added to it, as wait_for_connection does. With backoff: exponential the gap after each failed try doubles from sleep up to max_sleep, each gap a random point in its upper half so machines restarted together do not try in step. With steady above 1 the machine must answer that many tries in a row, steady_interval apart, which a machine just resumed or restarted that answers once and then refuses for a while does not; a refusal mid-streak starts the streak, and the backoff, again. It changes nothing.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait in total before giving up, counted from the start of the task, so the delay comes out of it. Must be more than 0.

params.name: delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait before the first try. Must be shorter than the timeout, which it is spent out of.

params.name: sleep
params.description: How many seconds to wait between tries, or with backoff: exponential before the second try, the gap doubling after each failed one. Must be more than 0.

params.name: backoff
params.description: How the gap between failed tries grows: fixed keeps it at sleep, as wait_for_connection does; exponential doubles it after each failed try, up to max_sleep, each gap a random point in its upper half.

params.name: max_sleep
params.description: With backoff: exponential, the longest gap between tries, in seconds. Not less than sleep; refused with backoff: fixed, where it would do nothing.

params.name: steady
params.description: How many tries in a row must answer before the machine counts as ready. Each is its own login. Must be at least 1, and the streak must fit in the timeout after the delay.

params.name: steady_interval
params.description: With steady above 1, the seconds between the answering tries. Must be more than 0; refused with steady 1, where it would do nothing.

params.name: connect_timeout
params.description: How many seconds one try may take before it counts as failed. Must be more than 0.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task, on a device reached over SSH. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How many whole seconds the task waited, including the delay.

returns.name: transport
returns.description: The connection that answered: ssh or winrm.

returns.name: tries
returns.description: How many tries the task made, answered or not.

returns.name: failures
returns.description: How many of those tries did not answer.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The connection that answered. Both halves are identical, since a wait changes nothing.

examples.name: Wait for a new Windows VM's first boot
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the Windows lab VM to let its Administrator in
  wait.connection:
    timeout: 1800
    sleep: 15

examples.name: Wait out a reboot
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Give the machine time to go down, then wait for it
  wait.connection:
    delay: 30
    timeout: 600

examples.name: Wait for a resumed VM that keeps answering
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait until the resumed VM lets its account in three times running
  wait.connection:
    timeout: 900
    backoff: exponential
    sleep: 2
    max_sleep: 60
    steady: 3
    steady_interval: 10

reversibility.notes: This method watches a path and changes nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo. That is the same fact that makes it report changed: false. It still records a diff whose two halves are identical, so a journal can tell an observation from a task that was never recorded.

wait.path.noCheckReason: what a wait waits for is usually an earlier task's change, which a check never makes, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits for a file path on the target to exist (or stop existing).
doc.description: Polls a path on the device until it exists, or until it is gone when state is absent, and fails when the timeout runs out first. It changes nothing: state: absent waits for something else to remove the path, it does not remove it. Anything at the path counts as existing, including a directory and a symbolic link whose target is missing, since the link itself is a thing that is there; that differs from wait_for, which follows a link and calls a broken one absent. The delay is spent out of the timeout rather than added to it, matching wait_for, so delay must be shorter than timeout. A run that gives up returns an error, because a task that waited for something that never happened has failed.

params.name: path
params.description: The path on the device to watch.

params.name: state
params.description: Whether to wait for the path to exist (present) or to stop existing (absent). started and stopped are accepted as wait_for's own spellings of the same two, so a converted playbook needs no edit. drained is refused, since it asks about a socket's send queue and means nothing for a file.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait in total before giving up, counted from the start of the task, so the delay comes out of it. Must be more than 0.

params.name: delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait before looking the first time. Must be shorter than the timeout, which it is spent out of.

params.name: sleep
params.description: How many seconds to wait between looks. Must be more than 0: a sleep of zero would probe the device as fast as it can answer.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The path this task watched.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How many whole seconds the task waited, including the delay.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The state of the path when the wait ended, holding its path, kind, mode, owner, group, size and modification time. Both halves are identical, since a wait changes nothing.

examples.name: Wait for a service to write its socket
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the socket to appear
  wait.path:
    path: /run/pleiades/api.sock
    timeout: 60

examples.name: Wait for a lock file to be released
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the package manager to finish
  wait.path:
    path: /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend
    state: absent
    timeout: 300
    sleep: 5

examples.name: Give a slow starter a head start
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the pid file, but not immediately
  wait.path:
    path: /run/app.pid
    delay: 10
    timeout: 120

reversibility.notes: This method reads the routing table and changes nothing, so there is nothing to undo.

wait.routes.noCheckReason: what a wait waits for is usually an earlier task's change, which a check never makes, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits until a router has a route to every prefix given and its routing table has stopped changing.
doc.description: A full OSPF adjacency is not convergence: shortest paths are computed after it, and a router can route the long way, or not at all, for a while after every neighbour is up. This waits for what a change needs: a selected route to each prefix (through the given next hops, when next_hops names any), and the routing table, uptimes aside, unchanged for stable_for seconds. At timeout it fails naming each route still missing, or saying the table never held still. It changes nothing.

params.name: prefixes
params.description: The IPv4 prefixes that must each have a selected route, e.g. 10.3.3.0/24; the IPv4 routing table is the one read.

params.name: next_hops
params.description: Per prefix, the next-hop addresses its route must use, e.g. {"10.3.3.0/24": ["10.0.12.1"]}.

params.name: stable_for
params.description: Seconds the routing table must stay unchanged.

params.name: timeout
params.description: Seconds to wait in all.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: waited
returns.description: Seconds waited.

returns.name: routes
returns.description: Each prefix given, with the next hops its route used.

examples.name: Wait for OSPF to settle
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Every router routes both LANs
  wait.routes:
    prefixes: [10.1.1.0/24, 10.3.3.0/24]

reversibility.notes: This method reads a file and changes nothing on the device, so there is nothing to undo. That is the same fact that makes it report changed: false. It still records a diff whose two halves are identical, so a journal can tell an observation from a task that was never recorded.

wait.search.noCheckReason: what a wait waits for is usually an earlier task's change, which a check never makes, so a check would wait out its timeout and fail where the real run succeeds

doc.summary: Waits for a pattern to appear in a file's contents on the target.
doc.description: Reads a file on the device on an interval until search_regex matches it, or until it stops matching when state is absent, and fails when the timeout runs out first. It changes nothing. The whole file is read on every look, so this suits a service's startup log rather than a file that grows without limit, and a file past 64 MiB fails the task rather than being matched in part. The pattern is matched in multiline mode, as wait_for matches it, so ^ and $ mean the start and end of a line; it is a Go RE2 pattern, so a backreference or a lookahead is refused when the task is read rather than silently never matching. Only a regular file is read: a path that is missing, or that is a directory, counts as not matching, which satisfies state: absent at once and never satisfies state: present.

params.name: path
params.description: The file on the device to read.

params.name: search_regex
params.description: The pattern to look for, matched in multiline mode against the whole file. Use wait.path when only the file's existence matters.

params.name: state
params.description: Whether to wait for the pattern to match (present) or to stop matching (absent). started and stopped are accepted as wait_for's own spellings of the same two. drained is refused, since it asks about a socket's send queue and means nothing for a file.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds to wait in total before giving up, counted from the start of the task, so the delay comes out of it. Must be more than 0.

params.name: delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait before reading the first time. Useful when the file still holds the previous run's matching line. Must be shorter than the timeout, which it is spent out of.

params.name: sleep
params.description: How many seconds to wait between reads. Must be more than 0: a sleep of zero would read the file as fast as the device can send it.

params.name: insecure_skip_host_key_verify
params.description: Skip SSH host key verification for this task. This removes protection against a machine in the middle answering for the device, so set it only for a target you have decided does not need it.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task read.

returns.name: search_regex
returns.description: The pattern this task looked for, exactly as the task wrote it.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How many whole seconds the task waited, including the delay.

returns.name: match_groups
returns.description: The capture groups of the match, in order, without the whole match itself.

returns.name: match_groupdict
returns.description: The named capture groups of the match, keyed by name. Empty when the pattern names none.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What the last read found: the path, whether it was a readable file, the pattern, and whether it matched. Both halves are identical, since a wait changes nothing.

examples.name: Wait for a service to log that it started
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the API to finish starting
  wait.search:
    path: /var/log/pleiades/api.log
    search_regex: "^Listening on "
    timeout: 120

examples.name: Capture the port a service chose
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Read the port out of the log
  wait.search:
    path: /var/log/app.log
    search_regex: "listening on port (?P<port>[0-9]+)"
  register: startup

examples.name: Wait for an error line to be rotated away
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Wait for the log to stop showing the failure
  wait.search:
    path: /var/log/app.log
    search_regex: "FATAL"
    state: absent
    timeout: 60
    sleep: 5

reversibility.notes: Extracting can write any number of files under dest, some replacing files dest already held, and this method does not list them as it goes; an undo would have to delete exactly what was added and restore what was replaced, which it cannot know, as archive.extract cannot.

doc.summary: Extracts a .zip, .tar or .tar.gz already on a Windows host into a folder there, over WinRM.
doc.description: Extracts src into dest, making dest when it does not exist, with the tar.exe Windows ships, which reads zip as well as tar and refuses an entry whose path is absolute or climbs out with "..". This is community.windows.win_unzip, and archive.extract for a Windows host: src must already be on the host. Idempotency is opt-in, as archive.extract's: naming creates skips extraction when that path is already there; naming none means every run extracts again and reports a change. remove deletes src once it is extracted. Every path is absolute and held to a pattern with no quote, wildcard or ".." before WinRM is reached. A check reads creates, src and dest and extracts nothing; a src not there yet, or a dest that is not a folder, makes the call unchecked rather than failed, since an earlier task may change either.

params.name: src
params.description: The archive on the host, an absolute path ending .zip, .tar, .tar.gz or .tgz.

params.name: dest
params.description: The folder to extract into, an absolute path or a drive's root (C:\), made when it does not exist.

params.name: creates
params.description: An absolute path whose existence means the extraction already happened; when it is there, nothing is extracted and the task reports no change.

params.name: remove
params.description: Delete src once it has been extracted.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds the extraction may take.

returns.name: dest
returns.description: The folder extracted into.

returns.name: extracted
returns.description: Whether this task extracted (or, in a check, would).

returns.name: diff
returns.description: Whether dest existed before this task and after it.

examples.name: Unpack Go, once
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Unpack Go into C:\go
  win.archive.extract:
    src: C:\Windows\Temp\go1.26.9.windows-amd64.zip
    dest: C:\
    creates: C:\go\bin\go.exe

reversibility.notes: A run that installed the capability emits a win.capability.remove naming it; one that found it installed, or pending a restart to finish installing, emits nothing. Either direction may need the restart reboot_required reports before it is complete.

doc.summary: Installs a Windows capability (a feature on demand) with DISM, run as SYSTEM so Windows Update will serve it.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows capability, what Get-WindowsCapability lists and Windows calls a feature on demand, is installed: ServerCore.AppCompatibility, OpenSSH.Server and the like. Its state is read first with dism.exe /get-capabilityinfo, so a capability already installed, or installed and waiting only for a restart, reports no change and nothing is sent; a name DISM does not recognize is refused. The payload comes from Windows Update unless source names a folder or mounted image holding the host's features on demand, and then Windows Update is left alone. The Windows Update agent refuses a WinRM logon (Add-WindowsCapability over WinRM answers Access is denied), so the install runs dism.exe as SYSTEM in a one-shot scheduled task in the \Pleiades\ folder, which this method registers, waits for and removes. A large capability from Windows Update can take many minutes: ServerCore.AppCompatibility took 23 on a one-CPU host. Many capabilities need a restart to finish, which reboot_required says, both on the run that installed one and on a later run that finds it waiting; win.reboot restarts the host. A run that installed it emits win.capability.remove naming it. A check reads the capability and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The capability's whole identity as DISM lists it, with its four tildes and version, such as ServerCore.AppCompatibility~~~~0.0.1.0 or Language.Basic~~~en-US~0.0.1.0 (Get-WindowsCapability -Online lists them). A name DISM does not recognize is refused rather than reported as already in the asked state, since that is nearly always a typo.

params.name: source
params.description: A folder or mounted image on the host holding its features on demand, such as D:\LanguagesAndOptionalFeatures, used instead of Windows Update. It may not hold a %, a quote or a line break.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds DISM may run. Task Scheduler stops it at that limit and the task fails saying so.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The capability this task acted on.

returns.name: reboot_required
returns.description: Whether a restart is needed to finish: DISM answered 3010, or the capability was found already waiting for one. win.reboot restarts the host.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What DISM reported about the capability before this task and after it, each holding name, exists and state. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Make Server Core run more applications
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install Server Core's application compatibility feature
  win.capability.install:
    name: ServerCore.AppCompatibility~~~~0.0.1.0
  register: appcompat

- name: Restart to finish it
  win.reboot: {}
  when:
    - result.appcompat.reboot_required

reversibility.notes: A run that removed the capability emits a win.capability.install naming it, which fetches it from Windows Update again: one first installed from a source needs that source in its rollback: list. One found absent, or pending a restart to finish going, emits nothing.

doc.summary: Removes a Windows capability (a feature on demand) with DISM, run as SYSTEM.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows capability, what Get-WindowsCapability lists, is not installed. Its state is read first with dism.exe /get-capabilityinfo, so a capability that is not present, only staged, or removed and waiting only for a restart reports no change and nothing is sent; a name DISM does not recognize is refused. The removal runs dism.exe as SYSTEM in a one-shot scheduled task in the \Pleiades\ folder, as win.capability.install does, which this method registers, waits for and removes. Many capabilities need a restart to finish going, which reboot_required says; win.reboot restarts the host. A run that removed one emits win.capability.install naming it, which fetches it from Windows Update again: a capability first installed from a source needs that source named in its rollback: list. A check reads the capability and sends nothing.

params.name: name
params.description: The capability's whole identity as DISM lists it, with its four tildes and version, such as ServerCore.AppCompatibility~~~~0.0.1.0 or Language.Basic~~~en-US~0.0.1.0 (Get-WindowsCapability -Online lists them). A name DISM does not recognize is refused rather than reported as already in the asked state, since that is nearly always a typo.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds DISM may run. Task Scheduler stops it at that limit and the task fails saying so.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The capability this task acted on.

returns.name: reboot_required
returns.description: Whether a restart is needed to finish: DISM answered 3010, or the capability was found already waiting for one. win.reboot restarts the host.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What DISM reported about the capability before this task and after it, each holding name, exists and state. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing.

examples.name: Remove Steps Recorder
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remove Steps Recorder
  win.capability.remove:
    name: App.StepsRecorder~~~~0.0.1.0

reversibility.notes: Reading is not changing: this reports the host's processors and alters nothing, so there is nothing an undo could restore.

doc.summary: Reports a Windows host's logical processors: which are performance cores, which efficiency cores, and how they group.
doc.description: Reads the host's CPU sets as its scheduler sees them, through the Windows API GetSystemCpuSetInformation, and changes nothing. Each logical processor is reported with its processor group, core, NUMA node, last-level cache and efficiency class. On a hybrid processor, such as Intel's with P-cores and E-cores, a higher efficiency class is a faster, less power-efficient core: the logical processors with the highest class are reported as performance processors and the rest as efficiency processors, with the affinity mask that selects the performance ones. On a processor whose cores are all alike, every logical processor is a performance one. No WMI class reports efficiency classes, so the host compiles a small call to the API with PowerShell's Add-Type; a host whose PowerShell runs in Constrained Language Mode refuses that, and the task fails saying so. A check is the same read.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds the read may take.

returns.name: processors
returns.description: Each logical processor as index, group, core, numa_node, last_level_cache, efficiency_class and parked, in the order Windows lists them.

returns.name: processor_count
returns.description: How many logical processors the host has.

returns.name: core_count
returns.description: How many cores they are on.

returns.name: hybrid
returns.description: Whether the cores are of more than one efficiency class.

returns.name: performance_processors
returns.description: The indexes of the logical processors of the highest efficiency class: every one, when the host is not hybrid.

returns.name: efficiency_processors
returns.description: The indexes of the rest, empty when the host is not hybrid.

returns.name: performance_affinity_mask
returns.returned: when the host has one processor group
returns.description: The affinity mask selecting the performance processors, as hexadecimal, such as 0xC03C3: what Windows' start /affinity and a process's ProcessorAffinity take.

examples.name: Find a host's performance cores

reversibility.notes: A run that enabled a disabled feature emits a win.feature.remove naming it. A run that found it already enabled emits nothing. What the inverse cannot undo is anything the feature's own presence changed on the system while it was enabled, and either direction may need the restart reboot_required reports before it is complete.

doc.summary: Enables a Windows optional feature or role via DISM, including its required parent features.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows optional feature or role is enabled. This is ansible.windows.win_optional_feature with state=present (or win_feature's default), built on dism.exe /online /enable-feature rather than the ServerManager PowerShell module, since dism.exe works on every Windows SKU and this platform's own DISMLogPath capability already commits to it. /all is passed, so enabling a feature also enables the parent features it requires, matching what the Windows GUI's own "Add roles and features" does by default. State is read before anything is sent, so a feature that is already enabled reports no change and no command reaches the device. A feature name DISM does not recognize is refused rather than reported as already enabled, since that is nearly always a typo. Many features need a restart before they finish taking effect; check reboot_required rather than assuming changed alone means the feature is fully usable. A check reads the feature and sends nothing; when the feature would change, its diff leaves out the state the feature would end in and reboot_required, since DISM decides between the finished and pending states only when it runs.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows optional feature or role's DISM feature name, such as IIS-WebServerRole, not its display name. The feature must be one DISM recognizes: a name it does not is refused rather than reported as already the target state, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The feature this task acted on.

returns.name: reboot_required
returns.description: Whether DISM reported that a restart is needed for this change to take full effect (its own ERROR_SUCCESS_REBOOT_REQUIRED). False on a run that changed nothing.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What DISM reported about the feature before this task and after it, each holding exists and state. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Enable IIS
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure the web server role is enabled
  win.feature.install:
    name: IIS-WebServerRole
  register: iis

- name: Restart if DISM asked for one
  win.reboot: {}
  when:
    - result.iis.reboot_required

reversibility.notes: A run that disabled an enabled feature emits a win.feature.install naming it. A run that found it already disabled emits nothing. Re-enabling it does not pass /all a second time from this inverse, so a parent feature the original install pulled in stays exactly as removing this one left it.

doc.summary: Disables a Windows optional feature or role via DISM.
doc.description: Makes sure a Windows optional feature or role is disabled. This is ansible.windows.win_optional_feature with state=absent, built on dism.exe /online /disable-feature. Unlike install, this does not pass /all: removing a feature should not silently remove the parent features it depended on. State is read before anything is sent, so a feature that is already disabled reports no change. A feature name DISM does not recognize is refused rather than reported as already disabled, since that is nearly always a typo. Many features need a restart before removal fully takes effect; check reboot_required rather than assuming changed alone means the feature is gone. A check reads the feature and sends nothing; when the feature would change, its diff leaves out the state the feature would end in and reboot_required, since DISM decides between the finished and pending states only when it runs.

params.name: name
params.description: The Windows optional feature or role's DISM feature name, such as IIS-WebServerRole, not its display name. The feature must be one DISM recognizes: a name it does not is refused rather than reported as already the target state, since that is nearly always a typo.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The feature this task acted on.

returns.name: reboot_required
returns.description: Whether DISM reported that a restart is needed for this change to take full effect (its own ERROR_SUCCESS_REBOOT_REQUIRED). False on a run that changed nothing.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: What DISM reported about the feature before this task and after it, each holding exists and state. Recorded even on a run that changed nothing, because "it was already like this" is what tells a later rollback to do nothing.

examples.name: Disable IIS
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Make sure the web server role is disabled
  win.feature.remove:
    name: IIS-WebServerRole

reversibility.notes: A copy writes a file, and a file it replaces is not kept; nothing here removes a file yet, so neither a new file nor a replaced one can be undone.

doc.summary: Copies a file from the project to a Windows host over WinRM and keeps it only if its SHA-256 matches.
doc.description: Makes sure path on the host holds the project file src, byte for byte. This is ansible.windows.win_copy for one file. The file is read from the project (at most 128 MiB; never from .pleiades, never through a link) and its SHA-256 worked out here. A file already at path with that digest reports no change and nothing is sent. Otherwise the file travels on the WinRM command's standard input as base64, never on a command line, into a file beside path, and is moved into place only once its digest matches; a mismatch leaves path as it was and fails. A file at path with another digest is replaced. Only the command line reads a project's files, so a Walk-tier Runner refuses src. A check reads path's digest and sends nothing.

params.name: src
params.description: The file to copy, a slash-separated path relative to the project directory, as dist/tree.tar.gz.

params.name: path
params.description: The absolute path on the host to write, as C:\pleiades\tree.tar.gz. Its folder must exist. It may not hold a quote, a wildcard or a control character.

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds the copy may take.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task made sure of.

returns.name: sha256
returns.description: Its SHA-256, lower case.

returns.name: size_bytes
returns.description: Its size.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The SHA-256 at path before this task and after it, empty where there was no file.

examples.name: Send a build to a Windows host
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Copy the tools archive to the host
  win.file.copy:
    src: dist/tools.zip
    path: C:\ops\tools.zip

reversibility.notes: A download writes a file, and a file it replaces is not kept; nothing here removes a file yet, so neither a new file nor a replaced one can be undone.

doc.summary: Downloads a file onto a Windows host over HTTPS and keeps it only if its SHA-256 matches.
doc.description: Makes sure path on the host holds the file url serves, verified by sha256. This is ansible.windows.win_get_url with a checksum it will not run without. A file already at path with that digest reports no change and nothing is downloaded. Otherwise the host fetches url with the curl.exe Windows ships, over HTTPS only, redirects included, into a file beside path, and moves it into place only once its digest matches; a mismatch leaves path as it was and fails, naming the digest it got. A file at path with another digest is replaced. The download is the host's own, so url must be reachable from it; nothing passes through the machine running Pleiades. A check reads path's digest and downloads nothing.

params.name: url
params.description: The https:// URL to fetch. It may not hold a quote, a space or a control character.

params.name: path
params.description: The absolute path on the host to write, as G:\iso\ubuntu.ova. Its folder must exist. It may not hold a quote, a wildcard or a control character.

params.name: sha256
params.description: The file's SHA-256, 64 hex digits, as the publisher lists it (Ubuntu's SHA256SUMS, for one).

params.name: timeout
params.description: How many seconds the download may take.

returns.name: path
returns.description: The file this task made sure of.

returns.name: sha256
returns.description: Its SHA-256, lower case.

returns.name: size_bytes
returns.description: Its size.

returns.name: diff
returns.description: The SHA-256 at path before this task and after it, empty where there was no file.

examples.name: Fetch an Ubuntu cloud image
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Fetch the Ubuntu 24.04 cloud image
  win.file.download:
    url: https://cloud-images.ubuntu.com/releases/noble/release-20260926/ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.ova
    path: G:\PleiadesLab\media\ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.ova
    sha256: 513a22ebe3982b9387b038f8a2a6dad1af980d4623dca03511312e55ba620b1a

reversibility.notes: A run that changed the profile undoes to the earlier value of each setting it changed. A setting Windows held as NotConfigured is put back as the value it had in effect, which behaves the same.

doc.summary: Sets, or reports, one Windows Defender Firewall profile over WinRM: whether it is on, its default actions and its logging.
doc.description: Names one profile, domain, private or public, and compares the settings the task gives with the machine's own (PersistentStore), changing only those that differ; a task giving none only reports the profile. A setting Windows holds as NotConfigured compares as what it does: on, block inbound, allow outbound, log nothing. The setting in force is read too (ActiveStore): one Group Policy sets to another value fails the task, naming it, since the machine's own setting has no effect there, after making the change if one was needed. The script is a constant and every value reaches it as JSON on standard input, held to its form first. The undo puts back the earlier value of each setting changed, as the value that was in force for a NotConfigured one. A check reads and reports what would change.

params.name: name
params.description: The profile. One per task, so its undo is exact.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether the firewall is on for this profile.

params.name: default_inbound_action
params.description: What it does with inbound traffic no rule matches. Windows' default is block.

params.name: default_outbound_action
params.description: What it does with outbound traffic no rule matches. Windows' default is allow.

params.name: log_allowed
params.description: Whether allowed connections are logged.

params.name: log_blocked
params.description: Whether dropped packets are logged.

params.name: log_file
params.description: The log file's path on the machine, as Windows takes it (%systemroot% may appear).

params.name: log_max_size_kb
params.description: The log's largest size in kilobytes, 1 to 32767.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The profile.

returns.name: settings
returns.description: Its settings before, as the machine keeps them, in this method's parameters' form.

returns.name: in_force
returns.description: Its settings in force before, Group Policy's included.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: How the machine's own settings differed from what was asked, empty when they matched.

returns.name: overridden
returns.description: The settings asked for that Group Policy held at another value.

examples.name: Log what the domain profile drops
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Log dropped packets on the domain network
  win.firewall.profile:
    name: domain
    log_blocked: true
    log_max_size_kb: 16384

examples.name: Make sure the public profile is on and closed
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: The public profile is on and lets nothing in
  win.firewall.profile:
    name: public
    enabled: true
    default_inbound_action: block

reversibility.notes: A rule this run made is removed by its undo; a rule it changed gets back the earlier value of each setting it changed; a rule it removed is made again with every setting it had, though not in the group it belonged to, which a rule cannot be put back into. Its display name and description are text the device holds, withheld from the journal, so an undo restoring either replays only from the task's own rollback: list.

doc.summary: Makes, changes or removes a Windows Defender Firewall rule over WinRM, or reports one as it is.
doc.description: A rule is named by its Name, its identity (OpenSSH-Server-In-TCP, not its display name), and read and written in the machine's own rule store (PersistentStore). With state present, a rule that does not exist is made, with Windows' defaults for what the task leaves out (inbound, allow, any protocol, every profile, enabled, its name as its display name); a rule that exists is compared on the settings the task gives and only those, and a setting that differs is changed, so a built-in rule's profiles can be widened without restating its ports or program. absent removes it; query only reports it. A rule that exists only through Group Policy is refused, since a change here would not be kept. Profiles, ports and addresses compare as sets, and an IPv4 network compares the same written as 10.0.0.0/8 or with the dotted mask Windows answers with. Ports need protocol tcp or udp, the task's or the rule's. The script is a constant and every value reaches it as JSON on standard input, held to its form first. A rule this run made undoes to its removal; a change, to the earlier value of each setting it changed; a removal, to making the rule again as it was, outside the group it belonged to. Lists may also be given as one comma-separated string, which is how an undo writes them; an undo restoring a display name or description is withheld from the journal. A check reads and reports what would change.

params.name: name
params.description: The rule's Name, its identity: letters, digits, space and ._{}()@,+-, at most 255.

params.name: state
params.description: present makes or changes it; absent removes it; query only reports it.

params.name: display_name
params.description: The name the firewall shows. A new rule takes its Name when this is left out.

params.name: description
params.description: Its description.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether it is on. A new rule is.

params.name: direction
params.description: Which traffic it matches. A new rule's is inbound.

params.name: action
params.description: What it does with that traffic. A new rule allows it.

params.name: profiles
params.description: The network profiles it applies in: domain, private, public, or any (all three). A new rule's is any.

params.name: protocol
params.description: tcp, udp, icmpv4, icmpv6, any, or an IP protocol number 0-255. A new rule's is any.

params.name: local_port
params.description: The ports on this machine it matches: ports, ranges (8000-8100), any, or a keyword Windows knows (RPC, RPCEPMap, IPHTTPS, Teredo). Needs tcp or udp.

params.name: remote_port
params.description: The other side's ports it matches: ports, ranges or any. Needs tcp or udp.

params.name: local_address
params.description: This machine's addresses it matches: addresses, networks (10.0.0.0/8), ranges (10.0.0.1-10.0.0.9), any, or a keyword (LocalSubnet, Internet, Intranet, DNS, DHCP, WINS, DefaultGateway).

params.name: remote_address
params.description: The other side's addresses it matches, in the same forms.

params.name: program
params.description: The program whose traffic it matches, a path, or any.

params.name: service
params.description: The service whose traffic it matches, by its short name, or any.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The rule's Name.

returns.name: existed
returns.description: Whether the rule existed before.

returns.name: group
returns.description: The group it belonged to before, as Windows names it, empty for none.

returns.name: rule
returns.description: Its settings before, as this method's parameters name them, empty when it did not exist.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: How it differed from what was asked, empty when it matched.

examples.name: Let SSH in on a domain controller
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: OpenSSH's rule covers the domain network too
  win.firewall.rule:
    name: OpenSSH-Server-In-TCP
    profiles: [domain, private]

examples.name: An app's port from one network
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: The app's port, from the office only
  win.firewall.rule:
    name: Pleiades-App-In
    display_name: App (TCP 8443)
    protocol: tcp
    local_port: [8443]
    remote_address: [10.20.0.0/16]
    profiles: [domain]

examples.name: What a rule allows
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Remote Desktop's rule
  win.firewall.rule:
    name: RemoteDesktop-UserMode-In-TCP
    state: query
  register: rdp

reversibility.notes: A restart cannot be taken back: once the host has restarted there is nothing to put back, so no undo is recorded.

doc.summary: Restarts a Windows host over WinRM and waits until it is back, as ansible.windows.win_reboot does.
doc.description: Reads the host's last boot time, has shutdown.exe restart it pre_reboot_delay seconds later (closing applications that do not exit, and recorded as a planned restart for maintenance), then waits until the host answers over WinRM again with a later boot time, which is what shows it restarted rather than only answered, and then post_reboot_delay seconds more. reboot_timeout bounds the wait from the moment the restart is asked for; a try the host refuses, or does not answer within connect_timeout, is made again five seconds later. A restart already scheduled on the host is cancelled and replaced by this one. A run always reports a change, and a restart cannot be undone. A check reads the boot time and sends nothing.

params.name: reboot_timeout
params.description: How many seconds the host may take to come back, from the moment the restart is asked for.

params.name: pre_reboot_delay
params.description: How many seconds shutdown.exe waits before restarting, at least 0 and at most 600.

params.name: post_reboot_delay
params.description: How many seconds to wait once the host is back, for services that start after WinRM does.

params.name: msg
params.description: The message shutdown.exe shows signed-in users and records, at most 512 characters on one line.

params.name: connect_timeout
params.description: How many seconds one try to reach the host may take.

returns.name: rebooted
returns.description: Whether the host restarted: true on a run, false in a check.

returns.name: elapsed
returns.description: How many seconds the restart took, from asking for it to the host being back.

returns.name: previous_boot_time
returns.description: When the host last booted before this task, in UTC (RFC 3339).

returns.name: boot_time
returns.description: When the host booted this time, in UTC (RFC 3339).

examples.name: Restart after a change that needs it
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Install Server Core's application compatibility feature
  win.capability.install:
    name: ServerCore.AppCompatibility~~~~0.0.1.0
  register: appcompat

- name: Restart to finish it
  win.reboot:
    reboot_timeout: 900
  when:
    - result.appcompat.reboot_required

reversibility.notes: A task this run registered is removed by its undo. A task it changed or removed is registered again from the XML definition it had, read before the change; that XML is withheld from the journal, so a rollback replays it only from the task's own rollback: list. The task's run history is not restored.

doc.summary: Registers, updates or removes a Windows scheduled task over WinRM, or reports one as it is.
doc.description: Reads the task first (Get-ScheduledTask, its XML definition and its last and next run), then: with state present, registers it with one action, one trigger and its principal when it is missing or differs in any of them, its description or whether it is enabled, and is no change when it matches; with absent, removes it; with query, only reports it. The script is a constant and every value reaches it as JSON on standard input, so a value can never be PowerShell syntax; every name is held to a strict pattern first. run_as SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE or NETWORK SERVICE runs as that service account; another account runs with S4U logon, so no password is stored with the task, and the task cannot reach the network as that user. A task this run registered undoes to its removal; one it changed or removed undoes to registering its earlier XML definition, withheld from the journal (xml, which also registers a task from a definition you give). A check reads and reports what would change.

params.name: name
params.description: The task's path: \Folder\Name, or Name in the root folder.

params.name: state
params.description: present registers or updates it; absent removes it; query only reports it.

params.name: execute
params.description: The program the task runs. Required with state present, unless xml is given.

params.name: arguments
params.description: Its arguments, as one string.

params.name: working_directory
params.description: The directory it starts in.

params.name: trigger
params.description: When it runs: at_startup, at_logon, daily (at, HH:MM, the device's local time) or once (at, an RFC 3339 time). Required with state present.

params.name: at
params.description: The time of a daily or once trigger.

params.name: run_as
params.description: The account it runs as: SYSTEM, LOCAL SERVICE, NETWORK SERVICE, or an account (DOMAIN\name or name) run with S4U logon and no stored password.

params.name: run_level
params.description: Whether it runs with the account's highest privileges.

params.name: enabled
params.description: Whether the task is enabled.

params.name: description
params.description: The task's description.

params.name: xml
params.description: A whole task definition, as Export-ScheduledTask writes it, registered as given with state present; what this method's own undo uses.

returns.name: name
returns.description: The task's full path.

returns.name: existed
returns.description: Whether the task existed before.

returns.name: state
returns.description: Its state before (Ready, Running, Disabled), empty when it did not exist.

returns.name: last_run_time
returns.description: When it last ran.

returns.name: last_task_result
returns.description: Its last result code.

returns.name: next_run_time
returns.description: When it runs next.

returns.name: differences
returns.description: How it differed from what was asked, empty when it matched.

examples.name: A nightly cleanup
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Cleanup
  win.schtask:
    name: \Pleiades\Cleanup
    execute: C:\Windows\System32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\powershell.exe
    arguments: -NoProfile -File C:\ops\cleanup.ps1
    trigger: daily
    at: "02:30"

examples.name: Is the backup task healthy
examples.runbookYaml:
- name: Backup task
  win.schtask:
    name: \Pleiades\Backup
    state: query
  register: backup
